speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

maintopic: CELEBRATION OF PEACE WHEN PROCLAMATION IS ISSUED.
speechtext: May I ask the Prime Minister whether it is the intention of the Government to have any official celebration of the signing of peace?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: CELEBRATION OF PEACE WHEN PROCLAMATION IS ISSUED.
speechtext: Only one treaty of peace has been signed so far. The signing of the treaty does not bring about peace; that can only be accomplished by royal proclamation issued after the treaty has been ratified. Under the terms of the Treaty of Peace, the proclamation cannot be issued until three of the Allied powers have concurred in its ratification. It is thought by the Government that the most appropriate time for the celebration of peace will be when peace has been proclaimed by His Majesty.

maintopic: CELEBRATION OF PEACE WHEN PROCLAMATION IS ISSUED.
speechtext: Is it the intention, then, when peace is proclaimed to have a Dominion celebration?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: CELEBRATION OF PEACE WHEN PROCLAMATION IS ISSUED.
speechtext: There will be eventually a proclamation of peace.

maintopic: CELEBRATION OF PEACE WHEN PROCLAMATION IS ISSUED.
speechtext: My hon. friend did not tell me whether or not there would be a Dominion celebration at that time.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: CELEBRATION OF PEACE WHEN PROCLAMATION IS ISSUED.
speechtext: Oh, yes; so far as I am aware, it is understood that there will be a celebration. I cannot speak for the United Kingdom or for the other Dominions, but I think we should celebrate the proclamation of peace when it is issued.

'On motion of Sir Thomas White (Minister of Finance), the House went into Committee to consider the following proposed resolution, Mr. Boivin in the Chair:
Resolved, That It is expedient to provide,-
1.	That the Governor in Council may, in addition to the sums now remaining unborrowed and negotiable of the loans authorized by Parliament by any Act heretofore passed, raise "by way of loan, by the issue and sale or pledge of securities of Canada, in such form, for such separate sums, at such rate of interest and upon such other terms and conditions as the Governor in Council may approve, such sum or sums of money as may be required, but not to exceed in the whole the sum of one hundred million dollars, for-
(a)	paying maturing loans and obligations of Canada;
(b)	carrying on of public works authorized by Parliament; and,
<c) meeting expenditures for general purposes authorized by Parliament.
2.	That when securities issued under this proposed legislation have been pledged as security for a loan, and the loan has been paid off and the pledge redeemed, the securities shall not be deemed to have been extinguished, but shall be deemed to be still alive, and may be reissued and sold or pledged as if the former pledging had not taken place.
3.	That the principal raised by way of loan under this proposed legislation and the interest thereon shall be charged upon and payable out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund.-The Minister of Finance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The purport of this resolution is to enable the Government to borrow moneys for the purposes which are mentioned and which are as follows:
(a)	paying: maturing' loans and obligations of Canada;
(b)	oarrying on of public works authorized .by Parliament; and,
<c) meeting expenditures for general purposes authorized by Parliament.
My view is that the money will be used tor the two first mentioned purposes only. 3 explained to the House the other day, in answer to a question, that the Dominion ''Government has a maturity of about $75,000,000 coming due in New York on August 1.
Is this the only loan for which the minister is to take authority at this session?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The only general purpose loan. I took authority for a loan for demobilization and war purposes. My [DOT]hon, friend will recollect that $350,000,000 *was the amount mentioned in the Bill, and ~we took borrowing powers in respect to that. That is not connected with this transaction. This is a general purpose loan, and the money will be raised and used, first,

for the purpose of meeting the maturity which I have mentioned, and second, for the purpose of meeting our capital expenditure. Before coming to the House I received a note from my deputy pointing out that the Main Estimates contain $86,000,000 of capital expenditure, and that the Supplementary Estimates will contain $12,500,000 more. It is not at all likely that all that money will be expended in the present fiscal year; but in my Budget speech I estimated that this year there would be $50,000,000 of capital expenditure which we would be justified in borrowing. We have in this resolution asked for just as small an amount as we can get on with. There is a residue of borrowing power provided for in the Appropriation Act of last year, and we shall, in this year's Appropriation. Act, show also the unexhausted borrowing power of the Dominion.
For the information of the House I might say that we are paying off in London tomorrow a loan of about $20,000,000. We are not renewing that loan, but paying it off in cash, by borrowing the money from the British Treasury and setting it off against the moneys they owe us here.

With reference
to the loan negotiated in New York about two years ago, the notes of which are due on August 1st of this year, I understand that this loan was issued at 98 and that the interest rate was 5 per cent. It has been stated in the New York papers that this loan has subsequently been put on a 6 per cent basis. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is an error. There was no change made, nor could there have been any change made. I remember however reading an article in the press which was most curiously confused respecting this loan. We put out two-year notes in 1917 bearing interest at 5 per cent, but the loan was issued at 98.

speechtext: I explained that a while ago, on the resolution, but evidently my hon. friend did not hear me. We have a maturity of about $75,000,000 in New York on August 1.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. We desire to pay that off, and to do that we shall have to make a new loan there.
Do you expect to make it at a better rate?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I can assure my hon. friend we shall do the best we can in that respect.
My hon. friend gave us the reassuring statement the other day that the Bank of Montreal would act as agent for the Government as usual.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The negotiations are being carried on by the Bank of Montreal, through Sir Frederick Williams-Tay-lor, and myself on the one side, and the parties with whom we are negotiating on the other. The Bank of Montreal has placed all our loans. I keep in constant touch with the situation as minister, but the immediate negotiations are carried out
by the Bank of Montreal through its general manager. I am anxious that the House should realize that in our New York financing during the war we were confronted with war conditions. I took the trouble some time ago of getting a statement from a very dependable firm in New York, the William A. Bead & Company, one of the largest firms of bond dealers in the United States, as to the rates of interest which prevailed there on high class securities during the war, and I should like to put it on Hansard because 1 think it would be useful to hon. members. The letter is dated July 15, 1918, and says:
(In the midst of the war) the Dominion of Canada 5 per cent loan of April, 1921, was quoted nominally around a 6| per cent basis; that was the offering price. The British Government 5i per cent notes due 1919-1921 were quoted on a basis around 7J per cent, and the French Government 5J per cents of April, 1919, on an 8 per cent basis; both these issues being secured by first-class collateral well regarded in these markets.
Look what that meant. Here was the British Government and the French Government on a 7i arid 8 per cent basis. We were able to float our loans in New York at a lower yield of interest than the British Government, or as a matter of fact, than the British and French Governments jointly on the Securities which they issued.
Did we put up any collateral?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, we have put up no collateral. Getting away from Government issues, let us see what the American Telephone and Telegraph Company did:
This company with its splendid credit has offered if40,000,000 seven-year 7 per cent notes to its stockholders with a syndicate underwriting of 3 per cent of the whole issue. Generally speaking, issues coming out in this market by corporations of the highest investment standing, have been offered around a 7J per cent to an 8 per cent basis.
Many business men here will appreciate the fact that when you are raising loans in the market you must face the conditions that prevail. When this loan was put out in 1917 we were obliged to have the money owing to the demands of the war and for our own purposes, and we faced conditions that were exceedingly difficult. The United States had just entered the war in April and had made their first Liberty Loan, and it was in August of that year that we floated this loari. We floated it for two years and paid a shade over six per cent, but in comparison. with the issues of other governments I have mentioned it was, on: the

whole, very favourable. I keep on record communications showing what the view of the Bank of Montreal was with regard to our financing at that time, so that the documents are available at any time for the information of the House. Sir Frederick Williams Taylor negotiated this loan, keeping, as I have said, in constant touch with me, and I believe he did the best that could possibly be done under the circumstances. He is a very conscientious man, anxious to the utmost to serve the interests of the Dominion, and he has had a long and wide experience. He said in his letter:
I am satisfied you have done the hest that could be done, and if the one-duarter per cent commission mentioned is conceded, it is in my opinion, a good piece of business, all things considered.
I can assure the committee that we feel very greatly the responsibility of placing these large loans, and we do the best we can in the financial conditions in which we find ourselves.

Of course, a loan is always to be deprecated, and I hope some day my hon. friend will keep himself out of the market. Much as I have confidence in his judgment and great ability, I must qualify that confidence by the statement that I am pleased to see my hon. friend negotiating this loan with the Bafik of Montreal as agent. The prestige of the Bank of Montreal is certainly on a par with that of the Bank of England and the Banque de France in the financial world, and it is undoubtedly to the credit of Canada that the Bank of Montreal should take up our business. What my hon. friend says about Sir Frederick Williams Taylor is perfectly true; he is the highest financial authority in the land. My hon. friend spoke of collateral securities a moment ago. It may interest him, if he did not observe the fact at the time, to know that in connection with the Anglo-French loan, which, as my hon, friend knows, was advertised in all Wall Street publications, one of the collaterals, to my great pride, was the province of Quebec bonds. The only province in the Dominion called upon to furnish collateral security was Quebec. Quebec bonds were considered exceedingly attractive, and at the time they were quoted at a higher rate than bonds of the Dominion. In connection with this loan, which the present one purposes to wipe out, will the holders of those notes be able to exchange?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
They will be paid off in cash. It is the only way the trans-

action can be carried out. If any of them desire to subscribe to the new loan, they can do so.
Will the minister explain clause 3?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The explanation I gave the other night was concurred in by the former Minister of Finance, the member for Queens and Shelburne (Mr. Fielding). The occasion of pledging these bonds is not at all likely to arise. This is what you might call a standard clause inserted in the Dominion's borrowing bill. The clause arose out of a decision in the House of Lords a few years ago, which held that where the debentures of a tramways company, secured upon the assets of that company, had been pledged to a bank, and were afterwards got in by the paying off of the amount borrowed upon them, they could not be reissued. It had been the practice, as it is to-.day, for a company once its issue is authorized by its shareholders, to borrow temporarily against the bonds. Let us assume that $100,000 of bonds were pledged for a loan of $50,000. The company, when the period arrived for the bonds to be sold, would pay off the $50,000 and get back the $100,000 of bonds and issue them to the public. That was done, I suppose, by all companies in the Empire at that time, but when that decision came out it was found that it was unlawful to sell the bonds once they had been pledged. This provides, therefore, that notwithstanding their pledge for a loan, upon the pledge being paid off, the bonds may be issued just as if they had not been pledged. In other words, this clause keeps the bonds alive.
Does this mean that bonds, if they are pledged to secure a loan, can be re-issued prior to maturity or after maturity?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It only refers to redemption. When securities issued have been pledged as security for a loan and the loan has been paid off and the pledge redeemed, the securities shall not be deemed to have been extinguished.

The great object which my hon. friend should have in view, in order to get as favourable a rate as possible, should be the re-establishment of the sound financial credit of the Dominion. I would not like to enter into any controversial discussion at the present time on the railway policy of the Government, although much could be said on the question, which would prove without doubt that the Govern-

ment's policy will ultimately have very serious effect on our credit. But if my hon. friend would only state that the Government does not intend to carry out the negotiations which were so much talked of at the beginning of the session about the Grand Trunk, he Svould certainly enhance the credit of Canada. I am told that in England the bondholders of the Grand Trunk have in the press and even in Parliament questioned very much the proposed legislation of the Government. We have not heard anything on the subject for some weeks, and I consider that if that project were abandoned, an announcement to that effect would certainly help the minister in negotiating any future loan.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I may say that the negotiations with the Grand Trunk are still proceeding.
Quietly?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, we have had several interviews with Mr. Kelley, representing the Grand Trunk Railway Board. We had a proposal from the Grand Trunk Railway Company, and have been making certain investigations as to allegations that in some respects the findings of Messrs. Drayton and Acworth were not entirely accurate, particularly with regard to the amount set aside for depreciation by the Grand Trunk from year to year, and the amount accumulated in reserves of subsidiary companies. Further than that, I am not in a position to make any statement to-day.

I am rather pleased
to hear the statement of my hon. friend and the public will read between the lines when his speech is presented to it. It seems to me that the Government has practically decided to deal fairly with the Grand Trunk Railway Company on this question and not to take the company by the throat and thereby involve Canada in a serious financial tangle.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Government's course throughout, I think has been very fair towards the Grand Trunk Railway Company having regard to its financial position and its heavy liabilities respecting the Grand Trunk Pacific railway. I stated in the House on more than one occasion that the Government desired to be fair but the Government is the trustee for the 'Canadian public and it is its duty to see that if the Grand Trunk railway is taken over it shall be on terms that will npt only be fair to the Grand Trunk Railway 'Company but fair also to the Canadian people whom we represent.

The minister has told
us that the expenditure, according to the Estimates this year, on capital account alone will be about $92,000,000. The Main Estimates make provision for an expenditure on capital account of about $80,000,000 and the Supplementary Estimates provide for further expenditures to the extent of about $12,000,000, making, on capital account, only, an expenditure of some $92,000,000. I would like to remind the minister that in 1910-11 the total expenditure of the Dominion of Canada for all public purposes was only $87,000,000 as shown by the public accounts. On that occasion the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden), then leader of the Opposition, stated not only in Parliament but out of it that the expenditure was prima facie evidence of reckless extravagance and incompetent administration. That was part of the manifesto of the then leader of the Opposition in 1911. I wish to remind the Minister of Finance that it is a startling state of affairs when we find that the expenditure on capital account this year, in the midst of hard times and difficulty in getting money, is $92,000,000. I do think that the Finance Minister could have held the Estimates down more than he has done this year. When expenditures are to be made, and money is to be raised, I can readily understand that the Minister of Finance has no alternative but to find the money as best he can but it is a good plan for the Minister of Finance to try and keep out of these difficulties and not allow the Government to commit itself to these extraordinary expenditures. I think, Sir, that during the war years-and this is called a war year-we have kept on too much 12 noon sail in the way of expenditure and that really very little notice has been given of the great necessity for cutting down expenditures. We could have done that. If the Finance Minister will look back to what is getting to be perhaps ancient history now, although it was only in 1909, he will find that we had a sudden drop of something like $12,000,000 or $15,000,000 in the revenue of this country. He will also recall that the Finance Minister of that day immediately dropped the expenditure so that we came out a little better than even that year. I wish to protest against keeping on full sail in regard to expenditure when we are not getting the money to spend, and when now, and for

the future, we should, as much as possible, live within our means and measure our expenditure by the amount of our income and avoid borrowing as far as possible.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I take no exception whatever to what my hon. friend (Mr. McKenzie) has said. I confess there is a great deal of wisdom in it. The expenditures on capital account are undoubtedly large but it has to be borne in mind that included in the amount is our shipbuilding programme which is 'keeping employed thousands of men in various parts of the country. I must pay a tribute to my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Carvell). I think that, remembering the pressure that has been put upon him from all parts of tha-country, he has had regard .to what my hon. friend has put forward. This is a war year and in all the nations that have been engaged in the war very large expenditures are being made. It is not' too much to say that in certain of the nations money is being poured out in order to prevent the disturbances which would occur if thousands of men were thrown out of work. In Great Britain they are paying out money at the rate of millions of pounds a day in order to prevent unemployment, notwithstanding which they have a very troubled industrial situation. In the transition period between war and the firm establishment of peace, all nations find themselves in the position that Governments are 'looked to to find work as far as they can and to prevent unemployment and hardship with consequent unrest and disturbance. We have a pretty large programme in this country. I have thought a great deal about it and I do not dissent very strongly from what the hon. gentleman has said. We must look forward to the period, as I stated in the Budget, in which the artificial character of our business in Canada must be changed and industry got back to a normal peace basis.
I would submit for the consideration of the Committee that if we had suddenly shut off expenditures after November last upon shipbuilding and other enterprises in which we were engaged, and, had refrained from going ahead with public works which give employment in cities, we would have had a very serious situation on hand, and, more than that and worse than that, there would have been a great deal of human suffering in this country. That is all I can usefully say.

The Treaty of Peace has been signed, we all heard the

guns this morning and the news was very welcome. Is the minister in a position to give the Committee any information as regards Canada's share of the German indemnity, how much it is going to be and when we may expect it to be paid?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am unable to answer the question of my hon. friend. Our claims have been filed by our representatives in the negotiations leading up to the signing of the treaty.
What is the amount of the claim?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There was first the amount of our war expenditure which was something like a billion and a half of dollars.
Then there was the capitalization of our pensions; I have forgotten the amount, but it was very large. Then, there were the claims for direct damage to our shipping and to some of our nationals through the illegal operations of German submarines. The claim has been put in, as I have stated, but what dividend will be declared I am unable to state. In my Budget speech I mentioned that it would be better for us, while pressing our claims against Germany, to depend upon our own resources for meeting our debt. I do not mean to say that Canada will not obtain a substantial indemnity from Germany, but how much and when obviously I cannot say.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported.

On motion of Sir Thomas White (Minister of Finance) the House went into Committee to consider the following proposed resolution, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
Resolved, That it is expedient,-
1.	To consolidate and amend the Acts respecting- the Ottawa Improvement Commission.
2,	To authorize the Minister of Finance to *pay out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada the sum of $ lfiO, O'O 0 annually, for a period not exceeding ten years from the first day of July, 1919; in four equal quarterly instalment®, payable on the first days of April, July, October and January, respectively, in each year; the first of such quarterly instalments to be paid on the first day of July, 1919, the amount of each instalment to be paid by the minister into a chartered bank, to be designated by him, to the credit of the Ottawa Improvement Commission, to be expended as prescribed for all or any of the purposes for which the commission is authorized under the proposed consolidated legislation to expend sums placed to its credit.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Under legislation of this House in 1899 and 1909, provision

was made for a grant, which finally amounted to $100,000 a year, to the Ottawa Improvement Commission, which was constituted for the purpose of the systematic planning and beautification of the city of Ottawa and the establishment of parks and driveways for the benefit of the people and of visitors to the Capital. During the war the work has been considerably interrupted; the amount which the commission received has been practically all required for the maintenance of existing parks, driveways and other properties which they have had under administration, and for the taking up of debentures which matured from year to year. The grant to the Ottawa Improvement Commission, while it was a recognition of the responsibility of the Dominion Government tow'ards the capital of Canada, was also, by the express terms of the legislation, a part of the consideration to the city of Ottawa for fire protection, water, and other services which the Dominion Government enjoyed from the municipality.
I stated that $100,000 was the yearly grant which was finally made under the legislation, and that amount has been paid for the last ten years. In addition to that there is a sum of $15,000 a year which is paid for the services or some of the services which I have mentioned. The agreement with the city of Ottawa respecting these services and the legislation respecting the Ottawa Improvement Commission terminated on June 30 of this year. It became necessary, therefore, to negotiate a new agreement with the city of Ottawa for the services which I have mentioned and to consider what grant should be made by new legislation to the Ottawa Improvement Commission. The two questions have been taken up in negotiations which have been carried on with the Ottawa municipal authorities by a committee of the Council of which the Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Carvell has been chairman, and I believe that an agreement has been reached. I am unable to give the details of that agreement; they will be given by the Minister of Public Works, who will introduce a Bill for the purpose of sanctioning the agreement. The amount of $150,000 which is provided by this resolution was part of the consideration passing from the Government to the city of Ottawa in the agreement which has just been negotiated; I am therefore asking the Committee to approve the resolution so that we may introduce a Bill for the purpose of defining the services which the Dominion Government will get and of setting forth the other consideration
which we shall pay. It was thought advisable, as the Dominion Government has a direct and intermediate interest in the Ottawa Improvement Commission, that the legislation respecting it should be separate. In order that the Committee may know the purposes to which the $150,000 will be devoted for the coming year, I may say that amount of $102,000 will be needed for maintenance, leaving only $48,000 for any new work. The whole of this balance could be expended, and probably will be, on the extension of the retaining wall of the Rideau canal from Laurier avenue southwest, a very necessary work which the commission is taking over from the Department of Railways and Canals. The plans of the commission are fairly extensive for the future, but it is not advisable that publicity should be given to them, as that might lead to speculation in land. The commission does not make public its plans in advance of acquiring properties; but for the present year, as I have said, the programme is a fairly simple one.
What was the vote at first, under the Act of 1899, and how has it been extended from time to time?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Speaking from
memory, I understand -that in 1899 the vote was $60,000 a year. The commission was given the power to issue debentures which were to mature not beyond a certain date.
Was the commission appointed by the Dominion Government?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, in 1899 the Government of that day created the Ottawa Improvement Commission and named its members, Sir Henry Bate being the chairman.
I may say that the laite 'Sir Wilfrid Laurier took a very keen interest in the work of this comiriission. I talked over a number of matters with him, and I do not recall anything in which he was more interested. In 1909 the amount was increased from $60,000 to $100,000 a year, and a further grant of $15,000 was given for water service for fire protection, I think, or for both. The grant therefore was $115,000 a year. That money was used ih Ithe first instance for the acquisition of properties, 'and the commission, by issuing 'debentures and raising money on them, employed those funds also for the same purpose. Then, when they acquired the properties and got their drives and parks established, the maintenance charges, of course, became considerable, so that the $115,000 was practically spent in this way in recent years: $15,000 went direct to the

city of Ottawa for the services I have mentioned, and the $100,000 a year was used for maintenance and for the retirement, as they matured, of the debentures which had been issued by the commission. The last debenture matures on July 1, and will be taken up from this grant of . $150,000. I was talking to Sir Henry Egan the other day about the terms and he estimated that the maintenance charges, leaving out the payment off of this debenture, were about $75,000 a year. With the payment off of the debenture, I think something like $100,000 will be required this year, apart from expenditure on any new work, and the balance will be taken up in building retaining walls along the Rideau canal.
Does the city contribute anything towards the maintenance?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
Who is the president oi the commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Sir Henry Egan. During the last few years very little has been spent on new work.

In the reference made by my hon. friend I suppose he had in mind the results of the negotiations that have taken place between the very progressive mayor of the city, Mr. Fisher, and the Minister of Public Works. Might I ask, is the city of Ottawa satisfied with the offer, made by the Government? At the time the letters which were exchanged between the Hon. Mr. iCarvell and His Worship the Mayor appeared in the press I noticed that his worship was pleading very earnestly for better terms. Will this resolution embody a settlement satisfactory to the city?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I understand from the Minister of Public Works that they have practically agreed upon the terms, one of which is contained in the resolution which is now before the committee. I assume therefore, that the negotiations have been handled quite satisfactorily to all concerned. Of course, my hon. friend knows that there are always two parties to a negotiation.

I thought His Worship the Mayor made a strong point when he stated that the fact that Ottawa was the capital of the Dominion reduced the city's tax revenue and thereby prevented the city from giving the necessary aid to industries which otherwise would find their way to the city. Of course, Ottawa is magnificently situated and lends itself to the development of industries by reason of its enor-

mous water-power. That was, in my judgment, a very strong argument. Of course, I know there are two sides to the question, and that the seat of Government being here brings quite a population to the city and is a very great advantage. I suppose we shall hear from the Minister of Public Works as to what conclusions have been reached.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes.
Mr. McKENZIE": I always understood that we had certain control, and I would expect that a Government engineer, for instance, who is an expert in these matters should have something to say as to where this money should be expended and how. I am rather surprised that the Mayor based his [DOT] plea for more money upon the ground that the seat of Government should not be here at all-that it is a disadvantage to Ottawa I might instance the city of Halifax, which is happy to look after the Provincial Parliament and Provincial Government property. There are millions of dollars worth of Government property in that city not paying a single farthing of taxation. At one time a man introduced a Bill in the local legislature to impose a municipal tax upon Government property in the city, but when the Bill came on for its first reading he could not get anybody to support it. I am pleased to be a party to giving money for the ordinary beautification of the capital city of the Dominion, but I do not want the Mayor of Ottawa or anybody else to think for a moment that we are paying tribute to .the city to be permitted to stay here. I think the advantage is entirely the other way, and that any other city would be only too proud to be constituted the capital.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I may say, Mr. Chairman, that all expenditures by the commission have to be approved by the Governor in Council. An estimate is made of what the commission desires to do, and that is laid before the Government and approved before the commission proceeds with the work. That is provided for in the Bill which I will introduce afterwards.
I quite agree with the statement made by the leader of the Opposition. I was under the impression that the city contribute to the maintenance of the public parks-.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I was speaking only of the Ottawa Improvement Commission's properties. There are certain properties in the city which the city does maintain.

But I mean the grounds of the Ottawa Improvement Commission, which are very extensive as we all know, and a great credit to the commission. But it must be remembered that people who come to Ottawa from other parts of Canada spend the winter here as a rule, and the parks are no good to them.
During the summer season, when the parks are really an advantage to the citizens of Ottawa, and they have the use of them, the money is expended. That is one reason why they should not press too hard for those concessions for which the (Mayor of Ottawa has been asking. I am quite in favour of the expenditure in beautifying the city of Ottawa; we are all very proud of it, and we want to make it as fine a city as possible. What the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) said about the late leader of the Opposition is quite true. He took a very lively interest in the Ottawa Improvement Commission, and I remember hearing him say once that when he got too old to lead a party in the House of Commons, he would like to be Chairman of the Ottaw.a Improvement Commission.

I must not be misunderstood. The Mayor of Ottawa, Mr. Fisher, never regretted the fact that the city of Ottawa was the seat of the Government, but he, representing the citizens of Ottawa, had to speak of the tax exemption enjoyed by the'Government and realizing the very large amount which the exemption involved, he certainly had a right to comment on that. I repeat that the point he raised last winter was a very strong one. The fact that the Government enjoys a tax exemption, which tax, if the Government did not enjoy such exemption, would yield a very large revenue to the city of Ottawa, makes it so that the citizens are heavily burdened, and the city is unable to aid certain industries which would otherwise establish themselves here. Of course the Government does a great deal for Ottawa by the fact that it is here, but the city is unique as a site for a capital. There are I know arguments pro and con, but I claim the city of Ottawa is doing as much as is being done for the city of Ottawa. But this is a matter of business which can be settled, after friendly negotiations as was hinted by the Minister of Finance.

Is this sum supposed
to be spent only in the city of Ottawa? I understand that the law provides that it could be spent in Ottawa and in surrounding municipalities. As a matter of fact, in
1910 or 1911, the city of Hull received the sum of $5,000 out of this fund to improve one of its parks, and I presume we received that under the provisions of the Act. It is all right to make a beautiful city of Ottawa, but it would be too bad if visitors, after leaving the beautiful city of Ottawa, were to cross over to Hull and see such a difference between the two cities. The Government should see to it that the city of Hull-
The free city of Hull.

Yes, the free city of Hull, receives a share of this sum once more. I understand that the law permits the spending of this money not only in the city of Ottawa, but in the surrounding municipalities, including the city of Hull. As a matter of fact, when I was mayor of Hull, in 1911, we secured a certain amount of money from the Improvement Commission, but that, of course, was during the regime of the late Government under the leadership of Sir Wilfrid Laurier.
Sir THOMAS' WHITE: The Bill provides that:
The commission may purchase, acquire, and hold' real property in the city of Ottawa, or in the vicinity thereof, for the purpose of public parks or squares, streets, avenues, drives or thoroughfares.
It is for the Ottawa Improvement Commission in the first place to determine the plans which it will carry out, and as I stated, they are then laid before the Government for its approval.

Three years ago a magnificent plan was published in connection with the Improvement Commission. It was distributed to the members, and it, of course, involved a much larger expenditure than the one mentioned this morning. What has become of this plan, and has the Government reached any decision as regards those extensive improvements?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The plan was made in order that the city might have the benefit of a certain systematic development. The object of the plan was the beautification of the city of 'Ottawa as the capital of the Dominion. The planning was carried out by a commission of which Sir Herbert Holt was chairman, and on that commission were, amongst others, Mr. Frank Darling, a very eminent architect of Toronto; Mr. Cousins, of Toronto, an engineer of ability and standing, and Sir Alexandre Lacoste. They engaged a town planning architect, Mr. Bennett, of Chicago, and the result was a plan which, I think,

met generally with the approval of the pep-ple of Ottawa. The idea was that all interests, transportation, municipal and governmental, should, in connection with the buildings which they found it necessary to erect, or the streets which it was found necessary to lay out, follow that plan. That course was adopted in connection with the city of Washington which has had the bene-fit_ of working to a plan which was drawn for its development many years ago by a very distinguished French town-planning architect.
Le Captaine Lenfant.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The members of the 'committee wall realize what that plan has meant to the city of Washington, which is one of the most beautifully laid out cities in the world. As regards the Dominion Government, we shall endeavour to follow, in any buildings which we erect, the lines laid down in the plan mentioned, and it is hoped that the railway companies, and also the municipal authorities, will do likewise. During the war, expenditure naturally could not be made upon projects of that kind, and at the present time there is need for expenditure, more upon essentials than upon the matter of beautification, but I hope that the plan will mean much to the further development of the city of Ottawa, and that all parties concerned will work to it.

I should like to assure the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) that the citizens of Ottawa fully appreciate all the advantages of having the capital city in their midst. At the same time we are giving the Government of Canada many advantages for which the citizens of Ottawa think they are not fully compensated. As regards the present resolution, which provides for a grant of $150,000 for the Ottawa Improvement Commission, I pointed out to the House on a previous occasion during this session, that the city of Ottawa does not in any way control the expenditure of that sum or have anything whatever to do with it. While we do not directly contribute towards it, we do indirectly; the grant that is made to the Improvement Commission is partly in consideration of services which are rendered by the city of Ottawa in the way of fire protection, sewers, water, and other matters of that kind. The payment to the city of Ottawa direct is I understand now the subject of an agreement between the city and the committee of which the Minister of Public Works is

chairman. I always felt that the mayor made out a very good case for the Government's paying the city at least $800,000 a year in consideration of the benefits derived. I am told that the agreement which the city have reluctantly accepted provides for a very much smaller sum. However, as it has been agreed upon and accepted by the mayor and corporation I presume that Parliament will pass the Bill when it is brought down.

I am sure that the city of Ottawa will take all that is given to it by the Dominion Government, and apparently look for more. I should like to know whether this $150,000 is included in the agreement now under negotiation between the city and the Minister of Public Works for t|ie Government, or is it a separate item? My hon. friend (Mr. Fripp") considers the mayor has made out a good case for the Government paying the city $800,000 annually. On looking over the Estimates passed this session under the Department of Public Works I find that a total of $733,616.20 has already been voted to be spent in the city of Ottawa during the coming year. On page 70 of the Estimates, under item 115, I find $6,616.20 for local improvements on Carling Avenue; on page 72, under item 121, $450,000 for repairs, furniture, grounds, snow and street maintenance, etc.; on page 78, under item 132, $120,000 to replace the present Union bridge over the Ottawa river below Chaudiere, and on the same page an item of $7,000 for maintenance and repair of bridges and approaches. These amounts to be spent by the Dominion Government in the city of Ottawa during the coming year aggregate $733,616.20. So the interests of Ottawa are not being neglected.
I remember also that the Minister of Public Works explained that one of the items Parliament has voted included an amount of $11,000 for salaries in connection with the upkeep of one mile of Wellington street, for which stretch the Government is responsible, I submit that that is a pretty liberal contribution in wages alone; in addition to that there is the machinery, the road material, and other et ceieras. We are all interested in Ottawa, and would like to see it put on its best bib and tucker at all times, .so that visitors from the United States and elsewhere will have something worth while to look at, and will form a good impression not only of the capital but of the whole Dominion.
The members are enough for the visitors to look at.

So I do not think Ottawa has anything to complain of.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
*Sir THOMAS WHITE (Minister of Finance) thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 165, to consolidate and amend the Acts respecting the Ottawa Improvement Commission, founded on the resolution.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.
Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Minister of the Interior) moved the second reading of Bill No. 159, to amend the Dominion Lands Acft Amendment.
Would the minister give a general explanation of the proposed amendments to the Act?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I might say that we discussed them on the resolution which has been passed. The first section raises *the rate of interest on pre-emptions from 5 to 6 per cent; the second section makes the same change in respect of purchased homesteads. The third section provides for the sale of surface rights in the case of school lands in certain cases where mining rights have been obtained but could not be exercised without injuring the surface. The provinces, of course, are interested and have agreed to this amendment. Section 4 provides for greater latitude in the area of timber leased for pulp purposes. It has been found that the areas limited by the Act, which never had regard for pulp at all, are insufficient to warrant the establishment of any extensive pulp industry.
What was 'the area undei the old Act?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend will find it in section 59; I will send him over a copy. Another section provides for increasing the rate of interest on money payable in respect of timber lands. It is simply carrying out the principle we have adopted of making the regular rate of interest 6 per cent. The rate of interest on arrears is made 7 per cent. Section 7 amends section 10 of the present Act by accepting land reserved for soldiers' settlement. Section 10 of the Act as d't now stands provides for squatters' rights. This Bill will accept lands reserved for soldier settlement.

Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time, and the House went into Committee thereon, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 1-rate of interest increased on overdue instalments for pre-emptions:

Is the rate fixed in these
agreements?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, the rate of interest is fixed, and we do not alter any agreement already made. In these cases, I notify the party who is in arrears that he must pay up, and if he is not ready to do so I submit to him a form of agreement in which he undertakes to pay interest on arrears at seven per cent. That has been the policy in relation to school lands ever since the House established seven per cent as the rate on arrears. I would suggest,, with the consent of the committee, that clauses one and two be allowed to stand: for the present. At the moment, it seems to me that it should be from five to seven instead of from five to six per cent. I am not sure why it is printed as it is.

Section agreed to.
On section 3-sale of surface rights in certain cases to lessee of mining rights:
Is it the object of this clause to recoup those who are entitled to the value of the land for the uselessness of surface as a result of mining operations.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, this does not purport to deal with any land alienated at all. This has reference to land unsold. It provides for the sale of surface rights where the mining rights have been acquired, without submitting surface rights to auction sale. The Dominion Lands Act provides that school lands must be sold by auction.. If it is found in certain cases that mining rights cannot be used for farming, and can be of value only to the owner of mining rights, it would not do to sell them by auction. So that we communicated with the governments of the three provinces and obtained their assent to an amendment to enable us to fix the valuation of the surface rights and sell them to owners of mining rights at these valuations. It does not apply to lands other people own, but only to lands owned by the Grown.
There are two separate interests, the surface and the mining. When a man acquires the mining rights, he has to acquire the surface in order to exploit his mine.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
He may have to acquire it if the mine runs close to the surface.
On section 4-limit of area to be included in timber permits:
I suppose this is necessary on account of the new industries of pulp and paper being established in certain areas of public lands?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Exactly.
On what law was this based: on the ordinary regulations of the provinces that lease their lands for pulp and paper exploitation?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think it is based on the regulations of Quebec. It enables the Governor in Council to extend the area that may be leased for purposes of pulpwood exploitation. At Grand. Rapids, in Manitoba,. 35,000 horse-power development is under way, and can he utilized certainly to the best advantage, and probably only, for the purposes of pulp mills. It is impossible for capital to invest in the magnitude it must invest to establish a pulp industry there, unless there are areas that can supply the industry, and which areas can be assured. The present regulations do not provide for any such area, and this enables the Governor in Council to make the necessary provision, dependent in each case upon the surrounding circumstances. The Government of Manitoba is most anxious for this alteration to be made. Naturally, they desire this industry to be established at Grand Rapids.

The section does not seem to me to be based to any great extent on the Quebec regulations, except in the fact that the lease will last only one year. The section reads:
Notwithstanding the foregoing subsection, if it is shown to the satisfaction of the minister that the establishment of a paper or pulp-mill requiring large capital expenditure is dependent upon the acquiring of the right to cut pulp-wood in the vicinity of such mill in sufficient quantity to justify such expenditure, the minister may, with the approval of the Governor in Council and subject to such regulations as the Governor in Council may provide, enter into an agreement granting the exclusive right to cut timber for pulpwood within a specified area until the specified quantity which has been agreed upon as justifying the expenditure shall have been cut.
In Quebec a man goes before the Government and makes application for the acquirement of certain timber limits. The 'Government advertises these limits for sale on a certain day, and the highest bidder secures them. Of course, the man acquiring them has to pay the ground rent yearly and stumpage according to the number of logs cut, but he does not get any concession from the Government by reason of the importance of the industry which he wishes

to establish. The first thing he has to get is the raw material, or timber, and he can secure this only in competition at public auction with all lumbermen or people desiring to obtain timber limits, and the sale is made on a day fixed by the Minister of Lands and Forests. He may ask the department to put a certain area on the market, but that is the only extent to which he may be considered as being privileged, all the rest being done by competition in the open market. In this case, if a man says he wants a certain area for the purpose of establishing a mill, and that he cannot properly and with any benefit exploit that industry unless he secures additional lands, the minister may recommend to the Government that such an area be granted to him. Is that right?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

So that the public are
excluded from any competition, and have no ojjportunity to buy the land if they desire.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The reason for that is
that the timber cannot possibly be used for pulp purposes except by those who are developing the power. The power is administered by the Water Power Branch of the department, and power rights were in some cases obtained years ago. The area could be of no value to any one else, and that is the position in which we find ourselves. If the area were put up for auction it would either mean that competitors who would otherwise go there for the purpose of forcing the hand of the owner, of power concessions would be bought off, or there would be no sale on account of these men endeavouring to make money out of the only ones who could establish an industry there and take advantage of the opportunities.
It seemed to me that the only thing that could be done-and this was the view of the Manitoba Government-was to enable the Government to place a valuation on it, by means of so much stumpage, the payment of rental and so forth, fix that at a fair price and give a lease on those terms to the owners of the power concession. I do not know when the power rights were given. They are conditional. Power rights are not alienated; they are conditional upon certain expenditures being made and on certain development going on. Power rights are given, wherever they are owned by the Crown, after the fullest engineer investigation to see that development along the lines proposed by the concessionaires is practically feasible. That is the method

of our power administration. Once you have them in the hands of a company there is no way by which you can usefully put the timber up and sell it except in connection with the power site. The reason is that it is so far from civilization and from the inhabited part of the province that it is useful only for the purposes in connection with the power site and it could not be developed profitably in any other way except by the use of the power in that locality.

This seems to be rather a drastic measure. I understand there is one case in which this measure would apply and that by an agreement which is to be entered into between the owner of a power and pulp mill ,and the Government he is to have the exclusive right to cut timber for pulpwood within a specified area and for a specified time. I do not see why a man should be held up by an act of this kind. If a man is going to invest money in pulpwood and if power is absolutely necessary to exploit this pulpwood, he is taking a big chance in the event of matters coming to a deadlock. I do not think there is a man who would be foolish enough to invest his money in the business on these terms if pulpwood is worth as much in Manitoba as it is in the region of the St. Maurice river.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It would be of no value otherwise and we would get no value for it.
Is it the fact that this power can only be used for the purpose of grinding pulp?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is the only purpose for which it can be used on account of its location. My hon. friend from Dauphin (Mr. Cruise) would know the location better than I would but any one who looks at the map will see that it could not be used for any other purpose.
Is this only an exceptional case we are legislating for now?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This is the only case we have in mind, but there may be others on the Nelson and Saskatchewan rivers and in some other similar positions.

If this is only to meet an exceptional case and to prevent a hardship to some important interest in Manitoba, well and good, but I think the principle is wrong if this legislation means that when a man goes and buys a water-power it will preclude anybody else from going into that region and buying pulpwood. There may be small mills operated by steam generated by the use of the refuse from the wood. This is not exactly a restraint upon trade, but it is an impediment to the development of the natural resources of a part of the country. Still, if it is an exceptional case, we will have to consent to this legislation because we do not want to block anything, but I would suggest that this special case should be defined. Grand Rapids, I understand, is the name of the place to which this legislation applies?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

Then Grand Rapids ought to be mentioned so that the law will apply only to the particular case that the Government now has in view, because people might try to create conditions that, in the opinion of the minister, or those interested, would be like those at Grand Rapids, whereas they would not be in fact.
At one o'clock the Committee took recess.
The Committee resumed at three o'clock.
I was asking the minister when the committee rose whether it would not be possible to specify the cases where forests might not be exploited unless the method mentioned in section 4 was followed.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have since had a discussion on the subject with the deputy minister, and he states that a pulp limit in the West, if you could call it a limit, would be virtually in the same position as -the one referred to here; there might be exceptions, but he thinks not. Our pulp timber in Western Canada is not like the pulp timber of Quebec. The northern areas of the province of Quebec comprise much solid bush, heavily timbered; ours is scattered and the bush is smaller, and it would be difficult to make up anything that could be called a pulp section unless there was power immediately adjoining. Very large areas will have to be given where there is a power site adjoining, but the deputy minister points out that unless the conditions obtaining are similar to those which obtain at Grand Rapids, of course the regular clauses would apply, and the department would put the land up at auction in the ordinary course. But there will certainly be other cases the same as the Grand Rapids case, and on that ground the clause should pass as it is.
Are these pulp areas adjacent to rivers and streams?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is a short river at Grand Rapids, near where the power is; but the concession will have to extend quite a distance from that.

Is there no means of carrying the logs down by water? In the St. Maurice region the logs are put in the small rivers and streams, and when the spring freshets cause the water to rise the logs are borne down to the main river where the power and mills are located.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They might go some distance down the Saskatchewan river to Grand Rapids; I am not quite certain of that. They would have to go through some lakes on the way.
That is easy.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, but the idea is not to give concessions up the river; it is to grant certain areas in the vicinity of the power section.
Section 4 agreed to.
On section 7-settling on lands reserved for soldier settlement.
Will the minister explain this clause?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The following is the clause in the Act as it stands, without the proposed amendment:
A person who has bona fide settled and made improvements on agricultural land before the survey thereof and is in occupation of and ordinarily resident on the land at the time of survey shall, if he is eligible under this Act to make entry for a homestead, or a purchased homestead, have a prior right to obtain entry for the land so settled on: Provided that this right is exercised within six months after notice in writing that the land is open for entry has been given by the local agent to the said person, or has been posted in a conspicuous place on the land; and that entry shall not be allowed for more than a quarter-section as a homestead.
By .section 7 of (this Bill the following proviso is added:
Provided further that no person shall obtain any rights under this section who settles on land reserved for soldier settlement after such land has been so reserved.
Without the amendment, we might reserve an area of land for soldier settlement, say in the Peace River District, before survey. Immediately men would go up there and forestall the soldier by getting on that land and securing squatters' rights; so we say that as soon as we survey, the squatter is precluded from going in and anticipating the arrival of the soldier.
Section agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Sections 1 and 2 were allowed to stand this morning. I move that the word "five" in the second last line of each of these sections he struck out and that the word "six" be substituted therefor.

Is it not somewhat
anomalous to have a general law providing for a certain rate of interest and then to have a special law providing for a higher rate in certain cases?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Six per cent is becoming the general law, but unless we make seven per cent the .rate of interest on arrears, the chance of getting the arrears in is practically nothing.
Why not take notes.
Amendments agreed to, and .sections 1 and 2 agreed to.
Why not take notes, which always carry 7 per cent?

We do not take notes.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

On motion of IHon. Arthur Meighen (Minister of the Interior) Bill No. 163, to amend the Indian Act, was read the second time and the House went into Committee thereon, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 1-leases of surface rights may be granted in connection with mining for precious metals:
Are there any provisions in the Indian Act as it now stands for the granting of mining leases?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.
This is a new law?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
This is new; that is,
there is no provision for the lease of surface rights without surrender from the Indians. The old section reads as follows:
Except as in this Part otherwise provided, no reserve or portion of a reserve shall be sold, alienated or leased until it has been released or surrendered to the Crown for the purposes of this Part: Provided that the Superintendent General may lease, for the benefit of any Indian, upon his application for that purpose, the land to which he is entitled without such land being released or surrendered, and may, without surrender, dispose to the best advantage, in the interests of the Indians* of wild grass and dead or fallen timber.
This ia amended so that:
The Governor in Council may make regulations enabling the Superintendent General with-

out surrender to issue leases for surface rights on Indian reserve, upon such terms and conditions as may be considered proper in the interest of the Indians, covering such area only as may be necessary for the mining of the precious metals by any one otherwise authorized to mine such metals, said terms to include provision of compensating any occupant of land for any damage that may be caused thereon as determined by the Superintendent General.
This is asked for by the Government of the province of British 'Columbia, where the mining rights, of course, are held by the province, to prevent mining operators being held at bay by the Indians.
Is there no provision made for the consent of an Indian tribe being obtained?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes. Wherever an
Indian tribe holds the mining rights it must surrender them before any mining leases are granted. But once the mining rights are surrendered-and there are cases where they have been surrendered-then the Indian tribe says, " You cannot go on the land to get the minerals out." This provides that leases for surface rights may be issued on making compensation therefor.

On what principle are
leases of mineral lands granted; for what length of time and on what terms and conditions?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am not sure that I
can answer the question in detail, but before mineral lands are leased or sold at all a surrender is secured from the Indians. I have had a few such cases and I will tell my hon. friend what occurred. The terms of the surrender itself contain the provisions under which the mining land is to be dealt with. Usually the Indian tribes are intelligent enough and capable of looking after themselves with the assistance of the agent, and they say: You must advertise the conditions, a long lease for so many years at a royalty charge ir a sale by auction, and the terms must be carried out. If there are no fixed terms in the surrender as to what is to be the method of handling the property, then the Superintendent General, with the approval of Council, provides the best way for dealing with the property in the interests of the tribe, and, of course, either tenders are asked for or an auction is held.
These mineral lands may be valuable in places?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Oh, yes.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There might be individual cases where it would be in the interests of the state to, what is -called, nationalize our mineral resources-that is, to go into the mining business, to put it in plain English. But if I may venture the opinion, in a great majority of cases, if the Government weie to go into the mining business, there would be no need of discussing in advance what should be done with the profits, because there would be no profits to distribute. There -might be individual cases where there would be profits, but I have not very much hope that as a general policy Government mining could be made a success. Mining is a most hazardous business.
But on coal might there not be a royalty?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That means private development on a royalty basis. That is the present system.
That is what the hon. member means.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: What the hon. member -means is, * rather, that the Government should itself undertake the mining, smelting, and so forth, and then sell the product.
Oh, no.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I know that is in the minds of some people in this country, and the Government has been importuned to adopt that policy. Very elaborate schemes have been worked out for the distribution of the profits in such an event, but I have never been bothered much on the question of the distribution of profits resulting from Government mining. I do not think their distribution would give any Government very much trouble. But there may be individual cases where that policy should be pursued, and, indeed, we have acted on that assumption. For example, there are large areas of oil lands now held from entry, the intention being that those lands should be reserved for the uses of the state-possibly to be developed privately, possibly to be developed under public ownership. It may be that the same policy should be pursued in regard to certain other minerals, but oil is the mineral in regard to which action hae been taken first.

I understand that the object of this clause is solely to allow the superintendent general, without the surrender, to issue leases of surface rights, to be used by the mine owners either as loads to and from the mine or for dumping purposes.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I would think that that was a pretty full statement of it. I do not think the surface rights would be needed for anything except dumping purposes.

Section agreed to.
On Section 2-Minimum with respect to amount to be paid to members of band struck out:
You are striking out " and not exceeding 10 per cent of the proceeds of any." Any what?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I will asik that this clause be allowed to stand.
Does the minister mean " of any," or " if any?"
It may be "of."

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It should be "of" if the amendment is gone on with at all.
Section stands.	.
On Section 3-Part Three-Soldier Settlement.

Would that have the same application as in the case the minister has just mentioned in the Dominion Lands Act, that wherever any surrender is made and the land is set aside for soldiers' settlement, squatter rights will not be considered as against soldier rights?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: What portion is the hon. gentleman referring to?
I see that the Soldiers' Settlement Act shall apply. This has reference, if I understand rightly, to the Indian Act?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

My question is if the application would be the same as in the case of the Dominion Lands Act when squatters have settled? The case I have in mind is this: Supposing a reservation is surrendered for the purpose of soldiers' settlement, all prior settlements will be void as against the soldier; he shall have priority? Or what cases are contemplated by the Act? I have not had time to read it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No, I do not think this has anything to do with what are called
[iMr. Meighen.1
squatters' rights. The old Indian Act contains provisions enabling individual Indians to secure farm lands on their own reserves, which they work as their own. This Bill provides that the proper sections of the Soldiers' Settlement Act shall be applied to the Indian Act, that the deputy superintendent general shall be enabled to grant to the Indian soldier lands on his own reserve, and then assist him on those lands as a returned soldier, thus taking care of the Indian as an Indian instead of endeavouring to take care of him as a white man under the Soldiers' Settlement Act. That is the sole effect of this.

Section agreed to.
On section 2-minimum with respect to amount to be paid to members of band struck out:

What is the effect of
the change?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It means this. Under the clause as it stood, in the event of a sale of Indian lands, the surrender might contain terms enabling the Governor in Council to distribute up to 50 per cent of the proceeds of any land and 10 per cent of the proceeds of timber, that being the maximum in each case respectively of the money, to the Indians. Now it has been found necessary to change the percentage as respects timber up to the same as that as respects land, and therefore, the special restriction with regard to timber should be struck out.

Section agreed to.
On the title:

We have a mining
branch, and as the Government of Canada owns minerals in the West and elsewhere, it is highly important that we should have a mining Act or legislation dealing specifically with mines. In Nova Scotia where we deal with coal largely, we have a very well considered mining law, but as regards coal mines in the West, I have never come across any proper regulations or mining Act which would govern the mines and the method in which they are worked. Unless it is the intention of the Government to pass over the mining rights, etc., to the provinces, in which case they will, of course, make their own mining laws, it is highly desirable that, while we own those minerals, we should have a mining law dealing with them. Such a law would be very desirable in the case with which we are dealing now. With us, if a coal mining company, for instance, wants land, they have to prepare a

plan, have it sworn to by proper engineers of the company, submit that plan to the Minister of Mines, and then he issues a summons to the owner of the land and to the company and they both appear before the minister and there is a hearing before him, and if after that hearing the mining company satisfies the minister that they should take the lands, an order is made to pass the land over to the mine owners. I believe some such proceeding is what the minister has in mind.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
While I would not like to give a positive acquiescence in the hon. member's suggestion, it is certainly worthy of consideration. Of course, our mining properties are at present administered under those provisions of the Dominion Lands Act which appertain to mining, and regulations are made in pursuance of the powers contained in that Act, and under those regulations the Mining Branch of the Department of the Interior administers all mining lands. That is our mining law today, and in consequence of that law, the property of Canada in minerals is wholly administered. We cannot, of course, have a mining law in the sense that it is asked for by some mining engineers of Canada, and that may be what the hon. member has in mind. We cannot do anything practical towards making uniform mining laws in the different provinces, and that is what they have in mind. It would be better if there were a little more statutory law as regards mining and perhaps a little less of regulations. I have taken occasion at this session to put in more elaborate form the statutory laws governing the administration of water-powers, and I am disposed to think similar action with regard to the administration of mines would be advisable, and it will be a consideration at the next session.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.

speechtext:
The House again in Committee on Bill No. 138, to amend and consolidate the Acts relating to British Nationality, Naturalization and Aliens, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 11-national status of married women.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext: Does this mean that a married woman, the wife of an alien, can be naturalized just the same as the husband can, and that if she becomes naturalized the children follow the nationality of the father?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext: Yes; this is put in more as a declaration to clarify the law.

Section agreed to.
On section 13-status of children.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext:
This is the section that affects the case I mentioned the other day.
It says:
Where a person being a British subject, ceases to be a British subject whether by declaration of alienage or otherwise, every child of that person, being a minor, shall thereupon cease to be a British subject, unless such child, on that person ceasing to be a British subject, does not become by the law of any other country, naturalized in that country.
Take the case of a child whose father is a British subject in Canada. The father crosses the border and becomes an American citizen. That child, being a minor, would lose his fiationality as a British subject.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext: Unless the law of the United States provides otherwise.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext: But suppose he keeps out of the reach of the law of the United States, and that while the child is still a minor the father comes back to Canada and becomes re-naturalized a.s a British subject; what then?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext: That is a pretty involved proposition, and I do not know that I could answer offhand. It might be a case for the consideration of the Secretary of State under section 4-a doubtful case.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext: We ought to make the law clear.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext: It is clear in my mind, but the question is rather an involved one.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext:
We passed a section the other night providing that if a man becomes re-naturalized the names of his minor children must be included in his certificate of naturalization in order to make them British subjects. Thousands of cases of this kind may arise in view of the intercourse between the two countries. A man may leave Canada to work in the United States, and take out naturalization papers while he is there. Under this section his child, being a minor, would lose his nationality as a British subject. When that father returns to Canada and becomes re-naturalized here, it is only in very few cases that the minor children would know that their names must be in-.
*4258

eluded to the father's naturalization certificates for them to become British subjects again. Why not provide that if the child when he reaches the age of 21 does not make a declaration as to the nationality he wishes to take, he shall follow the nationality of his father. That would make the law clearer, and would prevent a lo't of difficulty. Otherwise these children might go on living in Canada believing in perfect good faith they were British subjects, whereas really they would be aliens, and then if any law was passed affecting aliens they would be affected by that law. I think 'the child should follow the nationality of its father in a case of this kind, and we ought to amend the section accordingly.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext:
T think tlia't case is pretty well covered by sections 13 and 5. Section 13 says:
Where a person being a British subject ceases to be a British subject,-
We will suppose that the father and the children were born in Canada, and that the father removes his family to 'the United States.

every child of that person, being a minor, shall thereupon cease to be a British subject, unless such child, on that person ceasing to be a British subject, does not become by the law of any other country, naturalized in that country.
I am assuming that there is no law on the subject one way or the other in the United States, and that the child becomes an American citizen. Then his father comes back to Canada. Now under section 5 his father could then become re-naturalized as a British subject, and should include in his certificate all his minor children. If any of his minor children on reaching the age of 'twenty-one do not wish to become naturalized all they have to do is to make a declaration to that effect.
