The child has the option; he can remain an American or he can become a British subject. So I think that case is pretty well covered.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext:
A good many men will
become re-naturalized and will not think of including the names of their minor children in their certificate. Let me submit another case. A British subject goes to the United States, and before becoming naturalized a child is born to him on American soil. The father afterwards becomes a naturalized American citizen, and while the child is still a minor, returns to Canada and is re-naturalized as a British subject. Why not put it in the law that the child when attaining the age of

twenty-one years shall become a subject of the country to which his father belonged?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext: The child was to all intents and purposes an American citizen.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext: He was an American by birth.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext:
If his father comes
back to Canada and is re-naturalized he has the option, on attaining the age of twenty-one, of choosing his nationality. I do not think we should bind the child as my hon. friend suggests.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext: Suppose the father when he goes over to the United States leaves his family at home in Canada, takes out naturalization papers in the United States, returns to Canada and again becomes naturalized in Canada? The children never went to the United States, but remained in Canada. What will be their status? It happens in Quebec that large numbers of men go into the lumber camps in Maine and stay there for considerable time. Some men take out naturalization papers in the New England States, but their families never leave Quebec. Suppose a man made up his mind to come back to Canada, what would be the position of his children if they never left this country?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext: They are British subjects, there is no question about that. They never lost their nationality.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext: Another class will have to be provided for. Section 7 provides that if a Canadian citizen lives outside of this country for seven years he loses his naturalization. Suppose a man lives abroad for seven or eight years and decides to return, his family having been all born in this country. What will be the status of those children if they become of age by the time he decides to return?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext: They would be British subjects. But the father would not lose his nationality unless he severed connection with the British Empire.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext: The Act says distinctly that he does, if he has been resident, since the date of the granting of the certificate, for a period of not less than seven years out of His Majesty's dominions, otherwise than as a representative or employee of a British subject, firm or company carrying on business, etc.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext:
Further on it says "and has not maintained substantial connection with His Majesty's dominions." If his family were here and he communicated with

them, I would unhesitatingly say that he had maintained substantial connection.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext: Suppose he leaves the country and takes his family along with him, and after seven or eight years he loses naturalization. If he returns to Canada with'his children, who become of age during their residence abroad, although they were born in Canada, what will be the position?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext: His children, on attaining the age of twenty-one, would be entitled to declare whether or not they desired to be British subjects. The man would have to be re-naturalized. If the children had been born in Canada and went abroad as minors and the father became naturalized in a foreign country, they would take the citizenship of that country, but on returning here they would be entitled, within a year after attaining their majority, to elect whether they would be British subjects or not.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext: And if they do not elect they remain citizens of the foreign country?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext: Section 11 says that the wife of a British subject shall be deemed to be a British subject and the wife of an alien shall be deemed to be an alien. But subsection (a) provides that the wife of an alien may be naturalized "in like manner and with the same effect as if she were a femme sole." Is there any provision whereby the wife of a naturalized British subject applies personally for naturalization?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext: Later on there is.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext: I ask the question for the reason that when the Franchise Bill was under discussion in this House it was suggested that the wife should have personal naturalization in order to be entitled to vote.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext: Section 12 deals with the subject.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext: That applies only to widows.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext: It provides that a woman who, having been a British subject, " has by or in consequence of her marriage become an alien, shall not, by reason only of the death of her husband or the dissolution of her marriage, cease to be an alien."

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext: That is only as regards widows.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext: And further, "a woman who, having been an alien, has by or in consequence of her marriage become a British subject, shall not, by reason only^ of the death of her husband or the dissolution of her marriage, cease to be a British subject."

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext: It has already been suggested that to exercise the franchise a woman must be personally naturalized, and-not only be a British subject by reason of the fact that she is the wife of a naturalized citizen.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext: Under this Act it is most clear that the wife of a British subject, wherever she came from, shall be deemed to be a British subject, and that the wife of an alien shall be an alien. The declaration is quite plain. Even if a woman is Canadian-born, she is an alien if she is the wife of an alien.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext: According to my hon. friend the wife of a naturalized British subject shall be entitled to vote as well a3 heT husband under any franchise law?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext: There is no doubt about that.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext: If a young woman who is a Canadian citizen should marry an alien who is not naturalized, would she lose heT Canadian citizenship?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext: Yes, under section 11 she would be an alien. The law of all civilized lands is that the nationality of the wife is that of the husband, except in special cases provided for here.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext: The principle, then, is laid down, that for no purpose whatever shall there be a husband of one nationality and a wife of another.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext:

On section 18-capacity of an alien as to property; real estate may be held by aliens:

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext: I am strongly of the impression that aliens have no right to hold properly in this country, and I would not permit them to hold property until they are naturalized. I think it is time that we adopted some such policy as that. It has partly been adopted' under our homestead laws. Many aliens in this country prior to the war held land in Canada without becoming British subjects; in fact, held everything that a British subject could hold. They held on so well that they did not care for Canadian citizenship, did not need it, did not value it and preferred ,to hold the citizenship of the foreign country from which they came. I do not know that we will ever have another great war; I hope not, but it seems to me that it is time for the general advantage of Canada that, when we are dealing with the alien, we should prevent him from getting title to any land until he completes his citizenship and puts himself on the same basis as any other British or Canadian subject. While this may not be germane to the present Act, I cannot refrain from expressing the view that I have long held that we should not allow property, especially land, in this country to be held by aliens.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext:
I do not quite accept the view of my hon. friend from North Perth (Mr. Morphy) in regard to that matter. I think we are in a better position as we are [(Mr. Bureau.]
now by restricting our citizenship, not by enlarging it. I would not agree to the proposal to restrict the ownership of real estate to our citizens. We have been trying to induce capital to come into this country. The more foreign capital we get in the better, but if we insist that the property of the country shall be owned by citizens only we will greatly curtail the amount of capital coming in. Remember, that when the alien holds property we are in the best possible position; in case of war we can deal most expeditiously with his property, far more so than we can with the property of a British subject. The trouble we have experienced in the past results from the fact that we had granted certificates of naturalization too freely. The object of the Bill is that they shall be granted less freely and more carefully so that a man applying for naturalization shall be thoroughly approved before he shares the benefits of British citizenship.
I know that in many states of 4 p.m. the United States up to thirty years ago restrictions were put upon the rights of aliens to hold real estate. Up to 1890 the state of New York did not permit it hut a great deal of property there was owned by residents of Great Britain and held by various trust companies in New York city for them. That system did not work out well; the law was repealed in New York state and I think it has been repealed in almost every state across the line. Great Britain has always thrown the door wide open to investments in this country. She can control investments far easier than she can individual citizens and that is the policy which has been adopted in pretty nearly every country in the world. I think it is a good policy and I "would not favour exchanging it for the policies proposed by my hon. friend.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext: You would want the majority of the directors of a company to be British subjects.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext: The question is a big one and there are arguments to be advanced on both sides.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext:
My recollection goes
back to the beginning of the war when some of the boldest aliens were those who were permitted to hold property.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext: That property has all been seized.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext:
There are a great many things that can be done with property before you can seize it and there were a great

many alien property holders in the United States who were entirely opposed to that country going to war. With regard to extending the time for naturalization, I have long held the other view and I hold it still. I would make the time shorter and I would compel a man to be a citizen within a shorter period of time than five years, say, two or three years. This Parliament extends the time from three to five years. That provision of the law can be abused and I have always felt that it has been abused. If you compel a man to become a citizen and thus give him the right to hold property sooner than he otherwise would be able to he would be more likely to respect and obey the laws that other citizens have to obey. The reasoning that the longer you give an alien to become a citizen the better, does not work out in the way that those who advance the argument believe i't does. I know hundreds of persons in this country who have never taken out citizenship papers because they did not think they needed to. They were Amstrians, or they belonged to other nationalities, and 'they were never interfered with. They had their freedom in the country just the same as British subjects had and sneered at the citizenship of Canada. They held property under the same conditions as Canadians and British subjects held it. I would compel a man 'to be a citizen of Canada, or at least 'make him declare has intention of becoming a citizen within a year, and I would insist that he become a citizen within two years and that he should become a citizen before being allowed to hold real estate. The Solicitor General refers to the question of capital coming in. Capital will come in if the country offers advantages. Capital generally comes into the country in joint stock companies anyway, and in that regard the principle of nationality does not prevail. I remember not very long ago that some Americans were surrendering their citizenship to go and live in England. The day may come when they may feel like doing that in regard to Canada. They have their eye on the natural resources of Canada, resources that in my opinion should go to the citizens of Canada. I do not think that an American citizen or any other foreign citizen has any right to pre-empt or take over our valuable coal and iron mines unless he becomes a citizen of Canada. It may be as 'the Solicitor General has said that they have recently changed their laws in regard to the holding of real estate in the United States, but they have changed them after the public domain has been frittered away and everything taken out of it. Let us preserve for Canada and'for Canadians and British subjects the natural resources of this country, the like of which do not exist anywhere else in the world, and which must be developed to help out the nationalization of our railways. Let our forest, mineral, and agricultural wealth be devoted by the people of Canada to the purposes of Canada and handed over to our highways of commerce. The nationalization of our railways compels it. Notwithstanding what the Minister of the Interior said about the nationalization of all the splendid resources we have in this country, whether that day will come soon or late I do not know, but it seems to me that with the incubus of debt that we have before us we should throw everything as far as possible into the hands of our own people and every resource we have should be developed along national lines, kept free from the influence of the exploiter; the man who is called a coal baron who comes in and takes these great resources and develops 'them for nobody but himself. The national wealth should be conserved for the nation.

On section 23-proof of qualification:

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext:
This section provides
that the applicant shall appear before the court in person. Suppose there is no opposition to his application?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext:
This clause is taken
from our Naturalization Act passed in 1914 and adopted from the English Act. Formerly, if there was no opposition to the granting of the application at the sitting of the court, then the judge granted the certificate; now a man must appear before

the court, and the qualification is put in that he must be familiar with French or English. For that reason he must appear to satisfy the judge; if he does not take enough interest in the matter to appear, then I do not think the judge could make a favourable report. Personal attendance is one of the things that I look upon as very necessary. In Ontario courts I have seen as many as thirty or forty applications dealt with in half an hour-applications from men whose names you could not pronounce, who could not speak or write English, and who were not there themselves. The court sits for two days, and at the end of two days these men are British subjects, the certificates being granted without any attempt at inquiry, simply on the sworn statements made by the applicants before a magistrate. It is to avoid procedure of that kind that the new method is proposed and the attendance of the applicant before the court required so that the judge may see the man, inquire as to his knowledge of English or French, and pass upon it.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext: What facilities are afforded to those who desire to oppose applications for naturalization certificates? A man who lives two hundred miles away from the court-house may not know that an application is being made for naturalization by a person whose application he wishes to oppose.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext: I do not know, except the general notice that is given and the general knowledge one is supposed to have of what takes place in connection with judicial proceedings. A man who is interested can take some step to obtain information in the matter; if he is very anxious to take action he can make application from time to time to the clerk of the court for lists of those who are desirous of obtaining naturalization. If you took steps to provide that all the people should have actual notice of every application, you would reduce the law to a condition in which it would be impossible to enforce it.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext: I do not mean that. Why should notice not be posted also in the post office in each locality, so that when people go to get their mail they would know that applications for naturalization were being made by certain persons, and could take steps to oppose them if they wished to do so? There is provision for opposition of these applications, but there is no means of conveying the knowledge that the applications are being made.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext: A man who desires to oppose an application can obtain from the clerk of the court the names of the applicants. If he is really zealous in the matter he can certainly, without very much trouble, obtain the information which he desires. It would be a good deal of trouble to have these notices posted up in the various post offices.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext:
It may be very important, for business purposes or for inheritance purposes, that a man who, we will say, is very ill, should get his naturalization certificate. He cannot appear in court; yet his estate may go to the wrong persons on account of this provision. I admit that in certain cases the applicant should appear before the court to answer any objection that may be made in connection with his application. In such cases the judge, if he is not satisfied as to the qualifications of the applicant, may recommend that the certificate do not issue. I understand that when the issuance of the certificate is not recommended, the Secretary of State has no power to issue it; he has power only to refuse to issue a certificate which is recommended. But why require the personal attendance of the applicant when notice of his application has been duly posted and everybody has had an opportunity of finding out whether or not he is properly qualified ? Let us provide that if there is any doubt as to the man's ability to read or write, the tribunal shall have the right to require his attendance before the court; but let us not say that in every case the applicant must attend in person. The remarks of my hon. friend (Mr. H. A. Mackie) suggest the case of those who live hundreds of miles away from the place where the court sits, and who, if it was possible at all for them to attend, would be put to great trouble and expense if they did so.
Sometimes it is practically an impossibility,-they have to travel through country where no roads are open, and the distances are so great that they have to camp on the way to and from the court. Let us say that the judge shall have power to summon any man to appear before him before he makes any recommendation, but take away this kind of drastic provision that in every case a man must appear. I do not think under the section as now drafted we would be any better protected, and, on the other hand, it would work a hardship on the applicants.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext:
The application is not
to a judge in court; it is to a judge. I real-

ize though that in practice it would work out probably in nine cases out of ten that the application would be to a judge sitting in court. No matter whether in court or not, it is a judge who must make the inquiry, and I cannot conceive that any judge in this country would find it so inconvenient to attend a sick applicant that he would not go to his house and make the inquiry there.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext:
The application has got
to be delivered at the office of the clerk.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext: If a judge of that kind is to be found in Canada, he ought to be disciplined by authorities which are above judges, namely, this Parliament. Judges are appointed and courts sit for the convenience of the people. There has been abuse in regard to naturalization. I do not know how these matters are attended to in other parts of the Dominion, but I know that in the province where I live there has been abuse, and I think it is of the utmost importance that applicants should appear personally. Where I live we have naturalized scores of men who cannot speak a word of English, and do not want to, and who only became naturalized, I suppose, to get a vote, which they say is of value to them.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext:
What nationality were
those men, Poles?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext: They come from southern Europe. I do not want to refer to them more particularly as some of them are my friends. It is to stop that practice that this provision is inserted. If the man is anxious to become a British citizen, he will have to put up with the little inconveniences of travelling a mile or two. If he has no anxiety on the subject, let him stay at home. I do not think the idea of this Act is to extend citizenship to any one by any means; it is to restrict it.

The section says that the application shall be made to the judge. I gather from that that it shall be addressed to the judge, because the other section says the application shall be made at the office of the clerk or other proper officer of the
court during office hours. It is not before the judge that the hearing takes place, it is before the court; and it is not the judge that decides, but the court. Therefore the judge must be in banco. The only place where the word "judge" is used is in section 20, from which I would infer that the petition instead of to the court is to the judge; but after that the court is acting all the way through, and I do not think the court would move to the hospital.

I think the objection raised by the hon. member for Edmonton is well taken. It is very easy to have a subsection providing that notice should be sent to the applicant. I have no doubt that that is the intention. I think there should be provision for having notice served upon the applicant or sent to him by registered mail. Section agreed to.
On section 24-Order of naturalization.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext:
Before this clause carries, I would like to bring before the Committee a case from my own constituency. It is that of a man who has been a resident there for some twenty-two years, and about eighteen or twenty years ago he went before a magistrate, then the mayor of the town, and became, as he thought, naturalized,-in fact, he really made an application for naturalization. He went to another man who was then representative of the district in the Conservative interest, a responsible and respected gentleman known very well to my hon. friend from East Edmonton, Mr. J. W. Shera, who acted as his agent in making his application in court. For some reason or other it appears that the record of that application has been lost. The officials of the court think that, perhaps, owing to the subdividing of the judicial districts it may have been transferred to some other district in the province of Alberta. The man I have in mind has held the positions of councillor and trustee and is a very prominent citizen in that section of the country. He has always had a desire to be a Canadian citizen.
I can remember very well that in 1911 he was a very strong opponent of mine and a man of considerable influence; he was carried away by the fear that the reciprocity agreement might lead to annexation to the United States. When in the last election he tried to get a record of his naturalization, with the intention of opposing me again,- although, I must say, he is a good citizen -he found that he was not naturalized or could not get a duplicate copy of his naturalization certificate. He went before Mr. Justice Walsh and made application, and took with him ex-Mayor Langworthy, the man who had taken his application before. He made a sworn application to the judge, together with Mr. Shera, now customs collector in the city of Edmonton, who swore that he actually brought this man's certificate to court and paid tne fees. Mr. Justice Walsh recommended to the Secretary of State that a naturalization certificate should be issued. However, the department did not seem to be inclined to do so. About two months ago I had an interview 
with the Secretary of State and asked him if anything could be done.
Nothing has been done in the matter. Here you have a man who was a good citizen, a particularly active man in patriotic work, a large subscriber to Victory Bonds and who has every intention of being a good citizen, but who now, under this new Bill, may be compelled to wait for ten years longer before he can become a citizen. It is a hardship that this man should be placed in this position. He has been a resident of this country for some twenty-three years, and some provision should be made whereby in such a case, where the local judge is satisfied by sworn evidence that the man made application, he should be granted the rights of citizenship.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext:
I thank my hon. friend spoke to one about this case. I have forgotten the details now, but it is somewhat allied to cases that have come up for consideration during the war, namely, those of a very large number of men of alien enemy birth who were under the impression that they had been naturalized or made citizens, because for a very long time past they had been taking part in municipal and provincial elections and had been good citizens as far as we understand the ordinary meaning of the word, but who, it was found, had not actually been naturalized. The hon. member for Waterloo North (Mr. Euler) knows that in his constituency there were many cases of that kind. Two special Orders in Council were passed under the War Measures Act by which, in case of men of alien enemy birth who had been a long time in the country and who were under the impression that they were naturalized, the ordinary proceedings could be dispensed with and they could be naturalized. After the Orders in Council were passed, there were no applications at all for a while, but finally one came in and, as there was something technically wrong in his application, it was sent back to the judge, and when it came back corrected, he was granted naturalization. Then a very long list came in, about ninety-two or ninety-four, and although I confess I have a great deal of sympathy with men who have been a long time in the country and who have been peaceable people, good neighbours and citizens, at that particular time we had reached a point in the war when public feeling was very bitter-and probably rightly so-against everything German. It was at the time of the great German push

and when all sorts of atrocities were perpetrated by the Germans, and there was a strong feeling throughout the country that we should go slow about naturalizing Germans even if they had been a long time in the country. The Council, after considering the matter very carefully, decided that at that time they would not naturalize any more under the ordinary Act, and the matter drifted along until the fall. I pointed out that if they were not going to naturalize any more people of this kind the Orders in 'Council should be repealed, and they were repealed before this House met. Now the question is in abeyance, and men who are in that position and who wish to become naturalized can be dealt with under the provisions of the Naturalization Bill which the Solicitor General has before the House. The question whether we should naturalize men of alien enemy birth now is, after all, a matter of some policy. My hon. friend (Mr. W. H. White) raised a question whether the Secretary of State should be the judge whether a certificate should be finally issued when the judge had pronounced. During the past three or four years the judges of the courts have taken different views of this matter. The Chief Justice of Ontario laid down the principle that it was absolutely wrong and illegal to naturalize any man of alien enemy birth, and I think he did not pass such applications. Some judges in other provinces passed a very large number of them, and some of them, under the powers of the old Act, which ran concurrently with this Act, naturalized, I think, two or three hundred Germans and Austrians when that was within the power of the court under the three-year system. Of course, under the five-year system, such men would have to apply to the Secretary of State.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext: Do men who hail from alien enemy countries and who are within one year of getting patents to their homesteads, now have to wait for ten years before they can get patents?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext:
Under the provisions of the Dominion Lands Act I think that is right. I discussed it with the Minister of the Interior since the question was brought up by the hon. member for Victoria, Alberta (Mr. W. H. White), last week. Personally, I see no reason for continuing that condition in the Dominion Lands Act, but officials of the Department of the Interior are considering that point now. I do not know what the conclusion will be regarding
the matter, but I assume there will be no difficulty in amending the Dominion Lands Act so as to remove that restriction on the issue of patents owing to lack of naturalization. At the present time I understand the provision is that patents shall not be issued to those that are not British subjects by birth or naturalization. If that restriction is removed -and, in my judgment, it ought to be removed-that will overcome the difficulty. Whether it is necessary to do it now, or whether it could be done at the fall session, is another matter. 1 am expressing only my view, because the officers of the Department of the Interior are going to make a report on the matter.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext: If it be the case that men who should have received their homestead patents but for the declaration of war, must now wait for ten years, that is nothing but a shame. Within the last week, I have brought to the attention of the Government the fact that 150,000 aliens want to leave this country and1 have asked the Government to give them passports. The Government claim that because they are not British subjects, they cannot give them passports. If the Government are not willing to grant these men homestead patents and so keep them in the country, and want, in addition, to keep them in abeyance for ten years, why not deport these men? The Government cannot blow hot and cold. The Government must either make them citizens or make the laws reasonable, or allow these men to get out.

I think that in the case cited by my hon. friend (Mr. White), proof could be established under that section.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext: The trouble was they could not find the record. Mr. Shera swore he had taken this application to court and paid the fees, and the other man swore that the application was made before him. They satisfied Mr. Justice Walsh that the man was really naturalized, but for some reason or other there was no record of it. The application was made eighteen years ago.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext:
We have determined the procedure whereby a man shall obtain a recommendation to become a British citizen. We compel him to make application addressed to a judge, to file his papers, and to have his name posted for three months in the office of the clerk of the court. After all that has been done, we compel him to go personally before the court, and the court has to issue a certificate, if it thinks proper that the man is fit . to become naturalized. After the man has been before that tribunal where everybody had a chance to be heard, he is still subject' to the will of another man called the Secretary of State. That there may be no ambiguity about it the section provides that:	"The Secretary of State of Canada
may thereupon in his absolute discretion issue a certificate." I think that is giving too much power to any one man. We have not yet reached the millennium. In spite of all the good people who are in the Government, in spite of all their efforts to uplift the people, in spite of all their restrictions of evil and evil dispositions, in spite of their control of everything that is bad, we have not yet reached the point where I would trust this power in the hands of one man, especially when that man is a politician of one political party, I do not care whether it is Unionist, Tory, Nationalist, Grit or any other party that may be formed hereafter. We have seen things done by the powers-that-be that they would never have dared to do under different circumstances. Those circumstances may repeat themselves, because history repeats itself. We have had the War-time Elections Act, for instance. If any man had suggested before 1917 the possibility of the things being perpetrated under that Act which actually have been perpetrated, no one would have listened to him; everybody would have said " Impossible." Therefore, after the judge sitting as a court has heard all the evidence and passed upon the qualifications of a man for Canadian citizenship, after he has recommended that the applicant is a fit and proper person, why should we give the Secretary of State power to refuse or withhold the certificate on an ex parte judgment, which may be based upon the recommendation of a political

friend or a political foe? I say there is a tinge of immorality in that section, and it should not be put on the statute books.
I presume the Solicitor General will justify its being there by saying that it has been the law since 1914, but in 1914 we did not know of the political and administrative crimes that have since been perpetrated in the name of the war. If the people of Canada have reached the point where they have no more confidence in the judiciary of this country, I doubt whether they have any greater confidence in a member of a political party. I think that the judgment of the president of the tribunal before whom the application is made ought to be final. We have just passed a section giving the Secretary of State power to cancel a certificate of naturalization, and I certainly do not want to give him the right to refuse to issue a certificate after all the requirements of -the law have been complied with, and after the judge has recommended that a certificate be issued. The Secretary of State does not hear the case or see the man; he simply gives an ex parte judgment. My hon. friend from Victoria (Mr. W. H. White) has just submitted an instance in which a judge passed qpon a case and hi? recommendation was dishonoured I think I can use that expression-by the Secretary of State. Now, who is better able than the judge to pronounce upon these matters? He lives in the community where the applicant seeks naturalization and is acquainted with all the circumstances, being in an eminently advantageous position to secure the most reliable information about the man and his bona fides. I cannot adequately qualify this clause. To say the least, it is most arbitrary. Why is this right reserved to the Secretary of State? No ordinary man can come to any other conclusion than that this power is retained in the Secretary of State to be used as a club in political exigencies and as a means of distinguishing between friend and-well, I will not say. foe; at all events, it seems palpable that it will be used to differentiate between political friends and adversaries when applications are made for naturalization. I shall move that this clause be struck out of the Bill.

I support the objection taken by the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) to this section, for the reasons he has advanced, although I may qualify his remarks 'to this extent, that I do not believe that the present Secretary of State nor any Secretary of State, for that matter, would use this power for political
purposes. The fact remains, however, that it would be a source of temptation, and for that reason it is objectionable. There is a vital objection to the clause in so far as the revision of the judge's decision is concerned. The section provides that upon the applicant taking and subscribing the oath of allegiance the clerk shall deliver the certificate to him. Now, if the Secretary of State is to reconsider the judgment of the court, it will involve a considerable amount of travelling on the part of the applicant, in many instances, distances of even a thousand miles, to a court. It will necessitate two tjips of the applicant, and it is absolutely unreasonable and altogether too expensive, having regard to the distances that must he travelled, in our province at any rate. I do not see any reason for the clause, and I heartily support the objection of the hon, member for Three Rivers.

In answer to my hon. friend's criticism, all I have to say is that nationality and citizenship are questions which should come within the authority of the Parliament and Government of the country, And if they have at any time in the ' past been delegated to the judges, that in my judgment was an improper delegation of the rights of Parliament. Parliament should control the nationality of citizens and the question of their franchise. It is just as able to do so as the judges, if indeed it is not better able. It is true that this section vests in the Secretary of State an absolute discretion. The language is absolute in form, but in reality it is just a judicial discretion to be exercised as that of a judge would be, because it must be exercised in accordance with the plain meaning and intent of the Act. Those of us who happen to be members of the Bar well know that wills, trusts, settlements, etc., where trustees are appointed, case after case comes up in which absolute discretion to do this, that, and the other thing, is granted the trustee. " Absolute and unfettered discretion " is a commonly used expression, which the courts interpret to be discretion that must be reasonably exercised in accordance with the clear meaning of the document. So it is with an Act of Parliament. Under this section, the Secretary of State cannot act upon any mere whim, fancy, or caprice of his own; he is bound to act in accordance with the meaning of the Act. He is not by any means unaccountable or irresponsible. As a matter of fact, he is far more accountable and responsible than is any judge in the Dominion, because, if he does not act rea-

sonably,-if his action in granting or refusing a certificate is at variance with plain reason, or if he acts without good faith or goes beyond the letter of the law, he will be amenable to this Parliament at the very first session after his action is called into question. This is the high court of appeal in such a case as that which my hon. friend from Victoria (Mr. W. H. White) brought up to-day. Every case in which a wrong is done or is charged can be ventilated here and punishment meted out if the House sees fit. But you cannot take any action of that kind in respect of a judge. The judge in this case is not asked to decide. He is merely asked to inquire and report. It is the minister of the Crown who decides, and the minister is responsible to his own colleagues in the first instance and, next, to this Parliament. I do not know of any greater safeguard that can be employed. My hon. friend suggested that the reply could be made that this had been the custom for the last five years. It has been the law of the land for the last five years, and I will say that for twenty or twenty-five years preceding that, these certificates were granted by the judges. I want to impress this upon the Committee that, knowing as I do the method which was adopted in Ontario during those twenty-five or thirty years in the granting of these certificates, the whole practice became a joke and a by-word. It is to overcome that defect that we are bringing the matter within the province of the responsible minister, who can be held accountable for what he does. I have seen in the city of Toronto long lists of names of men who had been granted certificates at a single court and who never appeared in court,-cases in regard to which little or no inquiry had been made and to which absolutely no consideration had been given.
I have known of justices of the peace in Ontario going through the foreign quarters of a city and, at two dollars apiece, drawing, preparing and swearing affidavits, and filing them in court; and I do not believe that the poor applicants knew actually what they were doing. Eventually, however, they got the certificates, and afterwards voted. What is the procedure? At the opening of the court-I am referring to the larger cities-the clerk reads the list of applicants iwith unpronounceable names who want to become citizens of Canada, and now, if this law goes through, of the British Empire. These documents are filed and no one pays any attention to them. The court adjourns the next day, or a day 
or two after, and if no objection is taken before adjournment the applicant becomes a British subject. There is no inquiry as to his intelligence or his general fitness of character, moral or otherwise, and nothing is asked as to his education. They know absolutely nothing about the matter, but the judge grants the certificate, as he is permitted to do under the former law. Is it not fair and better, as is suggested in the present Bill, that an inquiry shall be made and that the man shall be required to attend and ibiing proof, and -that he shall be familiar with English or French? These questions will be ascertained deliberately by the court. There must be an investigation -and a thorough inquiry and the court will report to the Secretary of State, who then will have a discretion to act or not to act. Whichever way he exercises his discretion, he is responsible to Parliament, which can condemn him if he -has done wrong. I cannot suggest a better mode or one that will yield more satisfactory results from every point of view than the one laid down in the Bill. It is the law in England and has been so for many years, and we will do very well to adopt it in this country.

Is it not a fact that the applicant will have to go home and wait until the Secretary of State has decided whether naturalization papers will be granted or not, and must then come back and take the oath before the clerk of the court? Is it not true that he must go back to the court and fake the oath before the clerk of the court? If that is the case I submit that it is an absolutely unreasonable thing with the great distances that we have in this country.
I think that might be remedied because it does not say that he must take the oath before the court.

It says:
Upon the applicant taking- and subscribing the oath of allegiance the clerk shall deliver the certificate to the applicant.

The certificate might be presented to the clerk of the court as is usually done in numberless cases but that does not mean that the applicant .must go before the clerk of the court. I have no objection to embodying that in the clause because it would not be reasonable to ask a man to go before the court again.

My hon. friend claims that Parliament should control naturalization. We certainly do. We are enacting a law prescribing how a man shall go about it to become naturalized. Who is going

to witness that these conditions shall be complied with? The Solicitor General says that the court will report favourably if an applicant is a fit person to become a British subject and that otherwise the court does not so report. But, this clause says that the Secretary of State shall have "absolute discretion" to issue a certificate of naturalization. That is what I object to and I move that the clause be amended as follows:
By striking out the word1 "may" in the first line of section 25 and substituting the word " shall " and by striking out, at the beginning of the second line thereof, the words " in his absolute discretion."	,
It will then read:
The Secretary of State of Canada shall thereupon issue a certificate of naturalization.
My objection to that is that the law is now five years old and it has caused no wrong, injury, or inconvenience.
A case has been mentioned.

A case has been mentioned, it is true, but the evidence goes to show that it only requires the proof of an act that was done some years ago and that,
I have no doubt, could be established. But this has been our law for five years.
Section 25 is marked " new " is it not?

That is a mistake in the printing. The only change in this section is that the old section provided for a duplicate certificate, one to he kept by the court and the other to be given to the applicant. This provides for one certificate. The provision with regard to " absolute discretion " was in the Act of 1914. This is the system that has been adopted by Great Britain, although that would not mean that we should adopt it, and it is a system that has been in force here for the last five years.
It gives us everything we are entitled to, it protects every applicant and I would not like to consent to a change in the clause.

Upon what is the Secretary of State to exercise his discretion? Discretion is exercised by a judge in regard to the question of costs in a lawsuit.
If he finds that there is some blame on both sides, while he gives his decision in one way, yet there is not enough justification for the decision to allow costs and he exercises his discretion in that way. Under this section, a judge, we will say, sitting in

Toronto, hears an application and after hearing all the evidence he decides that the man is entitled to a certificate of naturalization. He sends his certificate to the Secretary of State at Ottawa. There is to be no hearing before the Secretary of State. There is nobody to appear before him; he is to have nothing before him but the decision reached by the judge. On what is he going to exercise his discretion? Is he to go on what is reported to him by the proper tribunal and on that is he to base his discretion? I always understood that discretion is exercised on some fact that the party exercising the discretion has the privilege of weighing in his mind. There is nothing before him other than the judgment of the court which says that the man is entitled to the certificate. I would like to understand- from the Solicitor General what material is submitted to the Secretary of State on which he is to exercise his discretion.

I do not assume that there is going to be merely the bare, bald report that this man is entitled to a certificate. I assume that the judge will produce an intelligent report stating the circumstances and reasons in each particular case. Judges are very human like other people and [DOT] there is no uniformity in the minds of judges throughout the country.
I thought that justice was an attribute of divinity.
Justice is but judges are not.
How much superior is the Secretary of State?
There is one central board which is responsible to this Parliament in the case of the Secretary of State and a judge is not responsible.
He is responsible.
No, he is not unless you impeach him and he cannot be impeached for a wrong judgment.
How are we going to deal with the Secretary of State?
You can charge the Secretary of State before this House upon any question you like.
And you will whitewash him.
You can hold him to the strictest account.
And you will whitewash him.
You should not assume so much as that. Some men will assume anything that is not fair.
I am basing my statements on past experience.

If my hon. friend is going to assume wrong-doing in the administration of the Act by one of the responsible ministers of the Crown, he is going to bring into disrepute the whole Government in its administration of the Act.
It cannot be worse than it is now.
There is no warrant for any insinuation of that kind.
Certainly there is.

My hon. friend (Mr. McKenzie) asks: How is he going to form his discretion? He is going to have a report showing on certain facts that a certain man is entitled to a certificate or he is going to have certain other facts in another judgment showing that a man is not entitled to a certificate. The Secretary of State will inquire into' these things. He will try to administer the statute in accordance with its provisions and he will exercise his discretion accordingly. If he has the complete report of a judge before him stating that a man is entitled to a certificate, there is no chance of exercising a discretion in a case of that kind, but a judge might hold that a man was entitled to his certificate without the complete evidence before him. Something might transpire to change the situation in the interval between the making of the report and the granting of the certificate.
It would be cancelled if it were not properly granted.
It is not the easiest thing in the world to cancel a certificate of naturalization after it has been once granted.
Does my hon. friend argue that the Secretary of State is going to read the evidence in all the cases of naturalization?
No; he is going to read the report.
In each case?
Yes.
He will be kept busy.
Oh, no.

The law, as provided by section 24, is this:
If the court decides-
After a full hearing.
If the court decides that the alien is a fit and proper person to be naturalized and possesses the required qualifications, a certified: copy of such decision shall be transmitted by the clerk of the court to the Secretary of State of Canada together with the application and such other papers, documents and reports as may be required iby any regulation made hereunder. (Naturalization Act, 19:14.)
With all due respect for my good friend the Solicitor General, I see nothing there about the decision of the judge. If he finds that an applicant is a fit and proper person to be naturalized he so decides and he sends the certificate to the Secretary of State. The Secretary of State has to reverse him or grant the certificate. That is all the latitude that he has; he has to reverse him without hearing a word of evidence and he has to reverse the decision of the judge who saw the man and heard all the evidence.

My objection to the section is that it implies a star chamber method of dealing with naturalization. It does not seem to imply that an appeal is to be granted. If the decision of the Secretary of State were subject to appeal-
There is an appeal here.

There might be an opportunity for arguing the case and presenting both sides, as is done in the law courts, but there is no provision for a hearing. The Secretary of State seems to be authorized to go behind closed doors, take up the decision of the judge and reverse it. That is altogether against the principles of British law and British fair play. If my hon. friend wants to organize a court of appeal and make the Secretary of State the judge of that court, let him make provision for that and let both sides be properly heard before any decision is given. That is my chief objection to this section, and I shall vote for the amendment.

It seems to me that the section is all right. There may be in the hands of the Secretary of State, of the chief of Dominion Police, or of some department of the Government, information concerning the character, disposition, criminal tendency or otherwise of an alien which, had it been placed before the judge who adjudicated upon the application, would have caused the judge to submit an entirely different report. Consequently, as a safeguard this section is necessary.
The Secretary of State has power of revocation.

That is also true, but an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure. The power of revocation might not be exercised until something happened that was inimical to the best interests of the country. I do not like the word "thereupon" in the section. What does it mean? If it relates to the preceding section only, I can understand it; but if it does, I think the section should read "may, upon compliance with the requirements of the last preceding section."
Or, "On receipt of the report and evidence referred to in the last section."

From my own experience I can speak in the highest terms of the provisions embodied in sections 24 and 25. I am not the only lawyer who is here from Nova Scotia; I am not very much of a lawyer, anyway. But I have been in politics for quite a number of years-and I am going to be frank and candid with this Committee. For some years the lawyer who was running an election in Nova Scotia was always prepared to naturalize a foreigner for the sake of getting his vote; and I was a sinner in that respect as well as the rest of them. If this section does away with some of that, then let us have it. I have known Huns, Austrians, Hungarians, and all the rest, to go into the court-house at Sydney, though they had not been long enough in the country to know east from west, and swear that they had been here three, four, or five years, just for the sake of getting clear of the fees that a lawyer who was not in politics would likely charge them. Now, if the Solicitor General, by this section, is doing away with that, he is doing well.

Mr. Chairman, I think that under the circumstances the hon. gentleman (Mr. Butts) should resign.
Amendment (Mr. Bureau) negatived on division; yeas, 23; nays, 43.
Does the minister intend to amend section 25 so as to avoid the necessity of a second trip on the part of the applicant?

Would it not be well that this be transmitted so that there may be a record that he has subscribed ? The granting of a certificate by the Secretary of State is no evidence that the applicant has complied with all that is required of him to become a British subject.
He cannot get the cerifi-cate until he has taken his oath.

Would it not be well for the clerk himself to take that oath. As a rule clerks are commissioners, but I think in this case the clerk should be named, as it is better that he should take the oath when the man comes for his certificate.

That is the objection on the part of the hon. member for Edmonton, that the applicant is going to have to make two long trips, one to prove his case, and another when he comes back for his certificate. It is to avoid the second journey that we are going to permit him to take the oath before a justice of the peace at his own home or to go to court, as he sees fit.
The certificate has got to be delivered by the clerk to the individual, has it ?
Yes.
Why not swear him when it is delivered ?
Is the Secretary of State required to report on the granting or refusal of these certificates?
I have not considered that point.
It would be important for Parliament to know if the Secretary of State did refuse those applications.
I suppose a member can always ask the question and get returns.

Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended, agreed to.
On section 32-Saving for letters of denization:
I would like to have an explanation about that.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman wants an explanation I must remind him that he should rise in his place and address the Chair.

I have not time, because the clauses are passed quicker than a man

can rise, even, if he had a spring to push him up.

Letters of denization are special privileges granted by a sovereign state for the residence of its nationals in other lands without prejudice to their citizenship. They are never granted in this country,-at least, I have never heard of such a thing.
That is because we are not a sovereign state.

Section agreed to.
On section 33-Definitions-British subject; alien; certificates of naturalization; disability; territorial waters; Secretary of State:
Would not that be right?
Is an inhabitant of that territory a naturalized British subject?
No; but because hi3 country is annexed he is a British subject.
Is not that an innovation?

I suppose it has been the law since there Was any law, that in case of annexation by conquest the people of the annexed state acquire the nationality of the conqueror. The particular words to which my hon. friend refers were put in the Imperial Act of 1918, I think, in view of the peace treaty, and I believe in South Africa some people will become British subjects who were formerly German subjects.
Mr. W. H. W1H1ITE: I understand that Bukowina and Galicia are now claimed as Polish territory. The Poles not being considered alien enemies, what status would the people coming from Polish Austria have?

Subsection (4) (B) of section 8 provides that no alien enemy shall be naturalized for a period of ten years after the waT, but that that provision shall not apply to members of a race or community known to be opposed to the enemy governments. That was inserted! in the Imperial Act, and is followed in our Act, by reason of the fact that the Czecho-Slo-vaks, the Armenians, and people in Poland were, it is said, absolutely opposed to the Central Powers in the recent war. It is not intended to deprive these people of their right to naturalization unless they were actually alien enemies. For that reason that subsection has been inserted in section 8.
In the opinion of the Solicitor General, would Poles coming from Polish Austria be considered as alien enemies?
I cann t tell that. That part of the law would have to be very carefully administered,

Clause 20 says that the application shall be made, not to a court, but to a judge, and clause 23 says that the applicant shall produce his proof to the court. Therefore, some definition of the word "court" should be inserted in clause 33, so that the proof may, if so desired, be produced before a judge sitting in Chambers.

If you had it simply:
The word " court " shall mean the court or a judge.
That is all that you require. There is no question in the world about that.

I really do not think any difficulty would arise if you do not

define the word. The two expressions are used "judge" and "court." They mean the same thing, and there would not be any conflict. The word "court" is not defined in the Imperial Act, and our language is the same.

Clause 20
reads:
An alien desiring to be naturalized shall apply for a decision establishing that he is qualified and fit to be naturalized under the provisions of this Act to any Judge of any Superior Court, or to any Judge of any Circuit, District or County Court, and in the Northwest Territories to such authorities or persons as the Governor in Council may prescribe.
Does that include the 1?ukon Territory?

Northwest Territories
would include the Yukon, I think.

No, the
Yukon is a distinct territory.
I am glad of that information. We can remedy that very readily by referring back to clause 20 and inserting the words " in the Yukon and " after the word " and " in the 32nd line.
That will be all right.

I will leave the other
section as it is.

My purpose is this.
Under clause 20 you can make your application to a judge of a Superior Court or of a county court, but you are told in clause 23 that it is only a court that can hear you. You can make your application all right to a judge sitting in chambers or anywhere else, but when you come to a hearing you are told that your hearing will be before a court. In some parts of Canada a court may sit only once or twice a year, while a judge may be there quite frequently, and the man should be permitted to go before the judge when he is not sitting in court. My object is that the judge shall have power to hear the evidence as a judge just as he has power to receive the application.

I move to strike out
paragraph (f) and to replace the said paragraph by the following words:
The expression " court " shall means "court" or "judge" where used in this Act.

Amendment agreed to, and section, as amended, agreed to.
On section 20-application to court:
I beg to amend this section by adding after the word "and" in line 32, the words "in the Yukon and."
That is putting the Yukon in the same category as the Northwest Territories. There is a judge in the Yukon, and wherever there is a judge he should be the authority.
Under the section as amended, would it be possible for an alien to appear before the judge of the Yukon territorial court?
He would have no authority at all under the section as amended.
The Governor in Council will have to prescribe the judge of the Yukon territorial court?
Yes.
If the Yukon is left in the same category as the rest of the country the applicants would go before the judge in any event.	>

That has
been the custom there.

I see no necessity for naming the Yukon, and therefore I beg leave to withdraw my amendment.
Amendment withdrawn.

Section agreed to.
On section 7-revocation of certificate of naturalization:
I beg to move to amend this section by inserting after the word "State" in line 3 of page 4 of the Bill the words "of Canada."

In the absence of my hon. friend (Mr. McMaster), who is the grammatic critic of the House, I feel called upon to say that there is quite a conflict of opinion as to whether we should say "Secretary of State of Canada" or "Secretary of State for Canada." Personally I think the latter expression is the better.
I looked up the revised statutes, and they say "of Canada."

"Secretary of Canada
for the Colonies," "Secretary for India," "Secretary for War"-these are all good English expressions. The word "for" is always used in the Imperial statutes.

Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 8-effect of revocation of certificate of naturalization :

I beg to move that the words " of Canada " be inserted after the

word "state" in line 10 of page 6 of the Bill.

Amendment agreed to.
Section stands.
I see that the territory of Papua is included with the Commonwealth of Australia in the schedule. I understood that Australia was given only mandatory powers by the League of Nations.
I could not give any information on that. The Imperial Act includes Papua.
May I ask whether the Imperial Act of 1918, the provisions of which we are adopting in this Bill, was submitted to the Canadian Government for approval before being introduced in the British House?

I do not know whether it was submitted directly, but all the provisions of the Imperial Act were, discussed at the Imperial 'Conference in England prior to the introduction of the Bill in the British Parliament, and all these provisions were assented to by the representatives of the Dominions. Two or three other points which were discussed at the Conference were not embodied in the Imperial Act, and we have not embodied them in our Bill, but I understand there has been some discussion in England as to the necessity of further legislation covering these outstanding points. All the provisions of our Bill were tentatively agreed to by the representatives present at the Imperial Conference in London last year.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: When the Committee rose on Saturday we were still discussing section 41. Since then I have given consideration to the various suggestions made with reference to the phraseology of the section, and I think it would probably meet the object desired if we eliminated the expression "unmarried wife." Objection was taken on both sides of the House to this expression, and we might strike it out from the second line and insert after the word "forces," in the third line, the words "or of a woman awarded a pension under subsection 3 of section 33 of this Act."

I have been doing some thinking, too, in regard to the phrase. My objection to it was very clear on account of its being a contradiction in terms. A "wife" is a woman to whom a man is married, and ah "unmarried wife" is a woman to whom a man is married and not married. The phrase is ridiculous. I understood that no hon. gentleman objected to the money going to a person occupying that position. Therefore, how would "conjugal dependent" do?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Will my hon.. friend note the suggestion I have made to strike out the words "unmarried wife" and insert in the proper place the words I have mentioned. It seems to me that removes all objection to this section, and later I will move that we return to section 33.
Instead of the words "unmarried wife," would it not be better to use the expression "outcast?"
For that matter, we might call them "Gretna Green brides."

Mr. Chairman, let me say once for all to the minister, that I do not think that this Parliament should recognize any rights in a woman who is improperly living with a man. If a woman chooses to break away from the laws of society and of morals, the laws of God and of this land, and to live improperly with a man, she takes all the responsibilities upon herself, and the law cannot recognize any rights in her. She could go into court and claim wages if she could show that she was not living with the man for immoral purposes. The law would help her to get her wages, but nothing else. If it is true that in every court in Canada such a woman is absolutely tabooed and cannot for one moment claim assistance from the law, is the House of Commons of Canada going to recognize her as having rights? It is absolutely impossible; let us once for all disadvise our minds of any such ideas. If the man with whom such a woman lives can provide for her, and if under the law they are permitted to live together, that is not our business; but this House is bound to see to it that the moral law as regards marriage and the proper relations of the family in this country are maintained; this House must stand by the sanctity of the marriage tie. If a man has money he has a right to do what he pleases with it, so long as he does not interfere with any one else. It is sad that people should be living together in that way, and if we have no law at present to deal with such a

condition, I suppose it must continue. But in the interest of good morals, in the interests of the rising generation, in the interests of the people as a whole, it must be understood without the slightest equivocation that the Parliament of Canada will not recognize any family relation except that which is sanctioned by the moral and social law.

I repeat what I said on Saturday on this subject, and in so doing I entirely agree with the remarks just made by the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie). I do not understand why my hon. friend the President of the Privy Council should insist on such an immoral clause. Sir, it is an insult to every mother as well as to the entire womanhood of this fair country, to think that the Parliament of Canada will discard all recognized principles of decency because, forsooth, it happens that some soldiers are living irregularly with women. What is the foundation of law? The elements of Roman law which is the foundation of our civil law and of the common law of England, are based on two principles: honeste vivere, to live honestly; neminem laedere, to injure no one. What are you doing by this legislation? Are you inculcating in the people of the country the injunction that they must live honestly in order to have the protection of the law? Are you giving them to understand that in order to be within their right they must injure no one? No, Sir! You are prostituting the name of every mother and of every honest woman in crystallizing such a principle, and I say that no synod, no conference, no church, no decent organization in the country, knows of this clause, because the Government would have been bombarded with petitions and protests foT having introduced such legislation. I do not understand the mentality of my hon. friend. Why, this is putting a premium on immorality. Some people think that because it affects the returned soldiers we must give way. Well, is it the course to be pursued by a Government to give way to every whim and passion of people? The Government must resist and say, even to these returned soldiers: You are wrong; when you are right, we stand by you, but when you are wrong, we are against you and will resist. I would not be afraid to speak that way before a meeting of returned soldiers.

From the moral point
of view is the soldier who lives with a woman under those conditions not exactly in the same position as the woman, and
would my hon. friend go the length of refusing the man his pension on the same ground?

Because he went to the war, because he was at the front, because he exposed his life and came back maimed and a cripple he is entitled to his pension. But, he does not get his pension as a result of living with the woman. He gets it because he served his country at the front. The unfortunate woman, if she is in a position of dependence, while she is living an irregular life-and I have much human sympathy with her-under the law cannot claim the protection which she could claim if she were the honest and legal wife of that soldier. I think it is a most dangerous principle.
Mormonism.

It is asserting a most
dangerous principle when you sanction such a thing in this Bill because, forsooth, the returned soldiers ask for it. At the present time, in the Senate, there is a Bill amending the Criminal Code in such a way as to make the law more drastic than it ever has been just on account of the violation of this seventh commandment.
Sixth.

The sixth commandment. The legislation which is contained in this Bill violates first the law of God and second the law of every civilized country, the law of the land.
At six o'clock the Committee took recess.
After Recess.
The Committee resumed at eight o'clock.

Surely the President of the Council will reconsider clause 41 before he asks the Committee to adopt it in its present form. The amendment which he proposes is simply a play upon words; it does not strike at the root of the trouble. He suggests that the words " unmarried wife '' be struck out, and that after the word " forces " in the third line, the words " or of a woman awarded a pension under subsection 3 of section 33 of this Act " be inserted. Subsection 3 of section 33 reads as follows:
A woman who, although not married to the member of the forces, was living with him in Canada at the time he became a member of the forces and for a reasonable time previously thereto, and who, at such time, was publicly represented by him as his wife shall, for the purposes of this Act, be considered to have been his unmarried wife and may, in the oase

of his death and in the discretion of the commission, be awarded a pension equivalent to the pension she would have received had she been his legal widow.
I can only repeat what I have already said: This provision is placing a premium on immorality, and any law enacted by this Parliament, or by any Parliament in a Christian country, should be based upon morality. I mentioned the other day an article which was published in a Toronto magazine last week, which shows clearly that on this question of the relation between the sexes we are passing' through a revolution in Canada, and possibly in the world. But the standing of our nation so far has been very creditable and highly Christian, and tp crystallize into this Act any such principle as that which is proposed is to go against the Christian traditions of Canada-I should say, of the British Empire. But evidently there appears to be a lessening of the consideration for the matrimonial tie. The following few sentences from the magazine to which I have referred, will show how people have lost all sense of respectability now that the war is over. The article is published under the caption, " Three Million Husbands Wanted." I quote:
First, therefore, our divorce laws must be drastically revised and facilities granted for reasonably easy divorce on all reasonable ground. It should be possible to dissolve a loveless marriage without the necessity of making a public exhibition of "irregular incidents,"' in order to justify a divorce in the eyes of the law. This would at once set free a large number of men at present bound in marriage which is unhappy and sterile. These men would be free to remarry and very many of them would do so.
After all, would any one 'be the loser by the dissolution of all the existing definitely unhappy marriages? The old arguments are still heard urging that married misery must be perpetuated, and the parties to it held1 to their bond, for the various reasons familiar to most people. But are not these reasons more than a little old-fashioned, and do they not appeal to the past and passing generations more than to men and women of the rising generation, in whose hands rests the future?
The cancelling of existing unhappy marriages and permanent provision for easy dissolution of such marriages in the future, would help towards solving the problem of our surplus women. But far greater help would be given by making marriage altogether freer than it is at present.
There is only one valid, one legal, one moral relationship between the sexes, and it is that which takes place in some societies by the sacrament of marriage, and in others by the contract of marriage, because 'some claim that marriage is a sacrament; others that it is a contract. But

whether it is a sacrament or a contract, if it is admitted all over the civilized world, more especially in Christian countries, that it creates a spiritual tie between the parties concerned, how can we, in any legislation, go against that principle?
Why, our Criminal Code provides against such relations as are protected by this clause 41; and, as I stated this afternoon, a Bill has just been passed by the Senate, and will be before us in a day or two, whereby such illicit or irregular relations are branded as criminal, and may bring the parties to the bar,-not of public opinion only, but of the criminal courts as well; and yet by this clause we are putting a premium on these illegal and immoral relations. Matrimony should be encouraged by the State, because it is accepted by the Christian religion as the basis on which our social relations must inevitably rest. Even under the pagans of Rome there was a great distinction between concubinage and marriage. The state of concubinage created illegitimate children, and the concubine was never known as the uxor to the Roman law. There was not what the Roman law styles as the dignitas mariti on the part of the man who thus lived in a state of concubinage, and the issue were considered as liberi naturales-natural children; or liberi quasi sine patre nati-children who have no father. While the children born of a lawful marriage,-which even in Rome was dignified by a religious ceremony,-were considered as liberi qui patrem habent. It is so clear, that the sons of those immoral parents were and are inscribed in the registers as children born of unknown parents-they are not recognized by law.
According to our civil law-I do not know how it is in the other provinces-you cannot make a donation, for instance, to your concubine. There can be no contract validated by the fact that such relations have existed as between this woman and that man unless they marry. So the whole trend of our legislation is against such a mode of living. If I refer to the prayer book-and I think my hon. friend is more familiar with it possibly than I am-I find that it lays down the reasons for which matrimony was ordained: first, for the procreation of children; second, for the avoidance of sin; third, for mutual society and sympathy. According to all authors matrimony is the basis upon which civilized nations have built their social fabric, thus obeying the teachings of Christianity and, at the same time, furnishing themselves

with a sound position on which to treat the rights of succession to property and other cognate matters.
