Therefore, I say: You must not by this proposed legislation lessen the esteem in which the sanctity of marriage is held at present. This legislation is prejudicial to general morality, because the essence of marriage is spiritual. The Christian is moved-do not forget it, Mr. Chairman-by moral impulses and is guided by moral principles which are peculiar to himself. He cannot look on marriage, for example, from either the purely economic or the purely sensuous point of view, because piar-riage is an exalted state of society existing between two persons of different sexes. It is sanctified by God. I repeat, I cannot understand why my hon. friend, the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell), who is supposed to be austere in his views, should press this legislation. Perhaps he will tell me, "Well, the soldiers are clamouring tor it." Sir, I have the highest regard for the soldiers,-like them, I am human-and I do not believe that I am unduly austere or severe, but there must be a limit to our generous treatment of them. We must give liberally to the soldier what he is entitled to receive-and I claim, Sir, that the soldier in Canada, comparing his lot with the soldier who served in this war in the other countries, can say that he has been generously treated by a grateful nation, and I do not begrudge what the nation has done for him-but when it comes to infringing on the essential moral principle upon which our society is founded, and which draws its inspiration from Christianity, you must not go any further; it is time to say:	Halt! .Do not
listen to every passing whim and to every passion of the moment. Be stern.. Be firm. The Government must know how to resist when unjustifiable demands are made upon it. Will my hon. friend, in view of the gravity of this question, tell me if the Government has been requested or petitioned by any class of soldiers to enact this clause? I would be very much interested in knowing if this is the case. I would not, of course, ask for the names, but even if the Government had been petitioned, the Government could turn down the petition because it is not based upon any moral ground.

I think, in fact I know, that the hon. member (Mr. Le-mieux) has spoken from his heart and that he is absolutely sincere in the plea that
he has made to the House. Five years ago I would have made exactly the same plea, and probably I-would make the same plea to-night, had it not been for the fact that during the last few years I have come into personal contact with so many problems that I have altered my point of view to a considerable extent. Had there been no war, many veils would not have been lifted, we would probably have never known of many of the domestic tragedies that have necessarily been uncovered by this war. A great many men, in these days of migration, passed from one country to another because of unhappy domestic relationship. It oftentimes happens that a man living in the Old Country, let us say in England, does not live happily with his wife, and they separate, perhaps by mutual consent. Perhaps the woman abandons him; perhaps the fault is on her side. The man's home is broken up, and very often that man goes to some new part of the British Empire, to Australia or New Zealand or Canada, and starts again. He does not hear from his former wife perhaps for many years. He makes new affiliations; in the new land where he has his life to begin all over again, he finds another mate and they set up a home together. He is honest with the other woman; he tells her he cannot go before a minister and be married because he says: I have a wife somewhere; I know not where, who left me ten or fifteen years ago, but if you live with me, we shall be faithful to each other and our home will be to all intents and purposes that of a married couple. I do not think the hon. member (Mr. Lemieux) has any idea of the hundreds and hundreds of such families there are in Canada.
Nor would the question ever have been raised in this way had it not been for the war. Over and over again, branches of the Canadian Patriotic Fund all the way from Cape Breton to Vancouver have been faced with this case. A man would come in and say: "I wish to enlist; will you take care of my wife while I am gone." The Patriotic Fund officer would say:	" Will you ask
your wife to show me her marriage lines or her marriage certificate and the certificates of birth of her children so that I may know that the marriage is legal and that the children were properly born." The woman would say:	I am sorry but I can
show no lines." It was found necessary at the very beginning of the war for the military authorities to say that where such a case had existed, they would give the separation allowance and pay it to the de facto wife, to the woman with whom the man was

living, to the woman and children whom he was accustomed to support, whom he would have to leave when he enlisted and went overseas. When that woman would come to he Patriotic Fund and tell her story, we would say to her: "Yes, he may go overseas, and while he is gone, although you have not the necessary marriage certificate, the Patriotic Fund will help you and your husband's children." A pledge was made by the military authorities to that man that that woman would be regarded as his wife, and the same pledge was made and kept by the Patriotic Fund. If that man is killed and that woman is not in any way to be recognized by the Government or by any other organization because the marriage was not legal and because the children were not born to the first wife to whom he was originally married, then a very great hardship will exist. Hundreds of women, who were innocent women because they lived with a man not always knowing his previous history, oftentimes assuming that they were married to him or expecting to be married to him, and many of whom were faithful to the men with whom they were respectively living, cannot be left without any recognition by the Pension Bill or any other fund. I know it is a condition that from a moral point of view we deplore, but we cannot get beyond the fact that it exists and that it must be met, and this House, notwithstanding even the plea that has been so admirably made on moral grounds by the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux), should allow the clause to stand in the Bill.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Just a word or two in further reply to the hon. member for Maisonneuve. With all that my hon. friend has said about the importance of the sanctity of the marriage tie, I am in absolute agreement, and with all that he has said about the desirability of not incorporating in our legislation anything which would tend tb weaken the sanctity of the marriage tie I also cordially agree. Therefore, there is no difference of opinion between us on the importance of this question or on the sacredness of the relationship established by the marriage of two persons. Where I differ from my hon. friend, however, is in this: My hon. friend has expressed his amazement that I should present a Bill to the House, which, he says, encourages immorality. He asks: Is it possible that the Government has sanctioned and approved such a Bill? He asks: Have returned soldiers petitioned for it? If so, who? I will tell my hon. friend where this comes from, what is the origin of this clause. The clause

grew out of the necessities of the situation as explained by the hon. member for St. Antoine (Sir Herbert Ames), but it comes from a committee of this House appointed in the year 1916, of which committee my hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) was a member, and that committee reported this clause to this House and this House sanctioned the incorporation of this clause in the Pension regulations.
No.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I shall read to my hon. friend the clause in the report of the committee of 1916. The seventeenth paragraph of the report, to be found in the Votes and Proceedings of the House, 1916, sixth series, at page 727, reads:
That, in the event of an application being made for a pension on behalf of a woman who has, without being married to a member of such force, lived with him as his wife, or on behalf of the child or children of any such man or woman, the Commission be authorized to grant the customary pension for a wife or for a child or children, on being satisfied that the circumstances were such as to warrant the conclusion that the woman had at the time of enlistment and for a reasonable time, previously thereto, publicly been represented as the wife of said member of such Force, or if the commission is satisfied that Justice would be done by the recognition of such woman, for the purpose of pension, as the wife of such member; on the marriage of the woman 'her personal pension cease, but that she be entitled to draw a gratuity of an amount equal to one year's pension.

I am sure my bon. friend doees not want to be unfair to me. It is true that every member of the House is appointed to several committees. I remember having attended some meetings of the Pensions Committee two years ago, but I was not ia regular attendant last year or .this because I had so many other duties to perform. I have never personally sanctioned the principle which is embodied here, but that does not mean, that my hon. friend is wrong when he says that being a member of that Committee I was bound by its report. To a certain extent that is true, but the legislation is now before the House and I take my stand on this question freely. I was not present at the meeting of the Committee at which this particular point was discussed; I should have been present, but I am a member of so many committees and have so many duties to perform that I could not attend that Committee regularly. I admit, however, that my hon. friend is right when he says that I am bound by the report of the Committee of which I was a member.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I quoted that in .answer to my hon. friend's expression of surprise that I should have introduced and stood sponsor for this Bill in this House. My hon. friend wanted to know if the Government stood sponsor for such an immoral Bill as this, and I say to my hon. friend that the Bill is based in a report of a committee of the House of which he was* a member, which report was approved unanimously by the House at that time.
It is never too late to mend.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Quite so. Let me go a step further. This provision in the report of the committee of 1916 was unanimously approved by the House, not because the House did not recognize the importance of maintaining the sanctity of the marriage relation, but because a condition existed which the House felt it could not ignore, and which must be dealt with to prevent very grievous hardship. Last year there was a large and influential committee of this House which reviewed all these pension regulations, and they did not recommend any change in the regulations in this respect.

Has my hon. friend any information as to the number of these
cases?
There were 184 cases in Montreal alone where the marital arrangements of the dependent families were not normal.	.
That is no reason why we should encourage these irregular relations.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We are dealing with a condition that exists. This year this Bill was printed at the very opening of the session and distributed confidentially to all the members of the Pensions Committee. The Bill has now been in the hands of the members of the Pensions Committee for three months or more. It was before the committee for consideration at many meetings, and so far as this clause is concerned, it passed the committee without a dissentinng voice.
Was the point that is raised now raised in the committee, and was there any discussion on it?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There was an explanation by my hon. friend from Kingston (Mr. Nickle).
Was there any discussion?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The question came up and my hon. friend from Kingston explained to the committee the reasons why it was necessary to put such a clause in the Bill.
Was it objected to by anybody on the committee?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I do not recall that it was objected to by anybody, not because the members desired to lessen the sanctity of the marriage tie, but because the statement made by the hon. member for Kingston of the actual conditions existing apparently impressed the members of the committee that it was necessary to have provision made, and convinced them that the committee would not be justified in changing the law in that respect. So this comes to us with the backing of the Pensions Committees of this House for three sessions, and I think under these conditions it is deserving of the very serious consideration of the House.
The section now before us is not the one which authorizes the granting of the pen- ' sion to a woman in the condition we have been discussing. That is an earlier section of the Bill which has already passed the House. What this section provides is that in case of the marriage of such a woman the pension should cease, and I am sure that with that all the members of the House will agree. My amendment this afternoon was to strike out the expression "unmarried wife," to which strong exception had been taken, and 'to substitute therefor a reference to the prior section-"a woman granted a pension under subsection 3 of section 33."
tdr. LEMIEUX: In other words, as long as she is living an irregular life you pay her a pension, but the moment she marries and becomes an honest woman you cut the pension off.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We do exactly the same with the honest woman. The pension of a widow ceases if she re-marries.
Would you put those two on an equal footing?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
So far as cutting off the pension is concerned, if they re-marry, yes. The pensions of both are cut off if they remarry. Now a word with reference to the remarks made by the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) before six o'clock. If I understood him aright he said that we are putting a premium on immorality by legalizing such a relation. I think my hon. friend is under a misapprehension as to the effect of the earlier provision. We are
i

not legalizing such an arrangement. We are not giving such a person the right to a pension, but we do provide that in such a case the Board of Pension Commissioners shall have a discretion to grant a pension if they think the case is one in which the pension should be granted. That is as far as the clause goes. It does authorize them to grant a pension in their discretion if they think one should be granted. Those are the reasons why the clause was inserted in the Bill, and that is the history of the clause now before the committee.
I regretted very much to hear my hon. friend (Sir Herbert Ames) make the admission here this evening that there were 184 cases of unmarried wives in Montreal.
I did not say that.

Were there any such conditions in my county, and I represent one of the largest constituencies in Canada, I would try to hide them. Unmarried wife! Neither Shakespeare, nor Webster, nor any other man who wrote immortal English or compiled a dictionary ever defined an "unmarried wife." There are one or two words to describe them: "Concubine" is one; "strumpet" is another.
These are the only terms that have the same significance. I trust that our statutes will not be blemished with such an unworthy and meaningless expression as " unmarried wife ". Are we going to put a premium on immorality and infidelity in this country by statute of Parliament? Are we men sitting around the Council board here going to1 legislate' in such a manner as virtually to countenance a state of immorality? I hope not. Shakespeare was not only a great writer; he was a great philosopher, and a theologian of no mean repute. And hon. members will recall the words he put into the mouth of the Prince of Denmark, when he found the dishonest step-father praying at the bedside. He had dagger in hand ready to stab him, and expressed his wrath in these words:
No; Up sword and know thou a more horrid hent.
When he's drunk, asleep, or in the incestuous pleasures of his adulterous toed,
Then hit at him, that his heels may kick at Heaven,
And his soul he as damned and hlack as Hell whereto it goeth.
We are legislating to sanction a state of affairs similar to that which is reprehended in these tremendous words. At any rate, we are attempting to put through such legislation, and I sincerely hope that we
[Mr. Rowell.)
will not besmirch our statute-books and our moral records by passing such a section as section 41. For my own sake, and that of my family, I will not countenance it. I would be ashamed to face my wife and children if I voted for section 41.

I do not propose to take up much of the time of the House to-night in discussing this matter. I have too high an appreciation'of the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) to impute any unworthy motive to legislation which he supports. I can well understand the hardship which a strict adherence to legality imposes on a woman who has lived openly with a man as his wife when they are not married. I listened with the closest attention to what the hon. member for St. Antoine (Sir Herbert Ames) said, and the case he puts forward is this: A man comes out into a new country after an unhappy existence in the old land, perhaps through no fault of his own. His wife over in the old country may have deserted him. He comes to this country and becomes friendly with a woman to whom he discloses his inability to marry her. He takes her to his hearth and home as his companion, and they live openly as man and wife. Now, I was brought up perhaps in a severe school, but I was taught that the woman who contracted a relationship of that sort with a man who could not marry her was living in sin with him, and was doing what was morally wrong. I believe that attitude is correct, although I grant that it may cause hardship. But is that not the very foundation of our Christian conception of the relation between the sexes? I concede that it may cause hardship, but is not that hardship something which society must suffer for the preservation of the purity of the marriage bond? I think it is. The children are in an entirely different position. They have no responsibilities attaching to them, and are entitled to the full benefit from anything which the state may afford. I do not want to see these women starve. Charity, if they are able to look after themselves, will grant them relief, on the ground of charity. But this Act implies, nay, directs by permission, that the Pension Commissioners may grant a pension in such cases as these, if they think proper so to do. I cannot vote for this. I trust I have no harsh feelings against any persons in this position. We have the best authority that he that is without sin should first cast a stone, but we cannot, unless we are prepared to debase

the whole moral and spiritual level of the Canadian people, pass this clause.
May I ask the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) whether or not he thinks the State has a duty to perform to these dependents of dead soldiers?

The state has a duty to prevent any one suffering from 'hunger. The hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Peck) has failed to grasp my point, probably because I was not as clear as I should be. I trust I am not an unmerciful man. I would be sorry to see any woman suffering, but the claim of a sufferer must not be put upon a relationship which the law cannot and should not recognize. Let me put this case to the hon. member for Skeena. A man has been living with a woman as his concubine-for I must say in passing that the term "unmarried wife" is the most absurd term I have ever heard in my life; it means an unmarried married woman. The man has been dwelling with this woman as his concubine, and is killed in a railway accident. The law of this land would not allow this concubine to go before the court and get compensation, even though the railway was to blame; not because the state wishes the woman to suffer; but believing that the sanctity of the marriage tie should be kept inviolate, as the very basis of our whole social system the State says that if a woman enters into an irregular relationship of this kind the law will not recognize it, and no rights will flow from it. I do not want to see these people treated with harshness. I am not opposed to their receiving charity, but there must not be, on our statute books, even inferentially, a regulation providing that they have a right to receive aid from the State by reason of an irregular and improper relationship.

I believe that the argument on the morality or immorality of such a condition in our land is beside the question. According to the statement of the hon. member for St. Antoine (Sir Herbert Ames), and in my own understanding of the situation, these women who have been living with men as their wives and have probably borne children by them, have been receiving from the Government, whiie the men were overseas fighting, separation allowances. That constituted an absolute pledge from this Government that these women were going to be looked after if the men .should die. I observe that the other side of the House frequently takes the Government to task for the alleged breaking
of pledges. Well, I do not think that this is a pledge that we should break. To my mind, the moral aspect of this subject does not concern us in this connection. No one is attempting to defend the morality of such a condition of domestic life as is defined by this term. I do not like the term "unmarried wife," and I would vote against the use of it, but I understand that it is being discarded. I do not believe, however, that we, who are all so prone to sin, every one of us,-I have no doubt that no hon. member in this Chamber would be able to throw stones if he lived in the days when the Lord found the woman in adultery-should take .the high moral ground that we would throw these women out into the streets to the mercy of uncertain charity, compelled to hunt for a living, possibly immorally. I personally will support the clause as amended.

My hon. friend
must remember that we are here in a representative capacity and we have to deal with the public sentiment of this country in matters of this kind. My hon. friend may have a certain view upon this question, and so may I, but we are proposing to place legislation on the statute-book that is recognizing the rights of a concubine and placing her in the same position as a woman lawfully married. That is what we on this side of the House object to, and I am sure there are many hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House who have just as strong objection to it as we have. My hon. friend from Brome (Mr. McMaster) has pointed out that we do not recognize such women in relation to property. When a man dies, a woman of this character does not inherit his real estate. She does not get any dower rights, and she has no rights of this kind that have ever been recognized by law. The reasons are well known and they are as have been stated by my hon. friend from Brome. We are proposing to break away from that position in this case. I want to place myself on record as distinctly opposed to any such step. The only question that troubles me is that which relates to the children. We ought to provide for the children, and there ought to be some way found in which they can be cared for; but I do not 9 p.m. believe we have any call to place anything on the statute-books of this country that would recognize a woman who was living with a soldier as a concubine. By doing so we open the door to all kinds of trouble. Apart from the moral question, they will come by thousands and by tens of thousands and make claims on

the Government. How are we going to resist these claims? They will have the proof to a large extent in their own hands, and the department will not he able to say whether they are telling the truth or not. These claims will, of course, be investigated, but we are throwing open the door to all kinds of trouble if we once admit that a woman who has not been married to a soldier has the right to a pension. Besides, we are putting her on the same basis as the lawful wife. There is another Bill before this House in which we make it a crime to teach the doctrine that one may resort to force in order to get what he claims to be the rights of property. Twenty years in penitentiary for teaching doctrines of that kind. The rights of property are very sacred to this Government, but the Ten Commandments do not seem to be in the same class with them. I am opposed to this measure. But I would vote for a measure by which the children of the soldier can be cared for.

We are discussing clause 41, but as a matter of fact clause 33, paragraph 3, absolutely disposes of this question. Be that as it may, let us come down to brass tacks and decide exactly what we are going to vote on. Is it the attitude of hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House that they refuse to make any provision at all for the woman who has been living as a man's wife, or are they quibbling about the use of the word " unmarried wife"? Is it a question merely of the language that is being used, or is it a question of the fact? Do they propose to go out and absolutely state that in their opinion thesp women and these children shall not be protected by the State?

In order that there may be no mistake about it, let me say this: We recognize that the children should be looked after, but we say that there should be absolutely no recognition by the Parliament and the people of this country of prostitution and immorality of that class.

After that explanation let us go a step farther and see where we are in this matter. I commanded a battalion in which 6,000 men enlisted, and sub-quently a brigade through which 25,000 men passed, making in all about 30,000 men. A proportion only of these men came under my observation, hut I was made the recipient of the confidence of a large number of very excellent men. While I am not at liberty to discuss any of the cases that came under my observation, I will 
say this, that the House and the country would be surprised, as the hon. member for St. Antoine (Sir Herbert Ames) was surprised, to find to what an extent this sort of thing has been going on. For different reasons, most of which seemed to me to be quite sound at the time, men had separated from their wives, wives had separated from their husbands, and this relationship to which the hon. gentleman has referred, sprang up. I am able to say of my own knowledge that these people were living together, illegally if you will, but happily, honestly and properly, bringing up their children with the greatest possible care and attention, and there was nothing in their outward lives to suggest for a moment what actually was a fact. These men were splendid soldiers, they were urgently needed, their services were highly valued and highly considered, and many of them have been killed or become incapacitated. Probably these men would not have been enlisted at all if they had not known that the country was going to protect their wives and families, and in the end, protect them by way of pension. I cannot for the lifq of me see how any man, while he may object, while he may regard, as I am sure we all do regard, this relationship with the deepest possible objection, can fail to treat it, not as a theory but as a fact which has developed in our national life and which we must deal with. The leader of the Opposition has said that he would provide for the children but he would absolutely refuse to provide for the woman. Even with the lowest woman, it is generally admitted that she best can mother her own children, and for these women I unhesitatingly say that they are the only women who can bring up these children and look after them. Therefore, I desire to put before the committee in the strongest possible manner my belief that the obligation rests upon this country very heavily, in so far as these women and children are concerned, to make absolutely the same provision for them as we do for those who are legally and properly married.
Mr. H. A. MAC'KIE: I do not know that I can add anything of interest to what has been said this evening, but i was struck a moment ago when my hon. friend from Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) quoted us an authority which stands without an equal in this world but is also known to have been of immoral life. I am not at all surprised, Mr. Chairman, at the attitude of a portion of this House by reason of the fact that it is constituted of men alone and it

has been the duty of men from Christ down to the present time to throw the stone at woman. I will agree with the general principles enunciated by the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) and the leader of the Opposition, that marriage is a sacrament and that all legislation should tend in the direction of upholding Christianity in that respect.
But you did not tell the man who enlisted in this fight not to sacrifice his blood on the battlefield lest his widow and children should have no assistance from the State. You accepted everything that he could give, and now that he has paid the great price-
We stand by the widow and the children of any man who gave his life at the front, but we do not pledge ourselves to support a concubine.

When the military authorities accepted the services of a man who declared himself to be living in. a state of concubinage, you permitted him to go on the battlefield and sacrifice himself for your liberty and the liberty of the people of the Dominion; and if the sin ' of that man would cause you to say, com-mitto in inferno et in aetemam, then you lose absolutely the Christian spirit that has been inculcated in you when you do not say, absolvo te a pecatis tuis. Why do you say that, as concerns these two cases, there should be a difference between the treatment accorded to the women, and children? If the sin is to be visited upon anybody it must be visited upon the seventh, generation; why exclude children from the benefits of this provision because they were ushered into this world without their consent? You have accepted the sacrifices of these men, and I am surprised to hear hon. gentlemen say that because a man lived in a state of sin, his natural wife and natural children should receive no benefit whatsoever from the pension system of the State, although he made the greatest sacrifice that man could make in the defence of his country and of this Empire. -A little Christianity is about all that is needed in the consideration of a question that faces us as a bald fact. If our Saviour came to this earth, I wonder whether He would take the opinion of the leader of the Opposition and the member for Maisonneuve, or whether he would be prepared to say that such a man as we have been discussing had redeemed himself at least in a measure by performing his whole duty to his country, a duty which other men
failed to perform, although they were capable of doing it. I heartily support this measure, without adopting the principle that we do in fact support concubinage. We are dealing with one special case, and one that is deserving in the eyes of every Christian.

We seem to be discussing the propriety of granting pensions to a certain class; but is that the subject of section 41, which is under consideration? Section 41 does not grant pensions. It provides for what seems to be a marriage gift, one year's pension in the case of marriage or the remarriage of the women in the classes mentioned. But the main purpose of this section is to stop pensions which are already granted, and if you omit this clause you do not stop anybody's pension, but you prevent the commission from stopping any such pension when the marriage or remarriage takes place.
It was upon the expression " unmarried wife " that the discussion arose.
I understand that that has been amended.

The amendment is a
change of words, but it carries the same meaning.

I again make the point that this section does not grant any pensions, except that it provides for one year's pension as a marriage gift. If you omit this section you do not refuse pensions to the classes of women mentioned; you continue them. The object of this section is that, in a given condition, the pension may stop.

My hon. friend (Mr. J.
H. Sinclair) is, I think, incorrect in his assertion that if these sections pass in relation to the status of the unmarried wife, we shall have " thousands and tens of thousands " of applicants for pension under this provision. Only 60,000 men were killed overseas-a multitude, in fact, but only those women can make application for pension who were the wives of men who were killed or died, and the statistics will prove beyond possibility of contradiction that the proportion of married men to those who were unmarried would not permit tens of thousands of applications to be made. Of many of the applications that will * be made and in respect of which pensions will be granted, the domestic relationship was quite regular and no dispute or question could arise.

Subsection 2 of section 33 says:
Subject to paragraph one of this section, the widow of a pensioner who, previous to his death, was pensioned for disability in any of the Classes 1 to 5 mentioned in Schedule A shall be entitled to a pension.
Is the unmarried wife also included in the word " widow " there?
Yes.
Then I would like to correct the hon. gentleman who said a moment ago that only the relatives, if I may use the word, of those who had fallen in France would come under subsection 3.

The hon. member is quite correct in directing attention to the error in my statement. I should explain to the committee wherein he is correct and wherein I was incorrect. There is a provision in the Bill under which, on the death of a man who was wounded to an extent of disability exceeding 80 per cent, the widow shall be entitled to the same pension as if the man had continued to live. That would give occasion for an award in those cases where a married man, having been awarded a pension for disability exceeding 80 per cent, died and left a widow. There are not a very great number of those cases, although there are some. I have been on these pension committees since 1916 and I doubt if any other members of the committee have given more careful consideration than I have to the domestic problems that have arisen in reference to the war and to the pensionability of men. It is not a theory we have to face; it is a condition. I know, as a member of the Central Executive of the Patriotic Fund, and the member for St. Antoine (Sir Herbert Ames) knows as the organizer and chief force behind that Fund, that the war has thrown aside the veil from many a home of which otherwise we would not have known anything, and we have found that conditions existed that we little suspected. But, as I say, we are facing a condition, not a theory, and the question is, what is to be done in reference to the unmarried wives1-if, in order to be brief, I may use that objectionable term-whose husbands were killed or died in the war? The member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) said there was provision in our law that made the relationship of a man who lived with a woman unmarried to her a crime against the law. If my recollection of the criminal law is correct, there is no provision in the Dominion criminal law, although there is in the criminal law of New
[Mr. Nickle.J
Brunswick, by which an adulterous relationship is made a crime. The hon. gentleman also directed the attention of the committee to the fact that a Bill was now before the Senate, and would shortly come before this House-

My hon. friend may be right on that point. I know that the Social Service 'Congress have on various occasions petitioned the Parliament with a view to having such a law placed on the statute-book. I think that such a Bill as I have referred to has been passed by the Senate; if not, it was at least discussed there the other day. Was it rejected?

Sentiment cannot be a basis for sound law, and even all hard cases as brought out by my genial friend from Skeena (Mr. Peck) are a poor argument indeed as a basis for law. Let us carry his principle a little further. You give a pension to this unmarried wife- what a strange expression!-because forsooth her man fought gallantly at the front and sacrificed his all for his country. You are ready to pass a sponge over this little irregularity of his living with the wife of



another man, or with a woman of bad repute, because, forsooth, he went to the front and fought. Now, suppose that on his return, instead of parading himself as the master of that woman, this soldier finds himself stranded in a large city. We promised before he left that he would be looked after; he cannot find employment,-as is actually the case in many large centres-; he is hungry; he steals some food from a butcher's shop or a grocer's store; he is arrested andj brought before a magistrate. My hon. friend can there again, I suppose, quote law based on sentiment and say: It is a hard case; the man was hungry and stole; hut, Your Honour, he must not be punished because he is a soldier who served at the front, and is now unemployed! There is as much law in this contention as in the other.
Notwithstanding the sermon of my hon. friend the pastor from Edmohton (Mr. H. A. Mackie) once you begin to depart from the only safe principle, once you depart from sound principles recognized since Christianity, then there is no more law and there is>
no more respect for the ethics of civilization. You might just as well say, if the new social conditions brought about by the war must prevail: Let us give passion, the senses, and contempt of the law, full sway in the land; war is our excuse ! Am I to be told by the two hon. members for Edmonton that I am playing the Pharisee because I stand by British law? I fear not to go before the soldiers themselves and to advocate the same principles I have advocated here this afternoon and evening. Have the courage of your convictions and do not give way to every whim and passion, even though you cater to the returned soldier. Teach him to respect the law. He fought for the respect of the law in Europe. I am really dumbfounded-when I read in the press and hear in this House such extraordinary statements. Let me read another passage from a magazine from which I quoted a moment ago and which is published in Toronto. The two hon. members for Edmonton spoke in similar language to that used by this writer vrho says:
Some of our prejudices will have to go, some of our dearly cherished notions of respectability will have to be thrown on the scrap heap, and some of our national reluctance to look actual facts in the face will have to be overcome.
We heard about "facts" this evening. We are facing "facts." Here are "facts":
But that is all. Our surplus women can be given full opportunity to satisfy their just claim to enjoy marriage and motherhood without any upheaval or revolution, if only we have 
the sense to see that it would be definitely wiser to broaden our views than to invite the disastrous results which are certain to come if we adhere rigidly to our present conception and deny our surplus women their clear right.
Let us look around us. Let us take from our eyes our prejudice-tinted1 spectacles. Let selfish and fortunate women force themselves to think just a little unselfishly. Let the strict individualist listen just a very little to the man who considers the good of the community before that of the individual. Let the rigid moralist face actual facts, whether doing so be pleasant or unpleasant. Let us be frank.
Free love.

I need not read it all
nor give the name of the magazine, but it shows us how we have become colour blind as regards what is moral and what is not moral, as regards what is regarded as Christian and what is unchristian, as regards what is traditionally British and what is unBritish. I will ask the President of the Council to tell me what is the pension law of the United States of America, what is the pension law of Great Britain. I should like to know if, in the Parliament of Great Britain, such a principle as that under discussion has been advocated, and I should also like to know if our neighbouring republic has advocated such principles. If I speak a little heatedly, it is because I resent the suggestions which have been made that those of us, the leader of the Opposition and others, who oppose this legislation, are playing the Pharisee. I am not a Pharisee; I am unfortunately a publican; I am a sinner; but I stand by the best traditions of Canada and also of Great Britain in opposing this legislation.

I feel that "the
pastor from Edmonton " is entitled to reply to the able and distinguished gentleman from Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) and I desire to do so in most unmistakable terms. What is he going to say about the Grey Nuns in the province of Quebec, the only women who are looking after bastard children in that province and in the other provinces of the Dominion? Are they encouraging immorality? In the whole Dominion there is no institution that deserves the credit that those women deserve for looking after those children. Are they to be condemned because they are looking after the progeny of men and women who lived in sin?
What has that to do with the question?

What has that to do with the question? Yes, I know philosophers such as my hon. friends who may distinguish as they may see fit for the benefit

ol their argument, but they cannot by any means put it over in that way. By the way, perhaps the hon. gentleman from Maison-neuve would like " the pastor " to be on his job and read what St. John says in chapter 8. I am not a Presbyterian like the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster), and I do not know that I am a Roman Catholic like the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux), but at any rate, I should like to read this - because " the pastor " must at least enlighten the Opposition to this extent:
When Jesus had lifted up himself, and saw none but the woman, he said unto her, Woman, where are those thine accusers?-
Not from Maisonneuve.

hath no man condemned thee? She said. No man. Lord. And Jesus said unto her. Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.
That is exactly what this Bill says to-day. We provide for the woman who has committed a sin, but we say in this law: Go, and sin no more. I do not understand the frame of mind of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lemieux), when he takes it upon himself to lecture the members of this House with a sort of ex-cathedra authority. There is no one on this side of the House who is infallible, and I dare say there is no one infallible on the opposite side. The hon. gentleman has no business to assume to lecture us when we are trying to do what Christ has told us to do in looking after fallen people. Their men gave the best that was in them, and the State accepted their services, and it is the business of the State to-day to see that those who were unfortunate, as we have heard their circumstances described to-day, should be taken care of properly.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must remind the Committee that the point raised a few moments ago by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) was well taken. The pension that is now being discussed was granted in clause 33 of this Bill, and no vote having been taken upon it, it must be considered as granted unanimously by this Committee. This clause 41 is to take away that pension after a certain time. I do not want to keep any hon. member from speaking, but I must hereafter insist that the discussion be strictly relevant to the clause under consideration.

I have already discussed many of the features of this question, and my intention on rising was to confine myself strictly to the provisions of clause
272i
41. It is my intention to vote for any amendment that will delete this clause from the Bill. My hon. friend (Mr. iH. A. Mackie) has referred in a sneering manner to those who differ from him on this question, and has quoted St. John, chapter 8, verses 10 and 11. While I am sure many of us on this side of the House are conversant with that portion of the Scriptures, it is not pertinent to the question under discussion. The point I want to raise now is in connection with the, provision that is made by this clause for the unmarried wife.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must remind the hon. member that an amendment has been moved by the minister striking out the words "unmarried wife."
I submit that a woman in that position may continue to -live in the same relation with another man, and in the eyes of the law she would be entitled to continue to draw her pension.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Oh, no.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must again call the hon. member's attention to the fact that this clause provides that upon the marriage or re-marriage of any such person the pension shall cease. That is provided by clause 41. The clause granting the pension is clause 33. Therefore the remarks of the hon. gentleman are certainly not in order, and I shall be obliged to so rule.

I have not the amendment before me, but clause 41 reads:
Upon the marriage or re-marriage of the mother, widow, unmarried wife or divorced wife of a deceased member of the forces.
The point I was making was this: If the man a woman of this kind is living with dies she could take up with another man and her pension would continue under this law.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The clause says very clearly that her pension shall cease.

There is another point. The minister a few moments ago called the attention of the House to the amendments made to the Criminal Code this session regarding unmarried people registering at hotels. What provision has been made to cover a man with an unmarried wife? Apparently they would be able to register at an hotel and travel all over the country.

I was not in the House when the clauses of this Bill were going through, and I should like to have the privilege of calling attention to one aspect of this question which I have not

heard discussed, and that is the position of the women and children of a very large number of men who came forward voluntarily and went to the front from Northern Ontario and from the northern parts of Canada generally, from one end of the Dominion to the other. I refer to the native Indians. I know several hundred Indians from the section of the country from which I come, all the way from the Height of Land up to as far north as Fort Churchill, who came forward voluntarily, and many of them have made the supreme sacrifice. Many o| them were living in the relation that has been referred to in the discussion of this clause, and a very great hardship would be done to many of these people who were living together according to the customs of their race if the Pension Bill was framed as it has been argued it should be framed. I know personally that several hundreds of these men have left large families, who would be absolutely cut off from any remuneration under the pension scheme were the provisions that have been outlined here to-night by the minister not in the Bill.

I wish to explain why I
intend to vote in favour of the amendment of the President of the Privy 'Council. As I understand it, if that amendment should carry the pension of an unmarried wife, *that is, a woman who comes within subsection 3 of clause 33, will cease after a year. But should the amendment not carry, as we have adopted clause 33, her pension would continue indefinitely. Therefore I consider I am justified in voting for the amendment.

I should like to draw
the attention of the committee to the fact that there is a precedent for such legislation as this. We have had legislation on the" statute books of British Columbia for a number of years providing for the concubines of old-timers in that country. In the early days many of the men in that country lived with Indian women as their wives, and had children by them; possibly in many cases there was no opportunity for them to get married. Now the [DOT] old-timers in that province thought it was only right and just that if a man had lived with a woman for many years and had had children by her and had died without making provision for the women and the children, legislation should be passed to take care of them. It may be that we were too broad-minded out in that province, but it was thought only right and fair that these women and children should be provided

for by law, and accordingly provision was made by statute for them.

I do not want to prolong this discussion and I certainly do not want to put myself for one moment in opposition to your ruling, Mr. 'Chairman, but surely it is an extraordinary ruling coming after the speech of my hon. friend from Maisonneuve, where he appealed to certain other countries. If he is under a wrong impression, surely one ought to have a chance of removing that impression and giving correct information to the committee. Again, it is contrary to your own previous practice, Mr. Chairman. You have again and again allowed the committee a certain latitude. It has been granted to certain members of the committee, and I think we should be able to bring the debate to a conclusion within a reasonable time.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is not the contention of the hon. member that the hon. member for Maisonneuve was in order. The discussion drifted very far from the clause under discussion, and after a certain amount of latitude had been given the Chairman felt it his duty to remind the committee that they must come back to the' clause under consideration. If, however, the hon. member for Red Deer feels that he has something to say in answer to the remarks of the hon. member for Maisonneuve, and that the ruling was not made at the proper time, I am sure that with the unanimous consent of the committee he will be allowed to answer the hon. member.

My hon. friend from Maisonneuve appealed to the practice of Britain. What I do know about Britain is that pensions were paid to exactly such people as we have been discussing here, described as " wives by habit and repute." That happened during the war, and that is exactly the practice which is recommended, under more humanitarian considerations, in the case of those women who have lost their support by the death of their supporters either at the front or afteT their return. So that his appeal to the case of Britain falls to the ground. In the debates on the subject in the British House, what I venture with all respect to call the narrow, somewhat sectarian', and church, view was taken by some very high churchmen of a very old Tory school. Such men, of course, would have a natural attraction for my hon. friend- the leader of the Opposition, but the broad humanitarian practice of Britain has been to pay pensions in these very cases to women de-

scribed as " wives by habit and repute." I venture to call that the broad, humanitarian and, I might add, Christian vierw. I add the word " Christian " advisedly, in the light of t'he passage of Holy Writ which was read to this committee by my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. H. A. Mackie) to-night. He who taught all of us our Christianity, if indeed we have been permitted to sit at His feet and receive the pure and unadulterated truth from its source, in the presence of such a woman uttered a dictate which should be the guide for men surely in all times: " Let him that is without sin cast the first stone." There is no other road for myself, Mr. Chairman, not being sinless, than to wonder at those who take what is the attitude of the sinless in the view of the founder of Christianity Himself. My hon. friend quoted the question: " Where are these thine accusers?" If he had read the whole passage, he could have brought home to this committee the fact that the accusers, under the appeal of the only pure and sinless One, had slunk one by one from His presence. They had gone out and left the woman to the only One who had the right to condemn her. That I take to be the Christian view, and it is also, as I have tried to describe it, the broad and humanitarian, view. I would like to support that just in a sentence.
My hon. friend the leader of the Opposition has the greatest regard, on many grounds, for the great Scottish poet. What did he say in such matters as to the attitudes assumed by hon. gentlemen in this House? He said:
Then at the balance let's be mute:
We never can adjust it.
What's done, we partly may compute But know not what's resisted.
The great American orator, Ingersoll, referring to a preacher of a Presbyterian body, of great eminence, who had made a posthumous attack upon George Eliot, to whose brilliant salons the elite of literature and science in London were proud and glad to resort; George Eliot, who lived exactly in those conditions with George Henry Lewes-said, quoting Shakespeare:
Lay her i' the earth,
And from her pure and unpolluted flesh let violets grow.
I tell thee, churlish priest,
A ministering angel shall this woman be,
When thou liest howling.
I take it these men represent the broad and humanitarian view. But I do not want to follow that line of debate, because I am debarred from judging my fellow-men
or my fellow-women by the highest sanction of Christianity itself. * Mr. Gladstone, on a famous occasion, said about a great Irishman, restraining his action to the purely political ground: "I sit in judgment upon no man." Surely, what guided Ingersoll, and Shakespeare, and Burns, and the founder of Christianity himself, should be a fair guide for us as to our attitude to our fellow-mortals whom we, forsooth, chose to describe as sinners and beyond the pale.
I leave that tempting line of thought apd , these considerations with my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition.
I want to say one word as to the attitude of the Opposition on this question. What is it they propose to do under the sanction of morality derived from one particular commandment? Morality is a broad thing. It tells me that the only thing I ought to do to a sinner is to help him or her if I can. But it also tells me that other people who, restricting themselves to one particular commandment, denounce a woman by the use of the strongest language in regard to her that parliamentary forms will permit, ought themselves to be sinless. What is it that we in this Parliament are asked to do? We are asked in effect to say to a woman of this particular class: You may go and starve, as far as we are concerned: You were a certain man's wife by repute: He died for our cause and he thought that what he had done for his country would send on to you some little support after he had left you. We in this Parliament are asked to say now that this great country of Canada should take the position in regard to this woman, for whom in a minor sense the man died, after his country, that because, forsootth, .she had not gone through certain forms, which I should be the last to speak with any disrespect of, she should starve. We are asked to say to her: You shall starve so far a= we are concerned, because in one of the commandments you have erred. I could not take that attitude. I should proclaim myself sinless if I used strong language about her; I should proclaim myself, in my judgment, wanting in humanity if I did not see that her ordinary creature wants were looked after, after her only support in the world had died.

Perhaps if the
President of the Privy Council would explain what the section really means, it might be found that there is no great difference of opinion in the Committee on th* subject.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The amendment simply strikes out the words "unmarried wife" because objection has been taken to that description of the relationship referred to, and we use other language which refers back to an earlier .section of the Act.
Do the unmarried wife and children get the pension under section 33? '

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The Pension Board is entitled under section 33 to give a pension to the unmarried wife and children if in their discretion they think it proper.
When does the pension cease?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Upon her marriage, or re-marriage if you choose 'to describe it that way; in the same manner as the pension to the widow ceases upon re-onarriage. I beg to move that .clause 41 be amended:
By striking out the words " unmarried wife " in the second line, by adding after the word " pension " in the third line, the following words, " or of a woman awarded a pension under subsection 3 of section 33 of this Act."

Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to on division.
On section 43-inducements to assign, charge or attach pensions:

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It has been suggested that we might amend clause 43 so as to allow the Canadian Patriotic Fund, or any other patriotic or benevolent corporation to make advances on account of the pension provided such corporation is approved by the Board of Pension Commissioners, these advances to be made without interest to tide the pensioner over in case of illness or for other necessity. I would therefore move that the clause be amended by adding the following:
Provided however that t'he provisions of this section shall not apply to loans, credits or consideration made or given without interest or other profit by the Canadian patriotic fund, or by any patriotic or benevolent corporation, society or association approved by the commissioner^
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 45-false statement under oath or otherwise:

I would suggest that in
view of the fact that the clause has been amended the words "or otherwise" in the margin be struck out.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Quite so.
Section as amended agreed to.

On section 46-supplementary pension on disability of members of His Majesty's Forces other than those of Canada, to effect equalization:

Mr. Chairman, I wish to make an amendment to this clause by adding, in the thirty-fifth line, after the words " His Majesty's" the words "or allied " so that it will read:
In any of His Majesty's or allied naval, military or air forces, etc.
This would include soldiers who fought in the allied French, Belgian and Italian armies. We have made provision further on in the Bill for the widows of those soldiers so as to equalize their pensions with those of Canadian soldiers. As these men have fought the same fight, have fought for the same cause, have shed their blood on the same soil of France and Flanders, they should be entitled, if they were bona fide residents of Canada before the war, to absolutely the same treatment as our own Canadian soldiers. Their pensions should be supplemented to make them equal to those of the Canadian soldiers. A distinction has been made by section
10 p.m. 46 between a British reservist or soldier of the other Allied armies, but there is no distinction made between the widows of soldiers of the Canadian, British and Allied armies who fell on the field of battle. If we want to be fair to the residents of Canada, whatever be their nationality provided they fought on the side of the Allies and in-one of the Allied forces, we should give them the same pension as we give our own soldiers.
Does my hon. friend refer to men who resided in Canada before the war?

The clause reads: .
When a person who was domiciled and resident in Canada at the beginning of the war.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The question raised by
the hon. member (Mr. Power) is one which received very careful consideration at the hands of the committee. I am quite sure that the members were sympathetic with the idea
Will the hon. gentleman explain what the idea is?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The idea is that men who were domiciled in Canada

Canadians?
Mr. ROWELL-Canadians, and who enlisted in any Allied force should have their pensions supplemented so as to bring them up to the Canadian pension.

That means those
who served in the British forces?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No; the clause provides for those who served in the British forces. The committee had before them the proposal to supplement the pension of all Canadians who fought in the Imperial forces and also the question raised by the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) of supplementing the pensions of all Canadians who had fought in the Allied forces-French, Belgian, Russian, Italian and Greek. The committee, after giving the matter very careful consideration thought that if we supplemented the pensions of the Canadians who had fought in any branch of the Imperial service that was as far as they could justify going at the present time, except in the case of the widows and children of Allied reservists.
Allied reservists resident in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Allied reservists resident in Canada. The increased pension charge created by this Bill will he in the neighbourhood of $5,000,000, and the Committee felt that that was as far as they were justified in going.

I do not wish to take up the time of the Committee, but I do wish to say a word in support of the proposition brought fojward by the hon. member for Quebec (Mr. Power). This matter came very close to me in connection with a French reservist who lives in my county. He had lived in Canada for at least seventeen years before the war broke out, and had been a naturalized Canadian for fourteen years. When the war broke out he wished to join the Canadian army, but he was advised by the French consul that he should join the French army. He did so. He fought very gallantly; received the Croix de Guerre from the French Government, and came back home with two of his hands partially shot off. That man is receiving a very substantially smaller pension than that which has been allowed to men who enlisted in the Canadian army. He was a Canadian citizen before he went over. He fought the same fight and in the same cause as the Canadians who joined the Canadian or the British army, and I ask on what score of fairness can you give a man who joined the Imperial army an augmentation in his pension and refuse to pay the same pension to a man who joined the French army?	.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: On the same principle that you grant a preference within the Empire.

That is no answer because this man before he enlisted in the French army was a naturalized Canadian. He wanted to enlist in our army, but he was told by the French Consul that he must enlist in the French army, which he did, and gave loyal service. I am not asking for justice for him because he is a French Canadian-and he only represents a class-I am asking for justice for him as a naturalized Canadian citizen who served in the French army instead of the British or the Canadian army. The Pension Committee has recognized that if he died his wife and children would be entitled to an augmentation of pension which would bring that pension up to the Canadian scale. How does the Government differentiate between the claim of the widow and children and the man's own claim? It may be said that to extend this provision to the class to which I refer would cost money. But after all, justice should prevail before financial considerations; besides, there cannot be a great number of men who were French, Italian or Russian reservists who went to fight for the Allies in the armies of their respective countries. I submit that in all justice and fairness a man in this position should be recognized.

The men who went from Canada and served in the British army, whether Canadian-born or naturalized Canadian citizens, did so with the consent of and by arrangement with the Canadian authorities. The soldier to whom my hon. friend (Mr. MoMaster) refers did not join the French army through the Canadian authorities; he obeyed the order of the French consul to recognize, not his Canadian nationality, hut the authority of France as superior to the authority of Canada. That sums the case up in a nutshell.
Is it not a fact that by the authority of the Minister of Militia and Canadian military authorities, Polish troops, consisting of men who were Polish reservists, were trained in Canada?

This was done at the request of the Governments concerned. But the British and Canadian soldiers who entered the Imperial service did so by arrangement with the British Government and on the authority of the Canadian Government; the others did not.

Take the case of an Italian who obeyed the call of his country and went to fight in Italy; because he did his duty in that way he would not obtain the same pension as that obtained by another Italian who, because there was higher pay in the Canadian army, refused to do his duty to his country as he should have done it. The man who did his duty conscientiously is entitled to a pension as well as the man who did not.

Many of these aliens came to Canada, lived here a long time, became naturalized, and instead of enlisting in the Canadian service-as they should have done, because Canada was the country they swore to defend- they went off and served in the army of their own country. Some did that from choice; a great many did it because it is a law of the country whence they came that their Canadian naturalization was of no effect and that they should return to their own country to fight. In other words, the law of their own country is such that our naturalization does not touch them at all. I am absolutely opposed to extending this consideration to them; a large number of nationalities are involved, and there is no telling where it would end. But there is substantial reason for extending this privilege to those who have enlisted in the British army. The President of the Council has given, perhaps, the best reason. We are all under the same flag, all in a family of nations which are Very closely connected. But there is absolutely no reason why we should pension men who served in other armies. If we saddle ourselves with such an obligation the time may come when, because of having undertaken this burden, we shall not be able to do justice to our own people. .	[DOT]

My hon. friend
does not use the word " aliens " as applied to those who fought in the Allied armies?
They are friendly aliens.

These soldiers joined the forces of their various countries at the very commencement of the war and I do not see any reason why they should not get the same consideration as soldiers who joined the Canadian army. This is the first war that Canada ever took any great part in, and these men from France, Italy, and other European countries probably had a better idea of what the war really meant than the Canadian people did. When the war broke out we talked of a force of 50,-
000	as being a huge army for Canada. These French or Italian reservists went to their own countries because they expected to be in the fight and because they supposed, perhaps, that the Canadian army would be absorbed by the British army.

The member for
Brome (Mr. McMaster) intimated that some soldiers joined the armies of their own countries by order of their own consul in Canada.

In some cases, possibly
they did.

In the case with which
1	was familiar the man desired to enlist in the Canadian army, but he was told by the French consul in Montreal that, having been a French subject, notwithstanding the fact that he had been a naturalized Canadian citizen of many years standing, it was his duty to join the French army. He did not haggle about the matter; he went overseas and was in France by the end of August.

The ex-Minister of Militia (Sir Sam Hughes) was one of the few men in Canada at the outbreak of the war who thought that Canada would have moTe than 50,000 soldiers in France, or who thought that we would have any soldiers there at all in time to take part in the war. These French and Italian and other reservists who enlisted to join their own units overseas took a more serious view of the situation than the Canadian people did. They were willing to make the sacrifice; they wanted to get into the fight as quickly as possible. They had been invited to make Canada their home; they were Canadians. For the sake of the paltry sum of $5,000,000 per annum, I would hate to put these people in a class by themselves and say they are not as good as Canadian-born or British-born men or others who happened to join the Canadian forces, possibly believing that they would not get to the field of battle as soon as the fellows who joined the French, Italian or other allied armies. I cannot see why these people should be legislated against and treated as a separate class, to the detriment not so much of ourselves as of the honour of Canada. I hope that the amendment will carry.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
One of our difficulties, in addition to those which I have mentioned, is that we have no reliable data covering all the cases involved. Some members of the committee' would have been glad to include French and Belgian reservists but

were not favourable to including certain other nationalities. The committee thought we could not undertake to discriminate bysaying that the reservists of one ally should receive this treatment and that those of another should not. We have this year included all Canadians who enlisted in the Imperial forces. Before another year is over no doubt we shall have fuller information and fuller data, and if it is decided that further action should be taken, the matter may be dealt with ano'ther year. The Pension Bill has to come up for review next year because this will only continue for a year. I submit that the House will be well advised to accept the considered report of the committee on this matter and leave the clause over for another year.

I would be very happy to support the amendment of the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) if he would confine it to the French and Belgian armies, and if it does not put such a strain on our finances that we will not have enough money for ourselves. I have the most profound admiration for the French army, as I fought beside it for a very long time, and I should very much like, if it is possible, to see that army and the Belgian army included in the benefits of this pension scheme. But with twenty or thirty nations in the Alliance, I do not believe we can extend the benefits of the scheme to all of them. Ecuador was in the Alliance and other countries that I had hardly heard of before.

I am quite willing to accept the suggestion of my hon. friend for Skeena (Mr. Peck) and to limit the application of this to the British, French and Belgian soldiers. If my hon. friend will support me in that, I will change my amendment accordingly.
Amendment (Mr. Power) negatived.

Section agreed to.
On schedule A:

I am not going to repeat what I said* the other night, but in regard to the two schedules, I do not think the amount is adequate, and I hope the Government will seriously consider raising it, especially the amount of the widow's pension.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
We have this year made two very marked advances in dealing with the widow's pension, and the committee thought it was as far as we could go this year; that is, we have increased it from $40 to $48, we have increased the pension to
the orphan child and have exempted the widow's earnings from consideration in dealing with the pension.
Schedule A agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Now I move that we revert to section 2, paragraph (c), and that we strike out the words "his child by his unmarried wife" in lines twenty-two and twenty-three.

Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I move that we revert to the sections 23 (4); 24, 33 (3); 35 (1); and that we substitute for the words "unmarried wife" the words "wife by habit and repute." I am advised that that is the description of a woman of this class which appears in the British Pensions Act.

I submit again, Mr. Chairman, that I am opposed to that amendment. A great deal of preaching has been thrown across the floor, and we have had a great deal of illegitimate use of Scriptures, if I may use the term-We are talking about illegitimate wives and illegitimate children, and surely we have had illegitimate quotations of scripture. When people ask "Who shall throw the first stone?" they must not lose sight of the punishment meted out by the Mosaic law to a woman found in that sin; she was to be taken beyond the camp and stoned.
That was Mosaic, not the Christian law.
If my hon. friend wishes to put himself up as the champion of this kind of morals in Canada, I want to know.
I am simply calling attention to the fact that that is not the Christian law.

I simply want to know if the hon. member for Skeena, with the distinction he has won in the army, wants to come back to this country and put himself forward as the champion of those who refuse to recognize the sacredness of the marriage tie?
I want to put myself forward as one who wishes to look after the dependents of those brave men who fought beside me in Flanders.

I am not going to be wiped out by this everlasting quoting of the war to justify everything, whether moral or immoral. I am not going to stand for it. I am as much a champion as any

one in this House of the women who are legitimately widows as a result of the war; I am as tenderhearted as any man in this House. But I want to be so without putting this class of women on the same footing as the married women of this country. Is there a member in this House who has a widowed daughter, or daughter-in-law, who wants to go home and tell either of them: I have put you in the same position as the concubine Indian women of Canada? That is what we have been asked to do here tonight. I want to help the Indian women by putting some money apart for them, if necessary.
I want to help the woman that was living in sin by putting money apart in some certain way to assist her, if that is necessary and proper. But I do not want to give her the status and recognition of the married women of this country. That is what I am opposed to. And I am to be told by hon. gentlemen that I am a " crusted Tory," as the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. M. Clark) calls me. I should like to know what he is. He ought to be a judge; he was on both sides and in the middle, so that he ought to have some idea now what sort of a man he is. He was but a short time with the Tories when they had to change the name of the party to get clear of him. They called themselves Unionists; they could not call themselves Tories while they had a man like him with them. Now he comes back and calls me a Tory. At least I know what I am; I am in the same place all the time. The hon. member for Red Deer used to go down to our part of the country to preach Liberalism; he and I have spoken on the same platform, and he then found no words strong enough to condemn the Borden Government. It was a Government of funks with the hon. gentleman in those days, and yet he comes back at me and calls me a Tory. And he puts himself in the class of those men who refuse to recognize the marriage tie between a man and a wife and their duty to their children. I am not against helping anybody in this country that requires help, far be that from me; but I do not want any woman who is living in this way illegally and improperly to be put upon the same basis as the honest widow who, by reason of the fact that she was properly married, is entitled to come under this law and to get this right. That is my position, and I cannot conceive of any member of this House being capable of calling such a woman a wife at all. She is not a wife, and surely no hon. member, who loves and respects his wife and who

calls her " my wife " and " my beloved wife," will use the same term " wife " in regard to this woman, who, perhaps, induced a man to leave his wife and his children and to become an outcast here with her. Is she to be called or blessed by this great Parliament of Canada as the wife of some one? She is not a wife; she is a woman who is, perhaps, in need and who ought to be helped; and if she ought to be helped let some money be set apart,'properly handled by this board or some other board, and let her be helped, but not as the wife of anybody, because she was never anybody's wife. I am told we have instructions and directions from the Holy Book in regard to " casting the first stone." Let people who are so familiar with the. New Testament as regards who a wife is and who thinks that a woman can be a wife to more than one man, go with the Master to the well when the woman came to where he was. What did He say to her? "Go, call thy husband and [DOT] come hither." The woman answered and said, "I have no husband." Jesus said unto her, " Thou hast well said, I have no husband, for thou hast had five husbands; and he whom thou now hast is not thy husband." That is Scripture, if hon. members opposite want the sayings of the Master. There was one legitimate marriage; there could not be five legitimate marriages, and he at once said to her: You have no husband at all.
