He would permit her to drink out of the well all the same, but he would not regard her as the wife of anybody. The word "wife" in this country is too sacred a thing. The word "children" and the word "family" are sacred things, things to be guarded at every standpoint; and while I am not opposed to using money for the purpose of helping these unfortunate people, I do not want to give it to them because the relationship of wife or family ties or legitimate obligations brings it to them. If we are going to use the word "wife" here, we are using a word that we have no business to use at all. Use the word "woman" or any other name you choose to take-help her if you can; but I am deadly opposed to using the word "wife." Why use the word "wife" in connection with a woman who was living with a man against the law, who was not his wife according to the law of Canada? Are such people to be regarded as man and wife? I was never more in earnest in my life about anything that has come up in this House than I am in regard to this. Are we to ignore the first principles of

right and law in this country? Is Bolshevism to be brought into this country? Is Parliament going to recognize what is a tenet of Bolshevism, that any man may pick up a woman and live with her and she with him? That is Bolshevism. Is Parliament going to recognize that principle to-day, and are we [DOT] to forsake the basic principle' of constitution and liberty and law in this country ? If so, what basis are we going to have, and how are we going to settle our standing? The Canadian people, those who are born and who live in Canada, who are brought up as Christian people and in Christian homes, must stand by those principles, not giving one whit in any way; and if we must deal with people who have forsaken those principles, let us deal with them individually and not on the principle that they are wives. I see the hon. member for St. Antoine (Sir Herbert Ames) laughing at my ideas of morality. I am not surprised at that at all. When it comes to a question of what can be done with money and the methods in which money can be used, I fail to accept the hon. member for St. Antoine as a guide in morals; I have heard too much of his doings. Those are the reasons why I am opposed to theword "wife being used and receiving the sanction of the House of Commons, the Senate and the King in this Parliament, to calling a woman a wife who is not a wife, who never was and cannot possibly be of the man to whom she was supposed to be a wife. Is there not some other word that can be used and some other way in which this woman can be helped without putting her in the class of the respectable women of this country? I am surprised that the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle), coming from that seat of learning and philosophy and education and religion, and Presbyterianism-I am of that famous body myself, and that is why I am fighting against the use of this term - should come and acknowledge that he has coined a phrase which is, going to go down the ages, to put a woman of this class in the same class as his wife and his mother. I do not think he should do it.

Do I understand that the words " wife by habit and repute " are to be employed throughout in all the sections?
Mr. ROWELL; Wherever "unmarried wife" appears, except section 41 where we struck it out and referred back, and except paragraph (c) of clause 20 where we struck it out entirely, as it was not necessary.

If the minister has
changed the wording in one place, why should he not continue that throughout? I was glad to hear the leader of the Opposition take common ground with what I believe to be the opinion of the whole House, namely, that he, as well as the Test of us want to see the women protected, and the whole difference as I see it now before the committee is the phraseology that is to be used in describing that woman. I think subsection 3 of section 33 can be amended so as not to refer to the woman at all in the highlv objectionable way in which she is referred to there. I would have that subsection read as follows:
A woman who although not married to a member of the forces, was living with him in Canada at the time he became a member or the forces and for a reasonable time previously thereto, and who at such time was publicly represented by him as his wife, shall be considered entitled to a pension.
It will be noticed I have struck out the words " for the purposes of this Act " and the words " to have been his unmarried wife." Then in section 34 I would strike out the words in lines 34 and 35-the lines are not correctly marked, but appear as lines 34 and 35-" unmarried wife who is entitled to a pension " and substitute therefor the words " other woman under section 33 entitled to a pension." We would then be simply legislating with respect to the woman whom the man had represented to be his wife, which is quite different from this Parliament going on record as recognizing her as a wife. I think the leader of the Opposition is entitled to the thanks of this House for standing out strongly against any legislative enactment that would give the status of wife-one of the most sacred words we have in the polity of our nation, and related closely to the motherhood of the nation-to a woman who is a concubine, who is living in adultery and prostituting the name of wife. We as a Parliament ought certainly not to give her the status of a wife. I am willing to give any woman who mothered the children of a soldier who fought for his country, any reasonable benefit that the country can afford to give to her and her illegitimate children, because they are entitled to it. I agree with the hon. gentlemen who have pleaded for them, but I also stand with the leader of the Opposition in no half-hearted way, and I am surprised that the hon. gentleman who is in charge of this Bill should not see the absolute necessity of divorcing any such language from the legislative enactments of this House. I believe he does see that

necessity. Otherwise, an " unmarried wife" would be exactly the sanfe as a legal wife so far as the effect on the minds of the people of this country is concerned. I do not believe that the phrase " wife by habit and repute " is very far removed from the phrase " unmarried wife." It is certainly not sufficiently removed to justify the use of the phrase when we can do without either. I hope the minister will see that the legislation is so changed that we shall not be in the position of putting upon the statute book phraseology that can only render this House ridiculous in the eyes of the country.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I have not the least objection to the suggestion made by my hon. friend (Mr. Morphy). As the hon. member knows, I discussed it before, and I intimated that I was quite satisfied with it, but subsequently it was suggested that we take the definition from the British Act, and I rather understood that that would be acceptable to the House. I am perfectly satisfied to accept my hon. friend's suggestion, but I would put it a little differently, although it will be the same in effect. What I would suggest is that we strike out the words commencing in line 43 of section 33, "shall, for the purposes of this Act, be considered to have been his unmarried wife and." The subsection will then read:
A woman who, although not married to the member of the forces, was living with him in Canada at the time he became a member of the forces and for a reasonable time previously thereto, and who at such time was publicly represented by him as his wife, may in the ease of his death and in the discretion of the committee be awarded a pension.
That is all right.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I therefore move that in lieu of the consequential amendment which I suggested of "wife by habit and repute," we substitute in the other sections the words "or woman awarded a pension under subsection 3 of section 33."

There is another way in which this could be accomplished, and I think it would be better drafting. That is by simply defining the widow in a definition clause. Simply say that widow means not only a woman who had been legally married to a member of the force, but as well, a woman who although not married to a member of the force had been living with him at the time he became a member of the force and for a reasonable time previously thereto and was publicly represented by him as his wife.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is open to the same objection as the other suggestions. The objection of the House, as I understand it, is to defining the status of a woman in that position by any recognized terms that indicate the position of one who has undergone the marriage ceremony according to the laws of the land. 'It would simplify it, I agree, but now that we have practically reached an agreement on the clause I think we had better pass it in that way.
I object to the use of the word "wife" at all in such cases. The relationship of wife can only be created in one way.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
"Unmarried wife" is
dropped out in every case, and we are substituting therefor "a woman awarded a pension under subsection 3 of section 33."

Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 34-pensions to parent or person replacing parent when dependent.

I regret I was unavoidably absent on the previous discussion of the Bill, through no will of my own, but through a somewhat tyrannical order of another court than this. I wish to support the plea that was made on Saturday on behalf of dependent mothers. I do not intend to make any lengthy speech. Even had I the eloquence of some other members of this House so that I could represent the case of the mothers as it should be represented, I merely wish to-night to give to the House as an easily grasped case a concrete one that arose not in my constituency but in a nearby one. The widow of a clergyman with two sons, one married and one unmarried, is entitled as the widow of that clergyman to the sum of $300 a year. The unmarried son before he enlisted was practically maintaining his mother. He went overseas and was killed.
Last autumn the married son died. This left the clergyman's widow with a daughter, incapable of earning anything. She received for some time a pension of $480 a year as the mother of a private who had wholly or in part sustained her. But under the regulation passed in December last, which is followed in this Act, the Pension Board, who I think had no option in the matter, deducted from the $480 the $300 which she had received as the widow of a clergyman, and paid her $180. Of course we are not legislating for particular cases and I merely quote that as one readily understood as a sample of many other cases along the same line. An amendment to this clause was sug-

gested on Saturday, and I can quite see the force of the objection raised; but I think we should so amend it as to avoid all objectionable features. I would therefore very strongly urge the favourable consideration of the Committee to this amendment. Section 34, subsection 4, provides that the pension to a widowed mother shall not be reduced on account of her earnings from personal employment. I move to add after the word " employment " in the seventh line, the following: "or so long as she is in a dependent condition." This would provide that the pension of the widowed mother would not be reduced so long as she was dependent. Under the interpretation clause, the widowed mother may receive from other sources income up to the amount of pension and yet be considered in a dependent condition. As I say, I do not want to take up the time of the Committee at this hour, but I should like to see this suggestion adopted.

The amendment proposed by my hon. friend (Mr. Cronyn) is in accordance with the amendment; which I asked my hon. friend from Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) to propose in my stead on Saturday. After having made provision for the unmentionable woman so that she may obtain a pension because her support is killed, we should at least extend the same consideration to the widowed mother of the boy who was killed at the front. We have now consecrated in this law the right of the woman who is outside the pale of society to obtain a pension, but we compel the poor widowed mother to prove her dependent condition and her case must be subject to review from time to time. The agents of the Board of Pension Commissioners may go, and in many cases have gone, into homes of widowed mothers, to inquire as to their incomes, and formerly as to their earnings. ' They ascertain from what sources their incomes are derived, and in fact put them through all the questions to which a lawyer would subject an ordinary witness. My hon. friend from Bonaventure (Mr. Charles Marcil) cited a case on Saturday last, and I know of a concrete case myself in the county of Rimouski. A widow had three sons, two of whom were killed at the front. The third son is still living. She applied for a pension and was given one of $10 a month which, at the request of some members of Parliament, was afterwards increased to $15. When she sought a further increase, she was told that she should derive a certain income from the salary earned by the third son.
who was then unmarried. Now although we recognize in this law the woman who is unmarried, the widowed mother, who in many cases is much older than the unmentionable woman, and who is less able to support herself, is placed at a disadvantage, , for you virtually prohibit her son from getting married, the reason being that he may -be free to support his mother. Such a condition is distinctly contrary to morality and public decency. It is not fair to ask a sole unmarried son to refrain from getting married in order to support his mother, when you allow a man to live with women with whom they are not married. If any woman in the country is entitled to consideration, it is the widowed mother, who should be considered before any of the prostitutes to whom we have given pensions.

I might mention a ease in my city of which I have personal knowledge, having known the family for thirteen years. The mother came to Canada about thirteen years ago bringing with her a son whom she was then supporting. In time the boy grew to maturity and was able to support her. Then he married and went, to the war, his mother and his family living under the same roof. He was killed and now, according to this Act, there will be only one pension which will be paid the widow and her child, although they and the mother live together. The mother is not taken into consideration. The argument will be raised that if you attempt to provide for such cases as this you will open the door to all sorts of applications and will not know where it will end. I think, however, this objection could be met by specifying that the pension will be payable only to a mother occupying the home of the son upon whom she was totally dependent before his enlistment.

I hope the Committee will very carefully consider the remarks of the hon. member for London (Mr. Cronyn). I know of a similar case to the one referred to by him, the difference being that the husband died while two sons were at the front. One son was married, and he returned safe and sound to his wife and the family he had left. The other son fell in the war. She is thus bereft of the support from this particular son, while she has no support from the married son. Because of the superannuation allowance in respect of her husband, who was a minister, she receives no consideration, and the allow-

ance given her is not sufficient for her to live on comfortably. In fact, it is not sufficient to keep her warmly clothed.* I think the Committee would be well advised to give these special cases careful consideration.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The point which has been raised by my hon. friend from London (Mr. Cronyn) was carefully considered, in the committee and settled in. this House in another form. The judgment at that time was that we would not be justified in enlarging it as proposed owing to the very large financial obligation which would be involved and. because it would have been a departure from the principle underlying the Pension Bill. I have just suggested to my hon. friend that he withdraw his amendment. I want to get the Bill through as soon as possible because I want to get it into the hands of the Senate so that it may have consideration there. In the meantime, I will taike the matter up with the Board of Pensions Commissioners with the view of seeing what will be the probable expenditure involved in making such a change. Then, if the amount does not appear to be a large one, and if the Government feels that it would be justified in making the expenditure, this amendment can be made in the Senate. At the present time I would not feel justified in departing from the position which the committee took.

Might I just add one word? I know that we are dealing with pensions on the line of justice only and that no action on the part of any outside body ought to influence this Parliament in arriving at a just conclusion. But we are feeling our way necessarily and this pension legislation we are passing to-day is not like the laws of the Medes and Persians, liable to remain unamended for the next twenty years. We may have to amend it in the light of experience. The Canadian Patriotic Fund has between $6,000,000 and $7,000,000 left in its hands. We are now authorized by Parliament to engage in -postwar relief. We are going to handle a great many of these post-war problems, now before the Pensions Board, in- the course of the next two or three years. The case mentioned by the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Wilson) is one which will draw from the Patriotic Fund $15 a mfinth. I do not mention that to Parliament with a view of in any way releasing the Government from its just obligation, but I do say that under any pension Act we may -pass there will be, just outside of its limits, a number of very

deserving cases, and the Patriotic Fund executive can utilize the re-
11 p.m. maining money that it has on hand to help out those families that are just outside the limits of the Act. We cannot do that permanently but we can do it as long as the money lasts.
How will you ascertain them?

Through the Pensions Board and also through our own office, but we will, with this money, for two or three years, take care of this problem of post-war relief that is just outside of the Pension Act. We can take care of these problems for that time, and Parliament can look after the future.

We will suppose the case of a woman whose husband was living and who had one son. The son went to the war and was killed. There is no pension coming to that woman because her husband " is still living. That is right, is it not? I assume that the husband is able to support her. There is no provision made for giving her a pension. She can get no pension be-cause_ her son was killed, for her husband is living and is able to maintain her. But a month, we will say, after the son is killed, the husband dies. Is any consideration given in a case of that kind? There is a case where the woman might properly say that if it had not been for the war she could reasonably look forward to her son maintaining her.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That case is provided for in the regulations as they stand.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Do I understand that the hon. member for London (Mr. Cronyn) withdraws the amendment that he proposed?
Would the minister sug-get that?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
What I suggested to my hon. friend was that he might withdraw the amendment on my statement that I will ask the Pension Board to- report at once- that means to-morrow, or at the earliest possible date-what charge this would impose upon the country. I will give my hon. friend the information and I will submit it to my colleagues with the view that if they think it is a case where they are justified in recommending to Parliament this additional expenditure, which the committee has not recommended, the Bill may be amended in the Senate. In the absence of that I shall have to ask the House to support the decision of the committee, because, the committee having reached that conclusion, I

do not think we would be justified in making an amendment without any idea of the financial charge involved. While I have not raised the point, and do not wish to raise it, I am not sure that the amendment is in order inasmuch as it involves an additional financial charge upon the country.
Amendment (Mr. Cronyn) withdrawn.

May I be permitted to draw the attention of the minister to section 23? This section refers to the pension allowed to children of the age of sixteen and seventeen years in the case of a boy and a girl respectively. Then' it goes on to say that if the child is unable owing to physical or mental infirmity to provide for its own1 maintenance, or where such child is following and is making satisfactory progress in a course of instruction approved by the commission, the pension may be continued until it has attained the age of twenty-one years.
I want to compare that with section 35 where the pension is given to a brother or sister, in which case there is no limitation to the age of twenty-one years. Why should there be a limit in the case of a child incapable of earning a living and no limit in the ca'se of a brother or sister?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That question was discussed by the Committee and the reason is this: Where it is a brother or sister, it is likely to be a person up in years and the charge will not be continued for a lengthened period. If an aged person is incompetent or imbecile or in such a condition as to he unable to earn a living the Committee thought it not desirable to impose the limitation that it did impose in the other case. That was pointed out in the Committee, and the Committee after considering it decided to impose the limitation in the former case.
It seems unfortunate that children absolutely unable to take care of themselves, after having reached the age of twenty-one years, should be thrown on the country without any consideration whatever.

Should there not be
some discretion left with the board?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The reason for it is that the legal obligation of a parent for maintenance ceases at that age. The legal obligation of the State which puts itself in the place of the parent for the purpose of this pension ceases at that date. It may be that the incompetent imbecile would then have to be put in some institution.
That would be the case regardless of whether the parent served in the army- or not.
Bill reported.

On motion of Hon. C. C. Ballantyne (Minister of Marine and Fisheries) the House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution, Mr. Boivin in the Chair:
Resolved, That it is expedient to bring in a measure,-
1.	To constitute and appoint a Board of Harbour Commissioners for the Port and Harbour of -Saint John in the province of New Brunswick.
2.	To empower the Corporation of the City of Saint John to transfer to His Majesty the property, privileges, title, interest and powers of the said City and the Mayor thereof, in, to and over the Harbour of Saint John and certain wharf and other -properties; such harbour privileges, powers and properties to be administered and controlled by the Harbour Commissioners.
3.	To provide that the consideration for the
transfer of the Harbour property and privileges to the Harbour Commissioners shall be two million dollars, payable as follows:	The sum
of one million, three hundred -and forty-two thousand, seven hundred and seventeen dollars and fifty-five cents, representing the present bonded indebtedness of the said city in connection with harbour development, shall be assumed and taken over by the Harbour Commissioners and that it shall pay the interest on the said bonds and the value of the same as they mature; and for the balance, that is to say, the
' sum of six hundred and fifty-seven thousand, two hundred and eighty-two dollars and forty-five cents, the Harbour Commissioners shall issue to the said city its debentures payable at the end of twenty-five y^rs from the day of issue and bearing interest at the rate of five per centum per annum, payable half-yearly, which debentures the Harbour Commissioners are to be authorized to issue, and the payment of which debentures and interest shall, if the Harbour Commissioners fail to pay the same, be paid -by His Majesty; and the assumption of the said bonded indebtedness by the Harbour Commissioners and the issue of the said1 debentures by the Harbour Commissioners of the said city shall be deemed to be payment in full for the harbour, harbour property, rights, rents and privileges to be conveyed as aforesaid.
4.	That the elevator, the property of His Majesty, and all wharves, the property of His Majesty in the right of His Government of Canada, within the limits of the Harbour of Saint John as defined in the proposed Act, shall be administered and controlled by the said Harbour Commissioners, upon the Harbour Commissioners paying in consideration -thereof to the Minister of Finance -of Canada the cost of construction thereof, and also paying to the said minister interest at the rate of three and one-half per centum per annum upon the said amount, or such portion thereof as remains unpaid, until the whole of the said sum is paid.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CREATE BOARD OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS.
speechtext: The object of this proposed legislation is to nationalize the port of St. John. Hon. members are aware that we have nationalized and have under commission at the present time the ports of Vancouver, Montreal and Quebec. The port of St. John is the second largest of our national seaports. The port of St. John holds a unique position, inasmuch as the facilities they enjoy there have been paid for almost exclusively by the city of St. John. The city authorities, the Board of Trade, and the citizens generally during the last year and a half have been representing to me as Minister of Marine that as the Dominion Government have advanced millions of dollars for the development of the ports of Montreal and Quebec, have spent millions on the port of Halifax and have recently voted $5,000,000 for the development of the port of Vancouver, it is only fair and reasonable that the citizens of St. John should be relieved of the burden which they are carrying and that the Dominion Government should advance the money for whatever further development is necessary at that point and thus treat St. John as they have treated the other ports that I have mentioned. The Bill to be based on the resolution provides for the taking over of the port of St. John and the creation of a Harbour Commission which will assume the bonded indebtedness of the port, amounting to $1,342,717.55, and issue Harbour Commission twenty-five year debentures, bearing interest at the rate of 5 per cent, for $657,282.45, making up the $2,000,000. A year ago I sent the Chief Engineer of the Marine Department and one of our auditors to St. John to report as to what would be a fair valuation for the facilities that that port enjoys, and also to look into the receipts and expenditures. In addition to that, about four months ago I asked the well known _ firm of auditors, P. S. Ross and Sons, Montreal, to make a valuation. The city of St. John also sent in a valuation; I will give-the committee the three amounts which were submitted. The city of St. John valued the port and its facilities at $2,506,966.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CREATE BOARD OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS.
speechtext: Who made that valuation for them?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CREATE BOARD OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS.
speechtext:
That is according to their own books and their own auditors. The valuation arrived at by the chief engineer of the Marine Department was $2,128,000, and by the firm of P. S. Ross and Sons, $2,297,620.32. It therefore appeared to the Government, after I had placed all the 
facts before them, that a fair valuation to offer the city of St. John would be $2,000,000. It will be quite unnecessary to put up any money, because as I stated a moment ago thb Harbour Coihmissioners of the port of St. John will assume the bonded inindebtedness of the port and will issue twenty-five-year debentures for the difference between the amount of the bonded indebtedness and the $2,000,000. The bonds which will be assumed by the Harbour Commissioners are long outstanding; they mature in 1923, 1938, 1942,	1944 and 1950.
The rate of interest is mostly 3i and 4 per cent, and there are a few outstanding bonds at 6 per cent.
I have also looked into the revenue of the port as it now exists. For 1918 the receipts amounted to $159,442, and the exexpenditure to $155,600. It will be noticed that there is a small surplus, about $4,000. I have also looked into what their estimated revenue will be, in as much as this Bill will turn, over to the harbour commissioners the wharves now owned by the Government, some of which were built by the Public Works Department and some by the Marine Department, and the grain elevator, which was built by the Department of Railways and Canals. Most of the expenditure the Government has gone to at the port of St. John, this Bill provides, the harbour commissioners will have to pay 3i per cent interest, and for some 3 per cent. So that the harbour commissioners will have the entire port under their control, which includes Courtenay bay. I think it will be in the national interest that this should be done, especially as St. John is our second largest port at the present time, a'nd as so much of our western grain goes out there. A still greater quantity will be exported from St. John this year, as none of our grain will be allowed to go by American ports unless the American authorities reinstate the coasting privileges which they cancelled. That, briefly, is the purport of the Bill that is based on the resolution now before the House.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CREATE BOARD OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS.
speechtext: The minister stated the receipts at $159,000 odd and the expenditure at $155,000. Did that include interest on the bonds?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CREATE BOARD OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS.
speechtext: Yes. I should have stated that the estimated revenue will be at least $225,000. That will enable them to defray all the expenses of the port, and to meet the interest, to pay 5 per cent interest on any future advances that may be made by the Government, and to establish a sinking fund.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CREATE BOARD OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS.
speechtext: I understood from the press of St. John some time ago, when a delegation was here from the city negotiating with the minister and also with the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Garvell) I think, that the amount agreed on was $2,200,000, and that the city authorities were very much dissatisfied to know that this was cut down by the minister to $2,000,000.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CREATE BOARD OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS.
speechtext: I have no knowledge of that, because I was ill at the time, and did not see either the mayor or the other representatives who came from St. John. No doubt they saw the Acting Minister of Marine, but I do not think he would make any definite offer to them. The first definite offer I made on behalf of the Government is the one I have just mentioned of $2,000,000, and this will have to be ratified by a referendum that the city of St. John will shortly take. No doubt they expected more than that amount, but in view of the reports that I have just referred to, the Government feels that $2,000,000 is reasonable and fair.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CREATE BOARD OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS.
speechtext:
Is that referendum by
provincial authority?

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CREATE BOARD OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS.
speechtext: Some years ago a statute was passed by the provincial legislature authorizing the city of St. John to sell their harbour after the matter had been submitted, first, to the city council, and, second, to a vote of the people. What is being done now will be the authority to purchase, providing the people of St. John themselves ratify that by referendum.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CREATE BOARD OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS.
speechtext: I am speaking subject to correction, of course, and I am only repeating what I saw in the newspapers, that the city commissioners and the citizens were complaining very bitterly, according to a very strong editorial in one of the papers, that the actual offer to the city when their representatives were here was $2,200,000, and they are very much put out to find it cut down to $2,000,000; indeed, they were arguing that it should not be accepted.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CREATE BOARD OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS.
speechtext: I think I am pretty familiar with all the negotiations. I have seen, I believe, every official of the city who has come to Ottawa, and I have met the commissioners and the officials in St. John on two or three occasions to discuss thisi, and I have no hesitation in saying that no such offer was ever made to the city. It is true they wanted it.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CREATE BOARD OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS.
speechtext:
It is in the papers.
273	1

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CREATE BOARD OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS.
speechtext: I am not responsible for what appears in the newspapers.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CREATE BOARD OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS.
speechtext: You saw that editorial?

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CREATE BOARD OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS.
speechtext: Oh, yes, I have seen many things in the newspapers. But I want to say no offer was made except the $2,000,000 offer.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CREATE BOARD OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS.
speechtext: I was present at that conference when the mayor and Commissioner Bullock came here with the idea of asking this Government for $2,500,000. The conference was held with Mr. Carvell and the representatives of St. John, and before they left the room that night they asked Mr. Carvell if he thought $2,500,000 was too large a sum, and he said he thought it was. Then they asked him what he thought of $2,200,000. Mr. Carvell stated that he would do the best he could for them. There was no direct offer of $2,200,000.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CREATE BOARD OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS.
speechtext: Do I understand the hon. gentleman from St. John is satisfied that $2,000,000 is enough for the harbour?

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CREATE BOARD OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS.
speechtext: As representing the city of St. John, I would like to see the city get considerably more than $2,000,000.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CREATE BOARD OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS.
speechtext: That is not the question.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CREATE BOARD OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS.
speechtext:
If the Government are determined not to give the city any more than $2,000,000 I am prepared to accept it on behalf of the city. In the reports as given by the hon. minister (Mr. Ballan-tyne) are not included certain articles that the city of St. John consider they are entitled to receive a valuation on. In making out their estimate of $2,500,000, they made it up on the basis of the valuation at which the city carry the property, namely, $2,008,000; on top of that is an amount of $75,000 that the city carry on their books for Partridge Island; besides that they took the revenue derived from the fisheries and the collections for the last four years and capitalized them at 5 per cent, which amounted to $120,000; they also took in the C.P.E. wharf-the Canadian Pacific Eail-way corporation owned a wharf commonly known as the C.P.E. wharf, in exchange for which the city gave the Canadian Pacific a 40-foot strip-at a valuation on their books of $200,000. That is the way in which the amount was made up. Eeally they have carried on their books a valuation of the harbour property at $2,900,000, but the amount they stated to the Government as $2,500,000. At the conference held between Mr. Elkin of the Board of Trade and myself last week, the Board of Trade passed a unanimous vote to accept this $2,000,000 for



the harbour. I know there is some question in the minds of the citizens about accepting it, but, as the representative of the city, if the Government do not feel disposed to pay any more than $2,000,000, I am prepared to accept this amount. I know that this has been a political football for both parties for a great number of years. Delegation after delegation came knocking at the doors of Parliament previous to 1896, asking that the subsidy that was given to the Elder-Dempster line running to Portland Maine, should be withdrawn.
The Hon. Mr. Foster at that time said: Prerpare your city; prepare the harbour; build your wharves and elevators; the subsidy that was going to Portland, Maine, is going to go to St. John and Halifax. The citizens of St. John, having faith in their city and realizing that it had a great future, were prepared to go down into their pockets to the tune of $2,000,000, and they have done that. But realizing the future of the port and the extension that will take place in the coming years, they feel it to be utterly impossible for them to carry on and to prepare the necessary developments that should take place, and, therefore, they are prepared to hand this harbour over to the Government to handle in the same way that the harbour of Montreal is handled.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CREATE BOARD OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CREATE BOARD OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS.
speechtext:
In answer to the hon. member (Mr. Copp) and in all fairness to the hon. member for St. John city (Mr. Wigmore), I may say that the latter was most anxious, indeed, just as anxious as my hon. friend that the city of St. John should get more than $2,000,000, and he has done his fair share to bring pressure upon the Government that we should increase the amount and endeavour to meet the views of that city. But I received a report from our chief engineer, Col. Anderson, who went down to St. John a year ago and went over every one of the sheds and piers; and in view of the considerable amount of money that would have to be spent on those wooden sheds and on the piers to put them into a proper state of repair, and after a consultation with my colleague, the Minister of Public Works, I felt that the Government was treating the city of St. John on very broad, and, I might almost say, generous lines in giving that city $2,000,000. If the piers and sheds were in a good state of preservation at the present time, and if the Harbour Commission would not have to spend money on them, as I am sure they will have to do, there might be some reason for the Government to offer the city more than $2,000,000. But in view of the money that will have to be spent on the wharves and sheds, the Government are certainly meeting the citizens of St. John fairly in offering them $2,000,-
000.	I want, however, to make it abundantly clear that the hon. members for St. John City ('Mr. Wigmore and Mr. Elkin) have done everything they can to get the Government to offer them more than $2,000,000, so that the citizens of St. John have no reproach to make against their representatives for not putting up as good a fight as they possibly could.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CREATE BOARD OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS.
speechtext: Inasmuch as the Government is taking over the harbour of St. John, I would suggest that the site of the old Fort Latour, the old Huguenot Fort, should be restored and turned into a public park. It would be a good memento of a very historic incident. The location is well known to the people of St. John, and it would be one of the historic landmarks of Canada.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CREATE BOARD OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS.
speechtext:
This is not a proposal to transfer the property to the commissioners; it is a proposal to transfer the property to His Majesty. We are purchasing the harbour of St. John by this transaction,

as I understand it, and I want to know whether we are getting a good bargain or not. Where do the people of Canada come in in this transaction? The hon. member for St. John City (Mr. Wigmore) says that the citizens of St. John dug down into their pockets and spent their own money. That was very creditable. I always thought they would do very well in St. John, but I am sorry they did not stick to their investment. They are now losing faith in it, and they want to turn it over to somebody else. Why do they not keep it and build it up and make it a good harbour as other cities throughout the world are doing? The whole , matter of transferring these harbours to His Majesty is a mistake. The harbours ought to be handled by the local people. It is all right for the Government to help, to guarantee the bonds. This is not the same transaction as we have in the city of Montreal, as I understand it. The Harbour Commissioners of Montreal own the harbour, not His Majesty.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CREATE BOARD OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS.
speechtext: The city of Montreal does not own a foot of land or anything in connection with the port of Montreal, at all.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CREATE BOARD OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS.
speechtext: Does not the commission own it?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CREATE BOARD OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS.
speechtext: No, the King. The commission have merely been appointed by an Order in Council to administer the affairs of the harbour during the pleasure of the Government. The port of Vancouver is also vested in the Crown, and so is the port of Quebec. As $28,000,000 has been spent by the Parliament of Canada in developing the port of Montreal, $11,000,000 on the port of Quebec, as we have a resolution for the expenditure of $5,000,000 on the port of Vancouver, and as millions of dollars have been spent by the Department of Railways and Canals in developing the port of Halifax, on which moneys the country will not even receive interest, it is a reasonable request for the city of St. John to make that it be treated in the same way as these other ports; and we shall get interest on all the money that is lent to that city.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CREATE BOARD OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS.
speechtext:
It is all very true that we have spent a great deal of money on Halifax and the other ports, but the port of Montreal has been able to finance its own affairs with the assistance of the Government, and it has been able to pay the interest. We are putting in this Bill language which implies that the port of St. John is not going to pay the interest; at all events, we are saying in this Bill that if
the harbour commissioners fail to pay the principal and the interest of this loan, His Majesty will pay it. The inference to be drawn from that is that the harbour commissioners are not going to trouble themselves very much about the matter, because His Majesty stands behind them and he will pay the bill. I do not think you will find language like that in the other charters. And why should that language be put in this resolution? It strikes me that it should not be there. The responsibility should be thrown on the commission to finance the development of this harbour, to pay the interest and to provide for the debentures when they fall due. If it is necessary for the commissioners to get the endorsement of the Government, let them do so, but why do we put language like that in the resolution?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CREATE BOARD OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS.
speechtext: It is just the same as in the others.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CREATE BOARD OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS.
speechtext:
If the harbour commissioners do not pay the bill, the country will pay it? That is not necessary, surely. I was glad to hear that the finances of the harbour are in good shape, and that the estimated revenue the minister makes is, if I understand him rightly, much larger than the proceeds of last year.
I was wondering how that could be, because last year, owing to the war, there must have'been more trade than in normal times. I have no doubt, however, the minister has reasons for the estimate he has made, and I am glad to hear the chances are that the harbour will pay its way. We all hope it will.
My idea of dealing with these matters is to leave them as much as possible under local control, but the custom seems to be growing of everybody coming to Ottawa for harbour improvements instead of looking after them at home themselves. The people of Halifax have come here and got $17,000,000 of the people's money, and they want $7,000,000 or $8,000,000 more to finish up the harbour. A good many people think that the money is being badly spent, that it is not improving the harbour at Halifax, that the money is not being spent in the right place, simply because it was not the people's own money under local control and they did not take sufficient interest in the work. As a result of it being managed from Ottawa we have a harbour built in an exposed place at George's Island where some ships last winter could not land their cargoes. They had to come into Halifax because they found it impossible to land

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CREATE BOARD OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS.
speechtext:
1 am afraid my hon. friend has not delved into this matter as deeply as he might have done, or he would have come to a different opinion from the one he has expressed to-night. In the first place the harbour of St. John is different from any other harbour in Canada, and probably in the world, in respect of its ownership. About 1895 the people of St. John started in to build up the harbour themselv.es. They have continued on down to the present time, and have expended something between $2,100,000 and $2,200,000 of actual money, practically in the construction of wharves. These wharves have been operated and maintained by the city, and the city has received the revenue from them. As the minister (Mr. Ballantyne) has stated, during the last three or four years the revenue has been sufficient to pay the cost of operation, the interest on the debentures, to provide a reasonable amount for betterments and improvements, and leave a small balance. Some years ago it was very patent that the city would not be able to go on themselves and develop the harbour as it should be developed, because next to Montreal it is the greatest seaport from a business standpoint in the Dominion. My hon. friend talks about Halifax. Why, Halifax even in wartime did not handle one-fifth of the value of the goods handled at the port of St. John. 1 think three or four wharves have been built in recent years by the Federal Government under the Department of Public Works, and as soon as they were built they were handed over for operation to the Department of Marine and Fisheries, as all these big wharves are. The revenue from the Government wharves have gone to the Government and the revenues from the city wharves have gone to the city, and that is why the
I Mr. Sinclair.]
minister states that when these are consolidated the revenue will be considerably over $200,000. Under this agreement the harbour will be managed by local people, just as my hon. friend desires. That is one of the reasons why I, as Minister oi Public Works, have been in favour of hand ing the harbour over to the commissioners. A man has only to occupy this position foi two or three years to realize how hopelessly at sea he is as to the requirements of any port in Canada. I thought I knew St. John pretty well; I think I do. I came here with certain ideas about improvements and * developments. My predecessor had certain ideas, and so had his predecessor, and so my successor will have. These things are worked out by men who have no real technical knowledge of the subject, and my opinion is that all these works should be placed under a commission of local men, because they are the ones who have knowledge of the subject; far better results will be obtained when they are all, consolidated under one body working along a certain well defined plan, and one body receiving the whole of the revenues. The way it has been handled for the last two or three years has been a real detriment to the trade and navigation of the country. In the first place, all of the wharves in the harbour are under the control of the harbour master, and it is natural that he should want to put every ship in the Government docks that he possibly can in order to get the revenue. It is a well-known fact that ships have been held up sometimes for twenty-four hours in the stream waiting a chance to go into a city dock instead of a Government dock. So it is really against the proper administration of the port the way it has been run in the past.
Just one other point. My hon. friend is under a misapprehension. We are not making any grants to the city at all. The city owns a certain property, which they are selling to the Government. There are bonds to the amount of about $1,350,000 outstanding, which the harbour commissioners will pay. In addition to that, there is $650,000 which the people have put up by means of taxation, and the idea is to repay them. Just figure it out and see where you are. They are handing over to the Government $650,000 of property, and in my judgment it is worth a good deal more than that over and above the debentures. They naturally want some guarantee that that money will be paid, and so far as this $650,000 is concerned, it is being provided that if the harbour commissioners do not

pay the interest and the principal the Government of Canada will be responsible, because the Government of Canada, is getting the property of the city of St. John. The harbour commissioners have no assets; their assets would be of no value unless guaranteed by the Government.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CREATE BOARD OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS.
speechtext: From whom did these proposals first come?

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CREATE BOARD OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS.
speechtext: From myself, probably. I was one of the first that I know of to work it out.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CREATE BOARD OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS.
speechtext:
Did the city oi
St. John come here to sell their property or did the Government go there to try and buy it?

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CREATE BOARD OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS.
speechtext:
I could hardly say. I
have talked the matter over so many times that I really would not like to say where it originated, but I think I had as much to do with it as anybody else. I had not been in this office very long before I realized what a hopeless mess the affairs of that port were in. It has been a political question in the city of St. John for a great many years. This plan is nothing new; I did not conceive the idea; I only realized the situation. I believe the city are anxious to dispose of their property if they can get a reasonable price for it. I do not think it would be reasonable to ask the city to hand over their property to the Dominion Government and get no security, because the bonds of the harbour commissioners, unless guaranteed by the Government, would probably be a very poor security.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CREATE BOARD OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS.
speechtext: The matter has been discussed in the House a good many times.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CREATE BOARD OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS.
speechtext:
Oh yes, and that is why I say I cannot answer categorically my hon. friend's question as to who first brought the matter up. It has been proposed a good many times in this House that the harbour should be nationalized, that is, put in the same position as Halifax is in. I would like to have that. I am sorry to see the port of St. John burdened with harbour dues, but that is only business. I have never asked the Government to do anything yet that is not business and that does not appeal to me as a business proposition, and I do not know why, because the Government might have made one great mistake in Halifax, we should be compelled to repeat it in St. John. As a minister coming from that province, and vitally interested in its welfare, I think it is a good fair business proposition, that the harbour itself should be
charged and the shipping pay its share of the expenses. No other city in Canada has-ever come under this condition because no other city ever owned a harbour and sold it to the Government. The city of Montreal never put a dollar into the harbour, or anything they put in would be a mere bagatelle. The city of Quebec never put a dollar into the harbour. This is in a class by itself. When my hon. friend understands the conditions he will realize that after all we have tried to make it a fairly good business proposition.	.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CREATE BOARD OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS.
speechtext: In answer to the hon. member for Antigonish and Guys-borough (Mr. J. H. Sinclair) I may say that this Bill is almost identical with the Bill that was introduced when the Harbour Commissioner for the port of Montreal was created, and also for Quebec and the port oi Vancouver. The Harbour Commissioners of Montreal issued debentures and the Government have to stand behind them. We are doing no more for the port of St. John than for those other ports. There was another point in connection with which the hon. member wanted an explanation, and that is, how I estimate the revenue to be $225,000 when for the year 1918 it was only $159,442. Well, there are various sources from which the harbour commissioners can raise revenue without injury to shipping. I find that the wharfage dues collected on the wharves owned by the Government amount to $59,331.37. That will be additional revenue for the harbour commissioners, and they will also get revenue from the fisheries..

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CREATE BOARD OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS.
speechtext: We are giving them that in addition to the grant?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CREATE BOARD OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS.
speechtext:
Yes, but these harbour commissioners for St. John have to pay three and a half per cent to the Government on the cost of construction of all wharves and the grain elevator there. They have revenue from the fisheries, and I am perfectly satisfied that they will be able to pay all operating expenses of the harbour, meet interest on bonds, pay five per cent on any moneys that may be voted in the future to the port; and while I won't make a definite promise I am reasonably sure that when the bonds come due they will have sufficient revenue to redeem them. I want to make it perfectly clear that this Bill is not different from the Bills in connection with Quebec, Montreal, and Vancouver. All the properties for these ports are vested in the King, and the harbour commissioners are simply trustees.

speechtext:
What strikes me there will be improvements at Government
as curious is the statement that if the harbour commissioners fail to pay interest on the bonds, His Majesty will pay it. Does my hon. friend say that that clause is in the charter of the harbour of Montreal?

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CREATE BOARD OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS.
speechtext:
I will not say that that exact phraseology was in it. But when these debentures of the port of Montreal come due-and I know that from experience while I was commissioner there- the Government take them up. I am responsible for having put that into the Bill because I knew that if we did not include that the city of St. John would naturally ask:	Who are the harbour commissioners
for the port of St. John if they cannot meet interest on outstanding bonds, and cannot meet debentures when tljey become due? The city of St. John would be in a rather unfortunate position, and therefore I had to put in the Bill the provision that if the harbour commissioners of St. John fail to meet these debentures when they come due, His Majesty will. When the debentures for the other ports come due, if the harbour commissioners are not able to meet them, in Montreal, Quebec, or Vancouver, the Government will also have to make them good.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CREATE BOARD OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS.
speechtext:
The enterprising people of the city of St. John have been willing to spend some money during the last fifty *years, perhaps longer, in creating a harbour to bring trade and traffic to the city. They were getting the benefit from year to year of that investment. They got good returns by the trade and traffic and the Canadian Pacific railway going to that port, having made certain development in order to fit that place as a terminus, I rather think those early investments are falling into decay. They have done their work and the enterprising live city of St. John has, in my judgment, received ample compensation and returns for those investments. They find that the burden is too big and they are asking us to send an engineer down to estimate the cost of those works.
iMr. CARVELL: No, the value. The report of Mr. Anderson is as to the present value of those works.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CREATE BOARD OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS.
speechtext: I don't know how a man can value an old wharf. He cannot put it up at auction.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CREATE BOARD OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS.
speechtext: These wharves have been kept in repair and good condition.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CREATE BOARD OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS.
speechtext:
Yes, but St. John will have identically the same benefit from these wharves and improvements after purchase as before. In fact, it will be better, because

expense. I am glad that the harbour of St. John yrill have better facilities, but I don't see why this country should return to St. John the moneys they expended on improvements which are necessary to carry trade and traffic to that harbour. I am willing that we should take it over, put it in good shape, and assume the debt in connection with it, and carry it along under a commission, but I cannot understand why we should go down into the depleted treasury and pay $2,000,000 to St. John or any other city for works which are still to be their property. There will be a change in name, but the utility will still be to the advantage of St. John. I do not see why merely because it will nominally pass to the King, we should pay cash for say the value of what remains of improvements that have been of a vast advantage to that city. I think the city of St. John should be perfectly satisfied if we took this business off their hands, which is bothersome to them, put it into good shape, and carry it along, and let them enjoy the use of it, without getting the money back.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CREATE BOARD OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS.
speechtext: The grain elevators and Wharves are being turned over to the harbour commissioners. Will the Government still retain control over the harbour commissioners as regards the regulation of rates?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CREATE BOARD OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS.
speechtext:
The Government certainly will. The same authority will prevail in the port of St. John as exists at present in other ports under commission. The rates on grain, the wharfage rates and everything else are subject to the approval of the Governor in Council.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in.
Hon. Mr. Ballantyne moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 169, relating to the harbour of St. John, in the province of New Brunswick.
Motion agreed to and Bill read the first and second time. The House went into Committee on the Bill, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
Progress reported.
On the motion of Hon. F. B. Carvell, Minister of Public Works, the House went into Committee on the following proposed resolution, Mr. Boivin in the Chair:

Resolved, That It Is expedient to provide that the Dry Docks Subsidies Act, 1910', be amended by increasing the subsidy on second-class dry docks to four and one-half per cent of the cost of the work, payable half-yearly during a period not exceeding thirty-five years after the work has been completed, but half yearly payments on account of the subsidy at the rate of four and one-half per cent on seventy-five per cent of the oost of the work done and materials provided at the time of such payment may be made during the construction of the dock, no such payment to be made until the work done and materials provided shall have cost the sum of five hundred thousand dollars, and no such payments on account to be made unless the Chief Engineer reports that the work is being proceeded with to his satisfaction.

The explanation of this is very short and simple. In 1910 the Dry Dock Subsidies Act was passed, which provided for three different kinds of docks. There was a first class dock which must oost a certain amount of money, $4,000,000 or $4,500,000. Upon that the Government was to pay a subsidy of three and a half per cent for thirty-five years. A second class dock was to cost $2,500,000 at least, and upon that the Government would pay a subsidy of 3i per cent for twenty-five years. Subsequently the law regarding first class docks was amended providing for the payment of a subsidy of 4i per cent for thirty-five years. Only one dry dock has been constructed under that provision and that is the dry dock at St. John. It does seem to me that some change must be made if we are going to get dry docks built in other places where they are required in the way of giving greater facilities. A number of applications Iiave been made during the last two or three years for the construction of second class dry docks. A second class dry dock would be one big enough to accommodate every ship that sails the seas except very large war ships and ships like the Aquitania and some of those monsters. The provision in regard to a second class dock also includes a floating dry dock. The place I have in mind in connection with this resolution is Sydney. There is a demand for a dry dock in Sydney and I am convinced that if we can change the law in accordance with this proposed resolution it will facilitate the construction of a dry dock at Sydney. Therefore, the proposal is that the Act be amended so as to provide for a subsidy of four and1 a half per cent for thirty-five years on a second class dry dock just the same as it is now on a first class dock. It also provides that no subsidy shall be paid at least until $500,000 has been expended on the work. The owners of a first class dock must put
up $1,000,000. The reason for this is obvious. The (xovernment would not be justified in guaranteeing interest on the bonds until the promoters had put up some of their own money because they might take the bonds, sell them, and not go on with the work. In the case of a $2,000,000 dock, if $500,000 were put up by the promoters, the Government would feel safe in guaranteeing the bonds. These are practically the only changes that are proposed by this resolution.
Will it be retroactive?

No. There is a special clause which reads as follows:
The provisions of section 2 of this Act shall not apply or extend to any agreement heretofore made for the construction of any dry dock.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in.
Hon. Mr. Carvell moved for leave to introduce Bill 170, to amend the Dry Docks Subsidies Act, 1910.

Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first and second time, considered in committee and reported.
